text:
Democrat Callie Barr is trying a second time to unseat incumbent US Rep. Jack Bergman, R-Watersmeet in Michigan’s 1st Congressional District.

In 2024, Barr earned 38% of the vote to Bergman’s 59% in a four-way race.

This time, Barr’s part of a seven-way race for the seat representing the northern Lower Peninsula and all of the Upper Peninsula in Congress. In addition to Barr, Bergman also faces Libertarian Arnett Satterla, independent candidate Zebulon Featherly, Green Party candidate LaVeta Davenport, US Taxpayers Party candidate Doc Kovaly and Working Class Party candidate Liz Hakola.

Barr spoke with WCMU about her goals for the district.

David Nicholas: Callie Barr, thank you very much for joining us.

Callie Barr: Thank you so much for having me.

DN: First question is, how would you define yourself politically?

CB: You know, I'm a patriot. I believe in representing the people of upper and northern Michigan to deliver what we need here. I often say this isn't a seat for Republicans or Democrats, it's a seat for the people of upper and northern Michigan, and being a fifth-generation Michigander from Cheboygan, Michigan, I'm deeply, deeply rooted here.

And so right now, to me, it's about returning this seat to the people who live and work here and just want a shot to be able to afford life.

DN: And what specific ideas or plans do you have to address affordability?

CB: Yeah, well, right now I'm running against an incumbent, Jack Bergman, who's done nothing but increase our costs while actually costing the taxpayer. I mean, he's the number-one spender, number-one out of 435 members of Congress, the number-one spending on lodging. I mean, even during COVID, when members were getting reimbursed like $600, he was reimbursed over $61,000. And along with that, he's done things like vote to cut Medicaid.

I would not do that, right? Medicaid funds our rural hospitals. He didn't extend the (Affordable Care Act) subsidies. I would not have done that, right? Because that is something that has increased our insurance premiums across this district.

He supports the war in Iran. That has increased the cost of gas and diesel, which has increased the cost of our food and our groceries and the things that we buy at the store.

He supports the tariffs, which has increased our costs for our small businesses and also for us, the consumer, and damaged our relationship with Canada.

So, when we think about decreasing costs, what we need to do is get someone out of Congress right now who is at every point increasing our cost of living here, while also at the same time using our taxpayer dollars to live a pretty lavish lifestyle.

And so, enough's enough. And so, I support policies that will decrease our costs, which means tackling insurance, making sure we can negotiate every drug price, making sure our rural hospitals are fully funded, not supporting a war right now that is driving up the cost of gas and everything else.

DN: And what is your position on US foreign policy specifically in Iran?

CB: So, no one's crying that we fight terrorism, right? And I want to be clear about that. The problem is, though, is when you go into a country and you have no plan, and when you are, like I said, increasing, the cost for us, right?

We're spending billions of dollars there. We don't have a plan. It's increasing our gas prices.

The other thing is, we're not at full military readiness. You know, I come from a military family. My husband is a Marine for 15 years. He served in Iraq and Afghanistan. And what concerns me is that we fired inspector generals. We fired JAG officers. We fired military leaders and commanders who had decades of knowledge and experience in the Middle East because they weren't yes men and yes women.

And so, that is also very concerning that we don't have a military that's at its full capacity and full military readiness to do the job that they're over there being asked to do. And frankly, I don't even know that they know what the plan is because there isn't a plan.

And so all of that, we need leaders in Congress right now, leaders in Congress that are going to have to take a look at this and figure out how we work to negotiate so that we're not in an endless conflict in the Middle East again, like my family was a part of for 20 years.

DN: What is your position then on tariffs and trade wars, specifically with Canada?

CB: I mean, this is ridiculous. Canada is a friend of ours and has been. We have been so damaged, not just with our friendships, but economically as well.

When we look at our Canadian friends coming across and sue Canada, they're not coming anymore.

We've seen just significant declines and it has resulted in the loss of millions and millions of dollars of economic benefit to us. These tariffs have not … these were not thoughtful. They’re chaotic. They've damaged our relationship with Canada. They've damaged our own economy. They were thoughtless and stupid. And we should not be supporting something that not only hurts one of our closest relationships, but also just hurts us too.

DN: And what is your position specifically on the construction of data centers in Michigan?

CB: We are the Great Lakes State and we have to do everything we can to protect our water. And we need regulation to protect our water.

We also need to make sure that there is strong local control that means something, that local communities can make decisions and have voice to actually realize that.

And that also means that we need absolute transparency. We need to know what risks are. We need to know what the impact on the environment is. And the other thing is that our local communities in no way are paying for any kind of energy infrastructure upgrades or costs associated with data centers.

DN: And finally, how would you address the ongoing debate over the Line 5 pipeline running under the Straits of Mackinac?

CB: Yeah, as a congressional representative, I think about, what are the things that you can actually do as a congressional representative? Because, of course, a representative is not going to, cannot by law, overturn a federal permit, a state permit, a state court decision, which is where that line is right now.

But what you can do is help to advance towards a clean energy future.

We had tax incentives and subsidies to do exactly that, to help us have the jobs of the future when it comes to working towards a cleaner energy future.

And this was supported by environmentalists. It was supported by our businesses. It was supported by labor because it was a way to have jobs and training and to start thinking about how we can diversify our energy sources, because we want to have reliable and affordable energy.

And of course, we want to continue to move towards energy sources that help protect this wonderful environment that we live in and that we are stewards over of.

And so, to me, that's really important, that we revitalize that effort, which this administration has pulled us back years in that kind of progress.

text:
The University of Nottingham will lead three projects as part of a new £20 million programme funded by UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) and led by the East Midlands Combined County Authority (EMCCA), to position the East Midlands as the leading place to develop and manufacture the next generation of clean power and propulsion technologies.

The programme, Advanced Manufacturing for Clean Energy (AMCE-LIPF), is funded through the Local Innovation Partnerships Fund, a £500 million UK government initiative delivered by UKRI to strengthen regional innovation economies.

The University of Nottingham is leading three of AMCE’s four projects, alongside the University of Derby’s INFINITY project, and will work closely with EMCCA, which is coordinating delivery to ensure integrated delivery across the programmes. Also involved are industry partners, Loughborough University and Nottingham Trent University.

The projects are designed to help the region seize time-critical opportunities in clean energy and decarbonising propulsion, as aircraft makers choose technologies for the next generation of single-aisle aircraft and large manufacturers look for digital, low-carbon supply chains.

The £20 million programme is an umbrella for a range of related projects to be delivered by experts in the Faculty of Engineering to offer businesses a pathway from idea to factory floor, with companies joining at whichever stage suits them.

The University is leading on three of these projects worth £13.6 million:

The Advanced Manufacturing and Clean Energy (AMaCE) Accelerator, which supports the commercialisation and development stage of the research-to-market pathway, helps entrepreneurs, start-ups and spinouts turn innovative ideas into investable products.

The Next Generation Single-Aisle (NGSA) Hybrid-Electric Propulsion Challenge responds to industry-led challenges, demonstrating and testing propulsion technologies against the needs of major aircraft manufacturers.

The Connected Factories Programme helps regional suppliers adopt digital, automated and low-carbon technologies so they are ready to manufacture new products at scale, including but not limited to those emerging from the other projects. This project has also been allocated £3.2m from the East Midlands Investment Zone initiative.

Across the whole portfolio, the programme is expected to add £325–340 million in gross value to the regional economy over its lifespan and will support up to 1,775 jobs. It will be matched by at least £36 million of private sector investment.

This LIPF funding complements the East Midlands Investment Zone’s Innovation Accelerator, whose second year was announced by the Mayor in September. The Accelerator funds university–business projects at an earlier stage of prototyping and demonstration, giving companies a further entry point into the region’s clean-tech support.

The programme will build on the East Midlands’ established cluster in advanced manufacturing for clean energy, which serves highly regulated markets such as civil nuclear, aerospace and defence.

Manufacturing accounts for 11% of the East Midlands workforce, and average manufacturing wages in the region are 21% higher than in the rest of the regional economy (Make UK). The wider Midlands is the UK’s largest aerospace cluster, with 30% of UK aerospace businesses and more than 56,000 jobs. The government’s Fusion Energy Strategy also identifies the East Midlands, around West Burton and the Trent Valley, as the UK’s second fusion cluster.

Professor Sir Ian Chapman, UKRI Chief Executive, said: “These projects in the East Midlands are all excellent examples of what can be achieved when world-leading researchers, innovative businesses and regional partners come together around a shared ambition.

"Building on local strengths and previous UKRI investment, they will create high-quality jobs, attract investment and deliver tangible benefits for people and communities across the region.

"Through the Local Innovation Partnerships Fund, UKRI is supporting partnerships across the UK to build on their distinctive strengths, translating innovation into impact that advances knowledge, improves lives and drives growth.”

The programme is also a practical example of the East Midlands University Compact, signed earlier this year by EMCCA and the University of Nottingham, Nottingham Trent University and the University of Derby. Through the compact, the partners have committed to work together on skills, research, business growth and innovation, and inclusive growth across the region.

Delivery is expected to begin later this year, and interested businesses can contact the University here: https://www.nottingham.ac.uk/workingwithbusiness/contact-us/contact.aspx

Dive Brief:

Lego has started using e-methanol or electro-methanol, a low-carbon fuel produced with renewable energy and recycled carbon dioxide, to produce over 90 products in a bid to cut its reliance on conventional fossil fuels.

The toymaker, known for its children’s plastic bricks, said in a Sept. 30 release that the e-methanol is being used to make a range of different products like steering wheels, connectors, cross axles and Minifigure hands. Lego hasmade over 4 billion Minifigures since 1978, according to a 2020 estimate, with the current production figure expected to be significantly higher.

Lego said the increased use of the renewable material was due to a2023 partnership it inked with Danish renewable energy producer European Energy and healthcare company Novo Nordisk, with the aim of substituting fossil fuel-based plastic with lower-carbon alternatives for some products.

Lego said the partnership supports the production of e-methanol on an industrial scale, allowing the retailer to use the renewable alternative to produce certain plastic components or “elements.”

E-methanol not only offers reduced lifestyle greenhouse gas emissions, compared to conventional methanol or petroleum fuels, but also helps create a circular carbon economy by utilizing captured carbon dioxide into a renewable fuel and chemical feedstock. The low-carbon alternative offersa “viable path” for cutting emissions in hard-to-abate sectors like shipping and chemical manufacturing, according to the World Economic Forum.

Lego said it introduced e-methanol into the production process of plastic after spending five years testing, learning and scaling the sustainable liquid fuel.

“This marks the latest step on our journey to increase the recycled and renewable materials we purchase to make Lego products, without compromising on safety, quality or durability,” the toymaker said in the release.

TheDanish retailer has set several sustainability targets in recent years, including a goal to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 and reduce its absolute carbon emissions by 37% by 2032, compared to a 2019 baseline — a goal it previously told ESG Diveit was on track to meet.

text:
The climate crisis is making extreme heat events hotter and longer, and California has prepared its power grid to keep up when extreme heat drives up electricity use. These results show how Governor Newsom’s investments in clean energy and reliability are helping the world’s fourth-largest economy meet those challenges.

California is powering the economy of the future

Since Governor Newsom took office in 2019, California has added more than 39,000 megawatts of utility-scale clean energy to serve the California grid. That’s helped make the grid more reliable and pushed the state further along its path in the clean energy transition.

The most recent numbers, from the end of 2024, show real progress: 67% of retail electricity sales in the state already come from clean energy. Last year, clean energy met 100% of the state’s electricity needs for at least part of the day on 279 separate days.

Solar and battery storage have been a key part of that progress, and are changing how California keeps the lights on. Since 2019, battery resources serving California grew from fewer than 700 megawatts to more than 23,000 megawatts — an increase of more than 3,100%. Batteries store solar power when it is abundant and deliver it after sunset. That reduces how often the state needs to run natural gas plants, which cuts air pollution and supports a more cost-effective electricity system.

California’s approach is also where the money is heading. Global investors are now putting roughly two dollars into clean-energy technology for every dollar that goes into fossil fuels. California is leading that shift while Donald Trump watches from the sidelines.

For California, that means investing in the good-paying jobs of the future. The Golden State is the 4th-largest economy in the world and leads the nation in total clean energy jobs, with 552,300 workers employed across clean energy technologies, nearly twice as many as the second-ranked state, Texas, according to a 2025 report from E2. California’s clean energy workforce grew by nearly 7,300 workers in 2024, outpacing job growth in the rest of the state’s economy by more than three times.

California plans ahead so the grid keeps pace with growing demand

California’s reliability gains reflect more than new construction. The state has strengthened coordination among the agencies that forecast electricity demand, plan transmission and oversee the purchase of new resources, helping ensure that available power can reach the communities that need it.

In December 2022, CAISO, the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) and the California Energy Commission (CEC) signed a memorandum of understanding linking resource and transmission planning, grid interconnection and procurement. The Newsom administration identifies that agreement as a foundation for preparing California to meet growing electricity demand, including from data centers, while maintaining reliability and advancing clean-energy goals.

The strategy connects decisions about which resources electricity providers purchase with where transmission capacity exists or is planned. It helps guide investment toward projects that can connect to the grid and deliver electricity where customers need it, rather than treating generation, transmission, and procurement as separate challenges.

The Newsom administration also built a backstop to provide additional energy reserves during climate emergencies. When the COVID-19 pandemic and supply chain challenges delayed the projects California needed to keep the grid reliable, Governor Newsom created the Strategic Reliability Reserve in 2022. The Reserve keeps backup resources ready for extreme heat and unusual conditions while new clean energy and storage resources continue to be deployed each year.

Keeping the grid reliable and bills fair as data centers drive new demand

This past summer, large loads, such as from data centers, added strain to power grids in parts of the Mid-Atlantic and Midwest, prompting emergency measures to prevent blackouts. California has not faced the same strain, thanks in part to safeguards Governor Newsom’s administration put in place, including the coordinated planning agreement signed in 2022 by CAISO, CPUC, and the CEC.

To build on those safeguards, Governor Newsom signed a legislative package in September to strengthen oversight of data centers and protect Californians from bearing the costs of the industry’s growing demands on electricity and water systems. The laws give communities more information about proposed projects while establishing safeguards for the grid, utility customers, and local water supplies.

With these new laws, California is helping to ensure that communities have the information they need to decide whether data centers are right for them, including:

⚡ Electricity, by making data centers pay their fair share of grid update costs, while preventing cost shifts to low-income customers. The new laws will also ensure data centers comply with California energy procurement requirements, bring new clean energy supply onto the grid, and pay for any upgrade costs. This legislation will prevent data centers from shifting costs onto everyday ratepayers.

🚰 Water, by requiring that proposed data centers provide information to local governments and water suppliers about water use, supply, efficiency, and drought planning. Any upgrades needed to supply water would be paid for by the data center.

🏞️ Land use, by making data centers ineligible for blanket environmental exemptions and instead requiring data centers to demonstrate that the project will not shift costs to ratepayers, but will meet state standards on energy, water, and fuel consumption before any judicial streamlining could be approved.

These protections complement California’s coordinated grid planning with a clear principle: innovation should move forward without leaving Californians to shoulder the infrastructure costs of data-center growth.

California chooses more affordable energy future, not coal-industry bailouts

Nearly two decades ago, California began moving away from coal, choosing instead to invest in a cleaner energy future that delivers reliable, more affordable power. That transition finally culminated last year, when the last coal-fired power plant supplying Los Angeles retired, ending the city and the state’s reliance on coal-fired electricity.

Meanwhile, Trump and Energy Secretary Chris Wright are handing the coal industry the bailout it asked for, forcing aging plants to stay open past retirement, sometimes over their owners’ objections, with electricity customers facing hundreds of millions of dollars in costs.

In Michigan alone, Trump’s forcing a coal plant to run past its retirement date had cost approximately $259 million before a federal appeals court struck down Trump’s unlawful order.

California is choosing a different path: expanding clean electricity and storage while maintaining the resources necessary to protect reliability throughout the transition. That commitment is delivering results, with clean energy supplying a larger share of the grid every year.

text:
The US is set to have access to about 110,000 US tons (100,000 metric tons) of battery-grade lithium over the next decade following a new agreement to produce the critical mineral using advanced lithium extraction technology.

The GET-Lit direct lithium extraction (DLE) and refining technology was developed by Energy Exploration Technologies (EnergyX). The Texas-based firm specializes in lithium extraction and critical mineral production.

1/1Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE

On Monday, October 12, EnergyX announced that it signed a binding, 10-year, take-or-pay agreement with Singaporean global commodity trader Trafigura to supply lithium from two major projects in Texas and Chile. The supply will support electric vehicles, energy storage systems, and other industries that depend on battery materials.

The company said commercial production is scheduled to start in 2028. “Offtake agreements are among the most important steps in taking a lithium project from development to production,” Teague Egan, EnergyX founder and CEO, disclosed.

A new extraction method

The US produces about 6,600 US tons (6,000 metric tons) of lithium annually. This accounts for less than one percent of the global production. Moreover, it relies on net imports for more than 50 percent of the lithium it consumes. To address this, EnergyX came up with the GET-Lit direct lithium extraction (DLE) technology.

More from Energy

See All

Backed by more than 150 patents, the approach extracts lithium from mineral-rich brines and refines it into materials suitable for batteries. The novel process works by separating lithium directly from liquid brines.

EnergyX has already tested the method in labs, pilot facilities, and demonstration plants in the US and Chile. In April 2026, it commissioned its Project Lonestar lithium production plant in Texas, which is the largest DLE lithium production plant in the country.

At the same time, the company is also working on another major lithium project in Chile called Black Giant. It has a planned annual production capacity of around 57,871 US tons (52,500 metric tons).

The two projects will produce different lithium products. Black Giant will supply lithium carbonate, while Project Lonestar will produce lithium hydroxide. Both materials are essential for rechargeable batteries used in EVs and energy storage systems.

Commercial operations

Under the agreement, Trafigura will buy 110,000 US tons (100,000 metric tons) of battery-grade lithium products over the next decade. The deal covers 66 percent of the planned first-phase output from Project Black Giant, as well as 30 percent from Project Lonestar.

Meanwhile, EnergyX is also talking to other potential buyers to secure customers for 80 percent of its planned production. At current lithium prices of about USD 18,100 per US ton (roughly USD 20,000 per metric ton), the deal could generate over USD 2 billion in revenue over its lifetime.

“A long-term purchase commitment from a counterparty of Trafigura’s scale and credit quality shows that the market wants EnergyX’s product,” Egan stressed in a press release. “It also gives lenders and investors the revenue visibility they need before committing capital to commercial construction.”

EnergyX has also secured financial support for its expansion plans. This includes a USD 225 million investment from energy company Eni for Project Black Giant and a USD 690 million letter of intent from the US Export-Import Bank for potential debt financing.

“We are pleased to support EnergyX as it develops its lithium projects in Chile and the US,” Daniel von Arx, Trafigura’s head of battery metals, stated. He added that long-term deals are important for starting production and securing reliable supplies of critical minerals.

text:
Gotion Power Morocco announced on 12 October that equipment commissioning and startup would begin during the week of 20 October at its plant in Kenitra’s Atlantic Free Zone.

The company says construction of the cell plant’s buildings and infrastructure is complete. The first phase is designed for 20 gigawatt-hours of annual production capacity, a planned figure rather than current output.

The facility will manufacture lithium iron phosphate batteries, commonly known as LFP batteries, for customers in Morocco and elsewhere in Africa, alongside Europe, the Middle East and the United States.

ADVERTISEMENT

According to TelQuel, which reported the company’s statement issued on 12 October⁠, commissioning will open the way to industrial cell production. Gotion Power Morocco chairman Khalid Qalam had previously indicated that sales of assembled batteries were expected before the end of the year.

From investment plans to factory operations

The announcement gives a more precise timetable for a project whose first production line had already been expected to start in October.

BI Africa

Commissioning involves bringing equipment into operation and testing its performance before production can expand. It should not be confused with the factory immediately reaching its full annual capacity.

ADVERTISEMENT

Gotion’s own project information puts first-phase investment at approximately $1.3 billion and identifies a planned capacity of 20 GWh.

The next commercial milestones will be consistent production, customer deliveries and the gradual increase in output.

Volkswagen adds a European connection

The factory’s progress comes as Gotion deepens its partnership with Volkswagen and the German carmaker’s battery subsidiary, PowerCo.

On 28 September, the companies announced plans for joint ventures in Spain, Slovakia and Morocco to expand production of LFP battery cells and cathode materials.

ADVERTISEMENT

The proposed Kenitra joint venture will manufacture cathode material, a key battery component. Gotion will hold 51% and PowerCo 49%, with the partners managing the venture together.

That materials project is separate from the cell-production equipment scheduled for commissioning this month. Volkswagen’s announcement did not establish an October startup date for the cathode facility.

Morocco is attracting investment in both finished battery cells and the materials needed to manufacture them.

Why Morocco matters to the supply chain

Volkswagen says its partnership with Gotion is intended to diversify supplies and strengthen Europe’s battery industry.

ADVERTISEMENT

LFP technology offers relatively competitive costs, a long service life and durability, making it attractive for more affordable electric vehicles and energy-storage systems. The companies see expanding European demand as an opportunity for their production network.

For Morocco, the investment provides an opportunity to move further into battery manufacturing while serving markets beyond its borders.

The project has also attracted African development financing. The African Development Bank announced approval of a loan in July to support an integrated battery-manufacturing facility in Kenitra.

Its financing documents describe an initial 10 GWh project, whereas Gotion’s broader first-phase description puts capacity at 20 GWh.

text:
NEW ORLEANS – Entergy is commemorating the 25th anniversary of its Environmental Initiatives Fund, marking a milestone in a long history of environmental commitment that began well before sustainability became a corporate trend.

For a quarter century, Entergy’s EIF has exemplified the company’s early and ongoing leadership in environmental stewardship. Established in 2001 as a shareholder-funded grant program, the EIF represents a proactive approach to protecting natural resources, reducing emissions, restoring habitats and strengthening community resilience across Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi and Texas. Over its 25-year history, Entergy shareholders have invested nearly $45 million in community-based environmental improvements across the region.

“Reaching 25 years of the Environmental Initiatives Fund is more than marking time; it’s a reaffirmation of a commitment our shareholders embraced long before sustainability was in the spotlight,” said John Weiss, vice president of sustainability and environmental policy. “The EIF has allowed us to support meaningful projects that improve local ecosystems, strengthen communities and advance environmental progress throughout our service area.”

In 2025 alone, the EIF provided $1 million in shareholder-funded support to 11 partner organizations working in areas such as wetland restoration, tree planting, biodiversity education and green infrastructure development. text:
Climate & Energy

A Vision for Western Solidarity in the Mid-Transition, Beyond the Resource Curse

10.13.26 | 12 min read | Text by Zoë Brouns & Erin Harrington & Craig Segall & Hannah Safford

The energy transition happens in real places with real people, and different regions face different obstacles in moving through the “messy middle” of the energy transition toward a more fully decarbonized economy. So while clean generation and capacity are growing fast across the country, continued progress depends on supporting that growth from the ground up.

Mid-transition challenges are particularly salient in Alaska and other Western states. Along with Appalachia, the American West has long been at the core of the fossil economy. Now, at a time of federal retreat with respect to clean energy, the American West can play an outsized role in driving a new kind of energy story.

The American West has a proud history: of policy leadership, environmental stewardship, and entrepreneurialism. However, the region is also largely dependent on resource extraction and fossil fuel production, industries that are deeply woven into its social, political, and economic fabric. This resource curse has concentrated economic and political power in the hands of a few companies at the expense of residents and communities. As new pressures like climate overshoot and geopolitical turmoil have arisen, the resource curse has complicated Western states’ ability to chart a more resilient future.

Complicated, but not compromised. The flip side of the resource curse is that Western states – as the bedrock of U.S. energy production – have a unique opportunity to reinvent not only their relationship to energy, but that of our entire country. Too often, the national conversation on climate and energy centers on the Eastern states that are geographically proximate to our nation’s capital. To the extent that policymakers look west, they often focus myopically on California. This essay broadens the aperture, exploring how the principles of regulatory ingenuity can position Western states beyond California to lead on mid-transition challenges and help a region transform itself in ways that can also create new possibilities for the country as a whole, starting now.

Escaping the Resource Curse

Escaping the resource curse means envisioning a future that does not simply replace oil with other extractive industries, but instead drives shared prosperity.

As home to significant domestic oil and gas production, Western states face complex pathways to decarbonization. In states like Alaska, Texas, Arizona, and Wyoming, natural resource extraction is inseparable from economic and government structures (e.g., sovereign wealth funds that underpin public services or gas industries as majority local employers), and that relationship directly impacts how these states go about the transition. For example, Alaska’s Renewable Energy Fund, which supports more reliable and cleaner energy sources for remote and Indigenous communities, is funded by state revenue and has historically benefited from windfalls resulting from global oil shocks. Boosts (or drops) in state funding are often driven by the volatility of resource markets, and the inconsistency of that revenue makes it difficult to sustain energy transition funds like Alaska’s.

Similarly, Wyoming’s mineral resources provide at least a third of the state’s annual public revenue (not counting earnings from its sovereign wealth fund). Though mineral extraction supports the development of clean energy technology, it has its own environmental impacts. In New Mexico, a recent oil boom has helped supercharge critical services, like universal childcare and public schools, but has also made it harder for the state to provide those services long-term without the help of fossil fuel revenue.

The legal frameworks of oil-producing states often favor investment in and subsidization of fossil fuels, including through tax incentives and below-market rate land leases. That limits market development for clean tech and renewables, and makes it harder to implement conventional policy tools that drive the transition in other states, like renewables mandates and supply-side incentives. Even where Western states are moving to accelerate renewables, existing regulation can favor incumbent fossil fuels over emerging clean sources because of the deep ties between resource revenue and public services and the higher bar to entry for clean sources versus subsidized energy sources. New Mexico has made significant progress on clean generation, but its budget still relies heavily on resource wealth.

In addition, the actual time, expertise, and resources necessary to reform an entire statutory and regulatory structure can be well beyond the capacity of any legislative body, even one with the best intentions. Many Western states have legislatures that operate on a biennial cycle of short and long legislative sessions; others have very short sessions every year (California is unique, with a year-round legislature). These structures can limit legislatures’ ability to dig deeply into existing legal frameworks and start untangling these dependent policies. Hyperpolarization nationally and electoral whiplash don’t help – state officials aren’t incentivized to try new things when there might be political consequences.

Alaska’s recent political wrangling to facilitate the construction of a new natural gas pipeline from the North Slope to Southcentral Alaska is an unfortunate example of how those pressures hinder progress. State elected leaders sparred in three special legislative sessions in 2026 over creating a more favorable tax structure for the pipeline developer, while also trying to safeguard the fiscal interests of the cities through which the pipeline would pass. Legislators otherwise largely ignored renewable energy policy, beyond one-time budget allocations. Given the revenue a gas pipeline represents for Alaskans and their public services, elected officials are incentivized to spend time figuring out how to create a friendlier environment for those developers, instead of for clean energy that doesn’t represent as much direct wealth for the state.

Turning the freighter of these policy frameworks risks very real impacts on communities. In Alaska, the singular dependence on oil and gas as the state’s economic driver for nearly 50 years has made it a classic resource colony, while exposing it to untenable long-term fiscal risk as the world energy system evolves away from fossil fuels. Early resource wealth helped build civic institutions that provide basic services to communities, like education, childcare, and safety. As those resource markets become more unstable, state and local institutions have contracted – the city of Juneau is facing a $10–12 million budget gap and Alaska’s projected deficit is $1.8 billion next year. The state is already prioritizing Permanent Fund dividends over things like childcare workers and increased Medicaid payments. Communities need reliable services, and dependence on fossil fuels or resource extraction won’t provide that stability long-term. But diversifying too quickly or haphazardly could upend the current system and leave Westerners unable to access basic needs, further damaging public trust in institutions, and hobbling the state’s ability to make it through the mid-transition.

Opportunity for Transformation

How, then, do Western states break their resource curse? The ideas below are a starting point for Western states looking to diversify – and thereby strengthen – their economies while simultaneously leading on environmental stewardship and an equitable, politically attractive energy transition.

The West has long echoed with calls for a more independent and self-reliant future, but often these visions, including the Sagebrush Rebellion of the 1970s and 80s, ended instead in frustration and constraints on the very government creativity needed to reshape economies – leading to neither local control nor shared prosperity. This is a chance for a more constructive path, aimed this time at creating fiscal room for democratic creativity.

Governance/Finance

Many Western states have unique economic instruments in their policy toolboxes. Sovereign wealth funds, for instance, are inherently tied to resource extraction but can also provide the capital needed to finance economic diversification and decarbonization. Resource wealth can be invested to derisk renewables markets, build more resilient infrastructure, and catalyze innovation – the building blocks of a modern, climate-smart economy. Resource wealth can also be invested in the enablers of that economy: e.g., better public engagement strategies that increase trust in government while producing better policy, new legal regimes that decouple state budgets from resource revenues, and accountability structures for reigning industries that force them to pay their fair share and keep benefits local. Initial approaches could include:

Collaborative finance. States can pool capital from green banks and infrastructure banks across the West into shared investments, or at least align on a shared strategy to reach the scale needed to shift markets while keeping capital in the region. Mutual lending and intra-West investing could shore up regional relationships and allow states to focus on what helps them grow instead of exporting resource wealth outside of the state. The West already has much of the capital it needs for economic growth, and being more strategic about scaling within the region would support independence and diversification.

Long-term revenue sustainability, including through resource stewardship. By diversifying their funding sources and investment strategies, Western states can secure truly permanent funds. Alaska’s Permanent Fund helps stabilize its budget, but is not large enough to sustainably support public services and relies on diminishing resources, while federal safety net cuts and natural risks like wildfires and floods increasingly burden public budgets. But Alaska – like many Western states – can provide valuable services to the country that extend well beyond raw resource production. Their land bases and locations position them to reduce global risks – and secure revenue for doing so. As an example, the Tongass Rainforest is a globally important carbon storehouse whose services warrant federal investment – not just in science but in enhancing its capacity on the ground by supporting continued stewardship in the state budget. Likewise, Alaska, alone among the states, can take meaningful action to lessen methane releases from permafrost that threaten trillions in global investments, or explore new climate interventions that may be able to protect globally important sea ice and the reflectivity of the Arctic. Other Western states have aligned opportunities in their land bases, from carbon capture to forestry stewardship to novel research and experimentation with public oversight. Monetization solutions are complex, nuanced, and need development – and can receive that attention through Western collaboration. The West can be a place that reduces national and global risk, reaps federal research dollars in exchange, and potentially secures longer-term financial support to maintain critical solutions.

These new strategies can also open up more opportunities for interdependence between Western states and the federal government, through federal capital transfers (when possible) supporting the West’s role in the national transition, as well as local governments, with increased funding shoring up responsive capacity at the city level. These could include new payments to manage public health and climate risks (e.g., forest management or underwriting community resilience investments like workforce development).

Western interdependence and solidarity. Creating a system where Western resources help build shared benefits within the West – not outside of it. Western state governors have already begun to weave together Western power grids, and they should look to other shared infrastructure and economic development projects, like new transmission lines connecting regional grids to the East and Canada. States can secure the benefits of these lines within the region by activating major new opportunities to build and sell clean energy projects (while capturing those benefits in enhanced state revenue) or new regional clean industrial zones to support advanced manufacturing.

Proactive transfer of governance to Tribes. Tribal governments play a unique role in Western governance and resource management. Transferring that role through compacts and co-management of federal lands, creative financing partnerships, shared workforce development, and increased Tribal authority and decision-making power can strengthen Western and Tribal independence from extractive industries and resilience to climate risks. Tribal leaders still face similar economic pressures, but have their own sets of policymaking tools – providing Tribal governments more policymaking agency could spur more innovation and allow for more supportive regional partnerships.

Energy

As pressures for energy generation and production mount, fossil fuels will continue to play a role in the West. But states also have unique opportunities to diversify their supply of affordable, reliable, and clean power and catalyze new Western economic engines. Geothermal energy and hydropower are uniquely abundant in the West, and vast amounts of federal land, if managed appropriately and sustainably, can unlock new development opportunities that don’t rely on extraction. State regulatory structures currently tilt the scales toward fossil fuels, so while states start the process of reforming those structures, governments will need to get creative in the short term to make sure renewables have a fair shot at staying competitive. Regardless of source, states will also need to invest in grid stabilization and modernization as prices and demand increase.

Some are leading already. The New Mexico Comprehensive Energy Transition Strategy is building out an integrated roadmap to support the state on its transition toward clean energy and net-zero commitments. Both Wyoming and Utah have made significant investments in renewables markets despite their reliance on fossil fuels. Utah’s DOE-sponsored and state-supported FORGE laboratory focuses on enhanced geothermal research, and groundbreaking geothermal developments across the state have helped kickstart the industry. Wyoming hosts major wind and solar projects alongside its coal production, and the state provides matching funds for innovative energy projects to attract outside developers. These states are not unique in the West in terms of political makeup, resource wealth, and generally limited government capacity, making them useful examples of how others can adapt to a new energy reality.

Resilience

The West’s tens of millions of acres of wilderness are a crown jewel of the continent and another unique opportunity for the region. Its intact natural systems are important not just as a focus of conservation or nature-based solutions, but also as a key component of economic development, built environment, and resilience. Joint strategies to build out learning and capacity for how to leverage that nature – for example, through public–private partnerships – could aid Western states in strengthening resilience to climate shocks. Turning nature into part of states’ economic engines (while stewarding the land responsibly) is a way to further aid the transition – and is something only Western states can do.

But the increasing risks of climate overshoot also complicate those efforts. Wildfires, floods, droughts, and changing landscapes result in massive cost increases and community disruptions. Current costs associated with climate-driven wildfire risks alone are in the hundreds of billions per year, to say nothing of the health costs of wildfires that are still difficult to quantify. There is tremendous need for wildfire prevention across Western landscapes, whether on federal, state, or private lands.

Broadly, more research is needed on both climate risk and stabilization approaches, especially, as noted above, because Western states functionally manage trillions in global climate risk (permafrost, forest carbon, etc.) and can do so in ways that drive state economic development. There are enormous opportunities to put public universities and science agencies in the lead on this front, securing federal appropriations to further support this work, and linking together collaboratives across the landscape. Imagine a cross-Arctic collaborative from Alaska on emergent ideas such as protecting volatile permafrost or restoring sea ice, along with paths to develop economies around these ideas, or a Pacific Northwest academic/government/industry collaborative to move the needle on forest and ocean carbon storage. With increased global attention on ecological systems interventions, Western states can be proactive leaders in research and governance on this front. Success in any of these efforts could reduce billions, or even trillions, of dollars’ worth of risk to the country and the world – making it vital to invest and creating a path for returns not just in knowledge but in careers for young people moving through public university systems.

Capacity and Expertise

To make this regulatory and economic transformation successful, the West will need smart and capable people to carry it out. In states where the dominant industries are fossil fuels, the workforce tends to be fossil fuel-oriented as well, but deep understanding of energy systems and skills with specific infrastructure or operations can be useful foundations for other industries (like geothermal). Professional expertise, mentoring and development, and training pipelines are all critical to workforce transition and economic diversification, including educational and vocational resources, workforce development programs, and good opportunities across the public and private sectors.

States can design both push and pull strategies for workforce development. Reinvesting resource wealth into clean job opportunities in technology, manufacturing, infrastructure, and energy; creating public sector openings for key expertise in permitting and utility regulation; and redesigning educational curricula to diversify pathways for students should all be part of the playbook. Interdependence among states can help expand pipelines for resource sharing, regional collaboration, and shared learning. Western state university systems – which are already linked through the Western Undergraduate Exchange (WUE) – can work together to create professional on-ramps for the next generation of energy leaders and workers.

Why now?

With many of them facing resource curses, increased natural disasters, and uphill political battles, Western states cannot afford to wait around for new policy tools. They have the know-how and the history to be able to lead in this moment – to reimagine economic and governance structures, to work regionally toward safer and healthier communities, and to build out cleaner and more reliable energy systems. This is a critical moment. Next month, nine Western states, including Alaska, will hold gubernatorial elections at a time when constituents are hungry for new ideas that actually deliver on government promises. Policymakers who can reimagine the existing paradigm will be the ones who usher in this new era of Western leadership.

text:
PARIS, Oct 13 (Reuters) – The US auto market will eventually embrace electrification despite a slow uptake of electric vehicles so far, Stellantis CEO Antonio Filosa said on ​Tuesday, predicting the shift will happen more slowly than ‌in other regions.

Speaking at an event on the sidelines of the Paris motor show, Filosa said EVs accounted for 7% of US auto sales this year, unchanged from five years ago.

“It has been a bubble driven ‌by ​regulation. But then, when the administration has ⁠decided to deregulate, the ⁠consumers have been preferring other powertrains”, he said.

For Stellantis, which counts North America among its key markets, interest is growing in the US for range-extender technology in large pickups and ​SUVs.

It is “not regulation driven, it’s customer driven”, Filosa said.

Despite the slower pace of adoption, Filosa said he “truly” believed electrification ⁠would eventually take hold in the ⁠US.

“The level of magnitude and the speed of ​transition is going to be lower for sure than other regions.”

He ​said Stellantis would be able to draw on lessons ‌learned from Europe’s EV rollout as demand develops in North America.

Filosa also said the automotive sector was becoming less global as trade barriers reshape markets.

“The recent trade regimens around the world ⁠have triggered the process of regionalisation. So, what was the global industry before, now it’s less global and more regional,” he said.

As a ⁠result, automakers need ‌to focus more closely on local customer ⁠preferences and regulations while maintaining global scale, particularly ​in ‌technology, which is playing an increasingly important role ​in the ⁠industry.

“Techs are important, so it’s very important for the companies to adapt to the trend and find a way. Our way is partnerships. So we see so many important partnerships that we can explore,” he said.

(Reporting by Giulio Piovaccari and Gilles Guillaume. Editing ​by Mark Potter)

text:
Comau and Intecells are presenting a roll-to-roll cold plasma surface treatment for battery electrodes and separators at The Battery Show North America in Detroit, October 12-15, 2026. Improving wettability speeds electrolyte uptake, which the companies say shortens filling, soaking and drying, reduces energy use and can lower battery cell resistance.

Comau, based in Turin, Italy, and Michigan-based Intecells are presenting a roll-to-roll surface treatment system for battery cell production at The Battery Show North America. The system uses Intecells’ cold plasma technology to speed up electrolyte uptake and reduce energy use in cell manufacturing. The show runs October 12-15 at Huntington Place in Detroit, where the companies are in Booth #3626.

The process treats the surfaces of battery electrodes, separators or both with cold plasma to improve their wettability. According to the companies, this lets the electrolyte spread through and penetrate the materials more quickly and evenly. That shortens the filling, soaking and drying stages and reduces the heat they require. The companies say this lowers energy consumption, factory floor space and associated costs, and can also reduce cell resistance.

Comau acquired a stake in Intecells in 2025. Intecells supplies the plasma technology, while Comau industrializes, integrates and scales the process for production lines. The companies also plan to explore uses for the surface treatment in other industries.

“For our customers, this means finding better ways to manufacture batteries at scale while controlling energy use, production time and costs. Our investment in Intecells addresses these needs with innovative technologies that deliver tangible benefits. Together, we will continue to bring plasma-based solutions to battery manufacturing and other industrial applications,” says Pietro Gorlier, chief executive of Comau.

“We need to transform battery manufacturing beyond iterative improvements in order to meet the energy demands of AI data centers and global mobility,” says Dr. Xiaohong Gayden, founder and chief executive of Intecells.

Gayden adds, “Intecells is excited to partner with Comau, a world-class industrial automation leader, to scale our atmospheric plasma technology and combine advanced manufacturing physics with gigafactory automation – enabling cell producers and OEMs to deploy lower Capex, higher efficiency production lines across the globe.”

Intecells is also developing processes for dry electrode coating and solid-state battery manufacturing. The company says it aims to cut battery manufacturing costs by 50% and carbon emissions by 70%.

At the show, Comau is also presenting a cell formation and testing hub it built for the National Institute of Chemistry (NIC). The semi-automated platform handles pouch, cylindrical and prismatic cells, from laboratory prototypes to high-power cells for automotive and industrial applications. It has dedicated formation chambers as well as climatic and room-temperature testing stations. The lab is open to academic and industrial users across Europe.

“The growth of cell manufacturing technology is creating significant opportunities across a market that spans batteries for both transportation and energy storage systems as well as renewables and electrification infrastructure,” says Gorlier. According to Comau, its target market is expected to grow at a compound annual growth rate of more than 15% between 2025 and 2030.

Comau will also exhibit at The Battery Show India, October 22-24, 2026, at the India Expo Mart in Greater Noida (Hall 7, Booth 115).

title: 'Power Islands' Tap High-Yield Market as AI Data Centers Go Beyond the Grid - Octus
description:
This shift addresses the growing electricity demand from data centers, which is expected to significantly strain existing power grids.
While high-yield financing for AI infrastructure power has lagged data center financing, power companies are increasingly tapping the high-yield market to fund the construction of behind-the-meter power generation, according to Kirk Roland, head of power debt capital markets at Citi.
Serial high-yield issuers, such as natural gas compression company Kodiak Gas, have led the pivot into behind-the-meter power, as they repurpose equipment and turbines to power data centers.
This year, Kodiak acquired Distributed Gas Solutions to expand its platform “into distributed and behind-the-meter power generation,” according to a press release.
Multiple other issuers outside the oilfield services group are considering high-yield financings to power data centers over the next six months, he added.
text:
Summary by AI at Octus

Solaris Energy Infrastructure, previously known for oilfield logistics, has transitioned to behind-the-meter power generation, issuing over $2.5 billion in bonds this year to support AI data centers with on-site power plants. This shift addresses the growing electricity demand from data centers, which is expected to significantly strain existing power grids. The high-yield bond market is increasingly being tapped by companies like Solaris and others, such as Kodiak Gas and VoltaGrid, to fund these power generation projects. Despite the potential for growth, the sector faces challenges including execution risks, regulatory hurdles, and the need for careful project management and technology assessment.

For years, leveraged finance investors knew Solaris Energy Infrastructure as an oilfield logistics provider. Now it’s in the business of powering AI. Solaris shifted to behind-the-meter power generation in the past couple of years and has issued over $2.5 billion in bonds this year, making it one of a handful of high-yield bond issuers to tap a fast-growing corner of the AI buildout: on-site plants known as “power islands” that keep data centers running without waiting on the grid.

The expected supply of high-yield issuance in the behind-the-meter, or BTM, space follows the massive electricity demand from data centers and the strain it could put on existing power grids, according to market participants interviewed by Octus.

A Surging Energy Need

Enverus, an energy data analytics platform, projects that 25.5 gigawatts, or GW, of energy demand will be served by behind-the-meter generation from 2026 to 2030, of which 88% will be driven by demand from data centers. Demand for BTM power in strained areas such as the PJM power grid, which covers the mid-Atlantic region, and ERCOT grid, which covers Texas, is expected to represent half of new BTM demand. For context, Goldman Sachs expects U.S. data center power demand to reach 66 GW in 2027.

“Politically, it gets tougher to tap power from the grid because of the perception that it drives up electricity rates for consumers, so [behind-the-meter] is an insurance play to make sure they are not constrained by either political or other constraints,” said Grant Moyer, head of leveraged finance at MUFG, on the demand for BTM power.

The pushback is already playing out. In the summer, NV Energy, Nevada’s energy utility, sued data center developer Tract, alleging the company would use large amounts of power for its own development while shifting costs onto Nevada residents and businesses. Last month, Nevada regulators approved two Tract gas power plants that will provide more than 360 megawatts, or MW, of on-site power generation, according to a local news report.

While high-yield financing for AI infrastructure power has lagged data center financing, power companies are increasingly tapping the high-yield market to fund the construction of behind-the-meter power generation, according to Kirk Roland, head of power debt capital markets at Citi.

“We need to build additional power to provide for these new users of power coming online, and that’s an inexorable megatrend that debt investors like getting behind,” Roland said.

The First Wave of Deals

“[Behind-the-meter power] is new for the high-yield market,” said Alina Golant, a high-yield energy strategist at SMBC, highlighting at least four issuers that recently tapped the market for BTM.

Solaris came to market last month with upsized $1.25 billion 7% senior notes due in 2032 to fund capital expenditures in the development of on-site power generation for data centers. It was the second time the company issued high-yield debt this year, following a $1.3 billion 6.375% note offering in May.

While new companies that were created specifically for on-site data center power, such as Tacanock and Thunderhead Energy Solutions, are entering the space, most behind-the-meter high-yield issuers so far have pivoted from another business.

Serial high-yield issuers, such as natural gas compression company Kodiak Gas, have led the pivot into behind-the-meter power, as they repurpose equipment and turbines to power data centers. This year, Kodiak acquired Distributed Gas Solutions to expand its platform “into distributed and behind-the-meter power generation,” according to a press release.

VoltaGrid, which began supplying mobile power to oil and gas operators before expanding into behind-the-meter generation for hyperscalers, was among the first companies in the sector to tap the high-yield market. In November 2025, VoltaGrid raised $2 billion of second lien notes due 2030 and a $3 billion asset-based revolving facility to fund its ongoing growth initiatives in the sector.

“[VoltaGrid] established the concept of the high-yield market financing these businesses that have stable, contracted long-term off-takes with hyperscalers themselves, co-located at data centers,” said Nick Fall, head of North America leveraged finance at Barclays.

But the field is now widening, Citi’s Roland said, as independent power producers, bitcoin miners and distributed generation companies are also pursuing deals. Multiple other issuers outside the oilfield services group are considering high-yield financings to power data centers over the next six months, he added.

The appeal of these deals to investors is that operators are signing long-term, take-or-pay contracts with data centers and hyperscalers, which means investors get paid almost regardless of how the AI buildout pans out, according to SMBC’s Golant. A buy-sider noted that these contracts offer cash flow visibility, while still paying investors a premium for the execution risk.

Behind-the-Meter Finds a Home in High-Yield

Despite having less of a track record and initially lower credit ratings than established energy names, BTM operators have solid contracts with off-takers, Barclays’ Fall said. If projects are built on time and phase in as planned, their cost of capital should eventually converge with that of larger power players, he added, calling these projects “mission-critical to the success of the whole data center ecosystem.”

“The high-yield market has been a very hospitable place for the overall power demand theme […] and it’s one of the first in the broadly distributed capital markets to be used for these buildouts,” Fall said.

Given their early-stage development, these deals price wider than benchmark high-yield power names.

For issuers, high-yield is flexible with fewer construction milestones and restrictive covenants than project financing, according to Fall. Roland said that developers are also counting on the bonds’ call option to refinance construction debt at a lower cost once projects are operating.

Options are immense for data center power buildouts, noted Aashish Mohan, head of energy, resources and infrastructure, Americas global capital markets, at BNP Paribas. After structuring deals for data centers and behind-the-meter facilities, banks can offer clients many pools of liquidity: the floating-rate bank market, the IG bond market (144A or USPP) or the high-yield bond market.

“We’re seeing a dispersion of solutions as the range of participants looking for financing grows,” Roland said. “But there is, without question, more high-yield financing for power for data centers in process now than there was, and there will be even more looking forward.”

Execution and Regulatory Risk

Despite expectations for growth in issuance tied to behind-the-meter power, the emerging sector is not without its hurdles. Developers still need to conduct diligence on the technology provider, fuel needs, pipeline access and permitting, a banker noted.

The main risk is getting projects built. That means scrutinizing termination clauses: whether the off-taker can exit, how many days of construction delay allow it to walk away and whether it can claim credits back from the developer, sources added.

Execution is the other concern, as some issuers are not fully ramped up yet. “Part of the challenge is the availability of turbines and other necessary machinery,” MUFG’s Moyer said, adding that investors want to know how developers will build and what access they have to equipment.

Other factors include who the off-taker is and whether the project can deliver power on schedule, the buy-sider added. They also noted that there is technology and residual-value risk, particularly if the contract expires before the debt matures.

Regulatory risk is growing too. In August, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott ordered an audit of data centers seeking grid connections, and in September he directed the state’s environmental regulator to halt data center permits until the audit is complete. Views vary on whether the halt applies to behind-the-meter gas plants, which the regulator also permits, and some suggest it could reach developers.

From Corporate Bonds to Project Bonds

Fall said he expects a real ramp-up in behind-the-meter high-yield issuance over the next year, since power is the big limiting constraint in the data center buildout.

The structure of the offerings could also evolve. Financings are likely to shift toward site-specific buildouts, with a separate special purpose vehicle for each project, which is expected to drive a lot more issuance, Fall added.

“What will be the next evolution in the high-yield market is when you start to see project financing high-yield bonds done for power for data centers […] and you will see that roll out, I’m going to say certainly within the next six months, if not a lot sooner,” Roland said.

text:
Republican-led states are using the courts to send a message to their Democrat-led counterparts: Your climate policies are going too far.

In at least one instance, the courts have been sympathetic to red states’ cause: A federal judge in August ruled in favor of red states and business groups in litigation against New York over its law to force polluters to pay for past emissions. Red states also intervened in a lawsuit challenging Vermont over a similar policy, and Iowa and Missouri also sued New York in May alleging the state’s greenhouse gas reporting program will harm out-of-state fuel suppliers.

West Virginia Solicitor General Michael Williams (R), whose state has led some of the red state coalitions suing blue states, said he doesn’t believe “blue states aren’t permitted to advance their own climate goals,” which is “fine as long as they sort of stay within their lane.” They become problematic when their policies impact other states and address interstate issues that fall under the federal government’s purview, he added.

“It’s not that the red states all got together in a room and it’s like, ‘What are we doing this week, guys? OK, let’s go bother the blue states,’” Williams said in an interview. “It’s purely a reaction to what we’re seeing and what our stakeholders and what our citizens are feeling.”

States’ efforts to challenge their peers’ climate policies come as the Trump administration has sought to reverse a spate of federal attempts to fight climate change. Blue states and cities’ policies could help fill the federal void, but cases filed by the likes of West Virginia and others trying to quash some of those policies could impact how much states ultimately can do to fight climate change.

The Evolution of Attorneys General

The country’s highly polarized political environment and past legal rulings curbing what plaintiffs can sue, thereby setting states up as ideal litigants, have contributed to states’ penchant to sue their peers over climate policies they feel go too far.

Paul Nolette, director of Marquette University’s Les Aspin Center for Government, said attorneys general from both parties have gotten more aggressive over the last roughly five years unlike decades earlier when they’d largely oppose each other in amicus briefs in Supreme Court cases. Now, “polarization just keeps getting deeper and deeper,” he said.

Attorneys general have also built on each other’s power and actions over the years, added Nolette, who has written a book on attorneys general and national policy.

“Over the last five years, the floodgates have kind of opened for these sort of state vs. state lawsuits,” he said.

Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway (R) said “a lot of it has evolved over probably the last 10 to 20 years as Congress has gotten more” gridlocked.

“We’ve seen states trying to put in place measures that they think their voters believe in and oftentimes there is conflict between red states and blue states and what they think the policy ought to be,” she said.

The legal fights between red and blue states are the result of “total integration” of state and federal partisan agendas, said Jim Tierney (D), Maine’s attorney general in the 1980s and now a lecturer at Harvard Law School. The Trump administration has dismantled environmental polices that red states fought the Biden administration on, so Republican attorneys general have now instead turned to challenging blue states.

“If you just ask the question, is it red states suing blue states over climate change in a way that’s never happened before? The answer is yes,” he said.

Attorneys general have also emerged as “the primary litigants” in place of potential plaintiffs hiring Washington lobbyists or localities and citizen groups filing their own litigation because courts have limited who has standing to sue, Tierney also said.

Sometimes, attorneys general also use their offices as stepping stones. The National Association of Attorneys General has jokingly been referred to as the National Association of Aspiring Governors, according to Hanaway.

“If you’re in a red state and you want to stand out to the Trump administration — maybe you want a prestigious appointment in the government or you want to be a judge — bringing these kinds of lawsuits that align you with one side or another is a way to do that,” said Andy Mergen, faculty director at Harvard Law School’s Emmett Environmental Law & Policy Clinic and a former Department of Justice lawyer.

Setting Precedent

Current litigation could have a lasting impact on what states can do on their own to fight climate change.

New York could still appeal the two federal rulings against its climate superfund law. The fate of litigation from Republican-led states and others against Vermont, along with Missouri and Iowa’s lawsuit against New York, is still unknown.

“When it comes to any sort of efforts to fight climate change in the courts, absolutely these cases can set precedents that may well limit state power and state AG power to both enact and enforce these sorts of laws,” Marquette’s Nolette said, adding that red states want “to create those precedents and prevent the blue states from carrying out these initiatives.”

A coalition of 26 largely Republican-led states also signed onto an amicus brief in a climate change accountability case before the US Supreme Court, Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder County, which attorneys for both sides argued last week, launching the high court’s new term. While Republican- and Democrat-led states have long indirectly disagreed in court through filing such briefs, the case is notable in that it could have wider impacts affecting states.

Phil Goldberg, office managing partner at Shook, Hardy & Bacon who helped write the National Association of Manufacturers’ amicus brief siding with Suncor, said how that case shakes out could affect state climate superfund laws.

“What the court ultimately decides here could certainly have implications for those kinds of statutes,” he said during an American Bar Association panel after the Supreme Court heard oral arguments.

title: Europe?s energy transition could save 34,000 lives and deliver 826 billion euros a year by ...
description:
“Climate action does not mean only cutting emissions” said Chiara Martinelli, Director at CAN Europe.
“It means lower energy costs, healthier homes, cleaner air and millions of jobs supported across Europe.
At a time when many ask what the cost of the energy transition is, the real question is what Europe stands to gain from investing in the transition.
The analysis also includes country-level findings, showing how the benefits vary across Member States depending on national energy systems, housing, transport and investment needs.
“This research shows that the transition can offer a way out: lower energy and fuel costs, nearly 300,000 jobs by 2030 and a stronger economy, if clean alternatives are made affordable and accessible to everyone.” For additional information:
text:
The report puts numbers on benefits of climate action that are often missing from debates focused on the cost of the transition: lower energy expenditure, new jobs, better health, fewer working days lost to illness and avoided global climate damage.

Key findings that energy-saving measures could deliver by 2030 in Europe:

826 billion euros in annual monetised co-benefits from energy-saving measures;

More than 8.5 million full-time-equivalent jobs supported, including around 6.5 million in construction and renovation;

Almost 34,000 premature deaths avoided every year, alongside around 8,000 fewer hospital admissions;

3.3 million fewer sick days due to lower air pollution;

Up to 713 per person in avoided end-use energy costs.

“Climate action does not mean only cutting emissions” said Chiara Martinelli, Director at CAN Europe. “It means lower energy costs, healthier homes, cleaner air and millions of jobs supported across Europe. At a time when many ask what the cost of the energy transition is, the real question is what Europe stands to gain from investing in the transition. Climate policies work when they improve people’s daily lives, now and in the future. Health benefits, cleaner air, better homes, improved transport and lower bills are not side effects. They are the reason these measures matter.”

The report finds that these gains increase over time, with annual monetised co-benefits reaching nearly 2 trillion euros by 2050. It estimates almost 32 trillion euros in cumulative monetised co-benefits between 2030 and 2050.

“The scale of the benefits is striking: more than €826 billion a year by 2030, over 8.5 million full-time-equivalent jobs supported, and almost 34,000 premature deaths avoided annually” added Corentin Bonte, one of the authors of the report, from Climact. “And these are conservative estimates: the modelling does not capture every benefit of climate action, nor the full economic losses avoided by limiting climate change.”

The findings come as EU governments negotiate the policies, budgets and governance rules that will determine delivery of Europe’s post-2030 climate targets. The report reminds that continued fossil-fuel dependence also carries major costs: the EU spent around 340 billion euros on fossil-fuel imports in 2025, while its climate investment gap stood at 344 billion euros.

The analysis also includes country-level findings, showing how the benefits vary across Member States depending on national energy systems, housing, transport and investment needs.

“In France, millions of people are still exposed to high heating and transport costs because they depend on expensive and imported oil and gas” added Alix Mazounie, Program Coordinator at Réseau Action Climat. “This research shows that the transition can offer a way out: lower energy and fuel costs, nearly 300,000 jobs by 2030 and a stronger economy, if clean alternatives are made affordable and accessible to everyone.”

text:
Lawmakers’ brief urges Ninth Circuit to reverse district court’s decision, issue preliminary injunction

Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senators Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works (EPW), Alex Padilla (D-CA), Adam Schiff (D-CA), and Representative Salud Carbajal (D-CA-24), led an amicus brief to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit in the case of California v. Wright, challenging the Trump administration’s illegal overreach to restart the Sable Offshore Oil Pipeline.

Last month, the lawmakers submitted a brief in this case to the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California explaining that the Trump Administration’s use of the Defense Production Act (DPA) to restart the Sable Offshore oil pipeline grossly misuses the statute’s national defense intent for a corporate rescue mission to bail out the Administration’s political allies. The U.S. District Court for the Central District of California ignored the evidence of pay-to-play corruption and allowed the pipeline to continue operating.

The lawmakers’ latest brief reasserts that the Administration’s DPA Order fails to justify invoking this extraordinary authority. “DOE relies on vague national defense justifications of questionable relevance for the Order but fails to articulate why Sable’s crude-oil production and operation … are ‘necessary’ for national defense …. The Order fails to identify any specific military need for crude oil or even explain how Sable’s crude will be refined and ultimately distributed for military use. …. Sable does not produce the type of refined products that the military purchases, and the Wright Order identifies no supply-chain mechanism that would ensure that Sable’s crude is ultimately used by the military.”

The Administration’s weak national defense justification “does not relieve a court of determining whether the Executive Branch has, in good faith, established the statutory prerequisites that Congress imposed on the exercise of national-defense judgments and associated statutory authority .… [The prerequisites] are safeguards that Congress deliberately built into Title I—and refined over decades—to confine extraordinary federal intervention into private enterprise to circumstances in which prioritization or allocation is objectively necessary for national defense.”

The Trump Administration has repeatedly invoked spurious national security or emergency justifications to favor fossil fuel production: halting offshore wind projects, exempting Gulf oil and gas activity from endangered species protections, exempting dozens of coal plants from pollution control requirements, and prohibiting planned coal pant retirements. This order to restart the Sable Offshore oil pipeline is the latest example of “an Administration hell-bent on expanding fossil-fuel production.” Moreover, the project was helmed by a Trump donor, raising the specter of pay-to-play politics; DOE “intervened to rescue a favored political ally from financial ruin and bypass the state-law obstacles that had kept its pipelines idle for nearly eleven years.”

The lawmakers concluded, “The district court erred by accepting DOE’s national-defense rationale at face value rather than testing it against the statutory prerequisites, the record, and publicly available information …. the Court should reverse the district court’s denial of the preliminary injunction.”

Joining Whitehouse, Padilla, Schiff, and Carbajal, the amicus brief is co-signed by Senator Tammy Duckworth (D-IL) and Representatives Zoe Lofgren (D-CA-18), Ted Lieu (D-CA-36), Nanette Díaz Barragán (D-CA-44), John Garamendi (D-CA-08), Robert Garcia (D-CA-42), Laura Friedman (D-CA-30), Mike Levin (D-CA-49), Dave Min (D-CA-47), Jimmy Panetta (D-CA-19), Brad Sherman (D-CA-32), and Mike Thompson (D-CA-04).
