Arevon is a U.S. energy leader committed to powering America with affordable, reliable, and secure homegrown energy. Headquartered in Scottsdale, Arizona, and with a regional office in New York City, the company's experienced and dedicated team develops, finances, builds, owns, and operates renewable energy projects nationwide. title: Construction Growth Hasn't Disappeared. It Has Moved - GroundBreak Carolinas
description:
Data Centers: The Industry’s Most Visible Growth Engine Perhaps no construction market better illustrates the changing economy than data centers.
FMI forecasts office construction spending will increase 13.7% in 2026, but that headline masks two dramatically different trends.
FMI forecasts power construction spending will increase 4.9% in 2026, followed by stronger growth of 8.1% in 2027.
The Bottom Line: Construction Growth Hasn’t Disappeared.
The companies that answer those questions effectively will be better positioned to navigate the current slowdown—and capitalize on the next cycle of construction growth.
text:
The U.S. construction industry is entering a period of increasingly uneven growth. While overall construction spending is declining, several important market segments continue to expand, creating a widening divide between contractors positioned for growth and those facing a more challenging environment.

According to FMI’s latest 2026 North American Engineering and Construction Outlook, total U.S. construction spending is projected to reach $2.167 trillion this year, a 3.4% decline from 2025. That represents a significant downward revision from the firm’s previous forecast of a 1.3% decline.

The numbers tell an important story, but perhaps not the most important one.

The construction market is not simply shrinking. It is shifting.

Of the 19 construction segments tracked by FMI, only four are expected to grow in 2026. Five are relatively stable, while 10 are declining. Manufacturing construction, one of the industry’s strongest growth engines in recent years, has weakened significantly. Residential construction is also under pressure.

Meanwhile, data centers and power infrastructure continue to attract substantial investment.

For contractors, developers, suppliers and other construction industry stakeholders across the Carolinas, understanding where growth remains—and why—is becoming increasingly important.

A $2.17 Trillion Industry Moving in Different Directions

The construction industry’s current challenges reflect a combination of economic pressures, elevated borrowing costs, changing investment priorities and uncertainty surrounding public policy.

Residential construction has been particularly vulnerable.

FMI projects residential construction spending will decline 5.9% in 2026 to approximately $881 billion. Single-family construction is expected to fall 5.8%, while multifamily construction is projected to decline a more modest 1.4%.

Higher financing costs, affordability challenges and cautious consumer sentiment continue to weigh on housing investment.

Manufacturing construction has also lost momentum after several years of extraordinary investment associated with semiconductor production, electric vehicles, batteries and domestic industrial expansion.

The slowdown does not necessarily signal the end of America’s manufacturing investment cycle. Rather, it reflects a transition from the initial wave of major project announcements and construction starts toward a more selective investment environment.

For contractors that expanded capacity to serve these markets, the implications are significant.

The next phase of growth may require a different mix of customers, project types and capabilities.

Data Centers: The Industry’s Most Visible Growth Engine

Perhaps no construction market better illustrates the changing economy than data centers.

FMI forecasts office construction spending will increase 13.7% in 2026, but that headline masks two dramatically different trends.

Traditional office construction is projected to decline approximately 11%, while data center investment continues to accelerate.

According to the Census Bureau’s newly established data center construction category, spending reached an annualized pace of approximately $75 billion in July.

This growth is being driven by the extraordinary infrastructure requirements associated with artificial intelligence, cloud computing and the continued expansion of digital services.

But the opportunity extends well beyond the data center building itself.

These facilities require substantial investments in electrical distribution, substations, backup power, cooling systems, controls, automation and telecommunications infrastructure.

They also create demand for the manufacturing facilities that produce the equipment necessary to support this expanding digital infrastructure.

In many respects, data center construction is becoming an economic ecosystem rather than simply another commercial building category.

For contractors in the Carolinas, this creates opportunities across multiple disciplines, particularly electrical, mechanical, civil, industrial and specialty construction.

It also introduces new challenges.

Data center owners and developers increasingly expect contractors to demonstrate capabilities in accelerated project delivery, prefabrication, supply chain management, workforce planning and schedule certainty.

Winning in this market requires more than construction capacity. It requires the ability to manage complexity at scale.

Power Infrastructure: A Long-Term Construction Opportunity

While data centers are generating significant attention, power infrastructure may represent an even more consequential long-term construction opportunity.

FMI forecasts power construction spending will increase 4.9% in 2026, followed by stronger growth of 8.1% in 2027.

By 2030, annual power construction spending is projected to reach approximately $273 billion.

Several structural forces are driving this investment.

Electric utilities must accommodate rising electricity demand, replace aging infrastructure, improve grid reliability and connect new generation capacity.

The rapid expansion of data centers adds another layer of urgency.

Large industrial facilities, advanced manufacturing operations and the broader electrification of the economy are also contributing to growing demand for electrical infrastructure.

However, the sector faces significant constraints.

Long lead times for transformers, turbines and other critical equipment are delaying projects. Some major electrical equipment now requires procurement commitments years before installation.

These challenges are changing how projects are planned and delivered.

Owners and contractors must coordinate engineering, procurement and construction decisions much earlier in the project lifecycle.

For electrical contractors, industrial construction firms, equipment suppliers and engineering companies, the opportunity extends from major generation and transmission projects to substations, distribution upgrades, controls, automation and ongoing maintenance.

Importantly, these investments are not entirely dependent on a single economic cycle.

They reflect structural changes in how electricity is generated, distributed and consumed.

What This Means for Construction in the Carolinas

North Carolina and South Carolina are particularly well positioned to participate in several of these long-term investment trends.

The region benefits from population growth, a substantial manufacturing base, expanding logistics networks, established utilities and a growing concentration of technology-related investment.

However, these advantages do not guarantee that every construction market—or every contractor—will experience growth.

Several opportunities deserve particular attention.

1. Electrical Infrastructure and Power Delivery

The Carolinas’ growing population, industrial activity and technology investments are increasing the importance of reliable electrical infrastructure.

Opportunities extend beyond large power generation facilities to include substations, transmission and distribution improvements, electrical upgrades and maintenance.

Contractors with strong electrical capabilities, utility relationships and experience working in operating facilities may find opportunities even as other construction categories weaken.

2. Data Centers and Supporting Infrastructure

North Carolina has an established data center presence, while additional opportunities are emerging across the broader Southeast.

The construction opportunity includes not only large-scale facilities but also supporting power, cooling, telecommunications and equipment infrastructure.

For contractors, the ability to participate in this market may depend on specialized technical expertise, relationships with major owners and construction managers, and access to skilled labor.

3. Industrial Modernization and Automation

Although manufacturing construction spending is declining nationally, manufacturers continue to face pressure to improve productivity, reduce operating costs and modernize existing facilities.

This creates an important distinction between new manufacturing construction and investment within existing plants.

Facility upgrades, equipment installation, robotics, industrial automation, electrical modernization and process improvements may create opportunities even when new greenfield manufacturing projects slow.

For contractors serving industrial customers, maintenance and modernization could become increasingly important sources of recurring revenue.

4. Healthcare, Education and Institutional Investment

Healthcare, higher education and other institutional facilities remain important construction markets across the Carolinas.

While these sectors are not immune to financing pressures and budget constraints, demand for facility modernization, renovations, infrastructure improvements and specialized spaces can create opportunities independent of large new construction programs.

Contractors with established institutional relationships and capabilities in occupied-facility construction may be better positioned to capture these opportunities.

5. Renovation, Retrofit and Service

One of the most important strategic implications of a slowing construction market is the potential shift toward work within existing facilities.

Owners may delay major new construction projects while continuing to invest in assets they already operate.

That can create opportunities in electrical and mechanical upgrades, energy efficiency, building automation, maintenance, equipment replacement and facility modernization.

For contractors heavily dependent on new construction, expanding service and retrofit capabilities may provide a more balanced business model.

The Growing Importance of Geographic and Market Selection

National construction forecasts provide valuable direction, but they can also conceal substantial differences between local markets.

The Carolinas illustrate why geographic analysis matters.

Charlotte, Raleigh-Durham, Greenville-Spartanburg, Charleston and the coastal markets each have different economic drivers, customer concentrations and construction demand patterns.

A contractor operating in one market may experience strong demand from utilities, technology companies or institutional owners, while another faces declining activity in residential or traditional commercial construction.

The challenge for construction executives is to move beyond broad industry forecasts and understand the specific investment drivers within their geographic markets.

That requires examining announced capital projects, utility investment plans, industrial expansions, public infrastructure programs, institutional capital budgets and customer relationships.

It also requires distinguishing between projects that have been announced and those that are funded, permitted and likely to proceed.

In a more selective construction market, the quality of the opportunity pipeline matters as much as its size.

Five Strategic Questions Construction Leaders Should Be Asking

The changing construction outlook raises important questions for executives developing their 2027 business plans.

1. Are we positioned in the markets attracting capital?

Historical market strength does not necessarily indicate future growth. Contractors should evaluate whether their current sector exposure aligns with emerging investment priorities.

2. Are we overly dependent on new construction?

A business model concentrated in large new construction projects may be more vulnerable to financing conditions and investment delays. Service, maintenance, retrofit and modernization work can provide additional sources of revenue.

3. Do we have the capabilities customers will need next?

Growth markets increasingly require specialized technical expertise, sophisticated project delivery, supply chain coordination and advanced construction methods.

4. Are we building relationships early enough?

In sectors such as data centers and power infrastructure, procurement decisions and project team selection may occur long before construction begins. Early engagement with owners, engineers and major construction managers is becoming more important.

5. Are we planning for multiple economic scenarios?

With construction spending weakening and uncertainty surrounding financing, public funding and material costs, contractors should develop plans that account for different levels of market demand.

The objective is not to predict the future perfectly. It is to build an organization capable of responding as conditions change.

Beyond 2026: Preparing for the Next Construction Cycle

FMI’s latest forecast highlights several risks that could influence construction activity in 2027.

These include continued financing pressures, rising project costs, equipment availability and uncertainty surrounding federal infrastructure funding.

At the same time, the longer-term demand for digital infrastructure, electricity, industrial modernization and essential facilities suggests that significant construction opportunities will remain.

The challenge is that these opportunities will not be distributed evenly across sectors, geographies or contractors.

For construction companies, this creates a strategic imperative.

Business development strategies, workforce investments, technical capabilities and customer relationships must evolve with the markets.

Contractors that recognize changing demand early will have more time to develop expertise, establish partnerships and position themselves for the next wave of investment.

Those that rely exclusively on the markets and business models that drove their previous growth may find the transition more difficult.

The Bottom Line: Construction Growth Hasn’t Disappeared. It Has Moved.

A 3.4% decline in national construction spending is a meaningful signal that the industry faces a more challenging operating environment.

But the headline number does not tell the entire story.

The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure, growing electricity demand, industrial modernization and the continuing need to maintain and upgrade existing facilities are reshaping the construction opportunity landscape.

For contractors across North Carolina and South Carolina, the central question is no longer simply whether construction spending will grow.

It is where investment is moving, which customers are making it, and what capabilities will be required to capture it.

The companies that answer those questions effectively will be better positioned to navigate the current slowdown—and capitalize on the next cycle of construction growth.

text:
October 13, 2026 Mactaquac, New Brunswick Natural Resources Canada

The world is changing rapidly. Global trade is upended, wars are ongoing in Europe and the Middle East, artificial intelligence is scaling at speed, and climate change is intensifying. In response, Canada is focused on what we can control: building a prosperous, secure and sustainable Canadian economy. Central to this mission is supplying and controlling our own energy. A reliable, affordable and clean electricity system keeps families’ bills affordable, makes Canadian businesses more competitive and will build a more secure and sustainable Canada for the long term.

That is why, today, the Honourable Tim Hodgson, Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, announced an investment of almost $270 million for clean and reliable energy in New Brunswick. This includes:

A $219-million site development loan from the Canada Infrastructure Bank (CIB) to NB Power for the Mactaquac Life Achievement Project to support technical studies, regulatory reviews, First Nations engagement and planning activities.

Mactaquac Generation Station is New Brunswick’s largest renewable energy asset and NB Power’s largest hydroelectric facility. The 672-megawatt (MW) run-of-river station supplies 30 percent of the province’s renewable energy requirements and 20 percent of its peak electricity demand.

Mactaquac has faced premature concrete deterioration that has affected critical equipment, including turbines and spillway gates. NB Power’s Mactaquac Life Achievement Project is a phased rehabilitation program that will enable the generating station to reach its 100-year lifespan.

$50 million from Natural Resources Canada to NB Power for the Static Synchronous Compensator (STATCOM) project at the Salisbury Terminal to strengthen southern New Brunswick’s electricity system.

The Salisbury Terminal is a high-voltage transmission substation that is key to managing the flow of electricity across New Brunswick’s grid. It will improve grid stability and reliability in southern New Brunswick while supporting the integration of additional renewable energy resources as electricity demand continues to grow.

text:
JOHANNESBURG (AP) — Climate activists picketed outside the African Energy Week conference in Cape Town, South Africa, on Tuesday, calling for an end to new oil and gas exploration across the continent and accusing energy companies of prioritizing profits over people and the environment.

Greenpeace Africa and Extinction Rebellion campaigners challenged efforts to position Africa as a new frontier for fossil fuel development, arguing that further investment would worsen climate change and threaten communities already grappling with its effects.

“Oil companies from overseas have made billions in profits this year alone at the expense of people’s lives, at the expense of ecosystems, at the expense of African lives,” Siya Myeza, a climate and energy campaigner with Greenpeace Africa, told The Associated Press.

Myeza branded the gathering “Africa Exploitation Week,” accusing the industry of driving environmental destruction and poverty. Police removed the protesters, who wore T-shirts bearing the slogan “Make polluters pay.”

The protests come as South Africa seeks to expand oil and gas development to attract investment and bolster energy security. The government presents natural gas as a complement to renewable energy, saying gas-fired plants could provide electricity when wind and solar output drops.

Despite legal setbacks, British energy giant Shell plans to drill up to five deepwater wells in the Northern Cape Ultra Deep block off South Africa’s west coast to explore for and assess oil and gas deposits. The project’s environmental approval has drawn appeals.

Protesters say such plans risk prolonging dependence on fossil fuels at a time when countries should be cutting emissions.

Judy Scott-Goldman, a representative of Extinction Rebellion in Cape Town, acknowledged that renewable energy would feature at the conference but said campaigners opposed promoting new oil and gas exploration.

She said expanding fossil fuel use would run counter to commitments under the Paris climate agreement to reduce emissions.

“We’re here to say we don’t want to see any exploration of oil and gas on this continent,” she told the AP.

She pointed to fires, floods and rising food prices as consequences of climate change, warning that its effects could also drive migration and social unrest.

text:
A surge in lithium production and the rise of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries are shifting demand for battery materials, while graphite, nickel and cobalt remain essential amid concentrated global supply chains and volatile prices

Battery production has expanded rapidly since 2020, driving up demand for the minerals and refined materials used in electric vehicles and energy storage. But the growth has been uneven, as changing battery chemistries reshape which materials manufacturers need and in what quantities.

Lithium production surged from 395 kilotonnes in 2020 to 1,500 kilotonnes in 2025, nearly quadrupling in five years, according to Benchmark Intelligence. Lithium remains essential across the major lithium-ion battery chemistries. Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries increased their share of the global electric-vehicle battery market from 19% in 2020 to 55% in 2025, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA). Unlike nickel-based chemistries, LFP batteries do not require nickel or cobalt, shifting demand towards other materials.

Growing demand

As LFP adoption expands, demand for phosphate-based battery materials is growing. Purified phosphoric acid production increased by 41% between 2020 and 2025, according to Benchmark Intelligence. China has played a central role in this transition: in 2024, it accounted for more than 98% of global LFP cathode-material and battery-cell production, according to the IEA's Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2025.

Although nickel-based batteries have lost market share, nickel production rose from 2,500 kilotonnes in 2020 to 3,600 kilotonnes in 2025, reflecting continued demand for chemistries that offer higher energy density and support longer driving ranges. Cobalt and high-purity manganese sulphate production also more than doubled over the period, according to Benchmark Intelligence. Their trajectories show how the expansion of battery manufacturing can sustain demand for established materials even as the industry's chemistry mix changes.

Graphite is a key component of lithium-ion battery anodes, making it essential to both LFP and nickel-based batteries. Global graphite consumption reached approximately 4.8 million tonnes in 2024, an 8% increase from the previous year, with batteries accounting for most of the growth, according to the IEA's Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2025. Supply is highly concentrated: China produced an estimated 78% of the world's natural graphite in 2024, according to the US Geological Survey. Graphite therefore remains a critical part of the battery supply chain.

Supply-chain risks

Rapid production growth has not eliminated supply-chain risks. In 2024, the three leading countries accounted for 93% of global graphite mining and 99% of graphite refining, according to the IEA. Meanwhile, expanding mineral supplies have put downward pressure on prices: lithium prices fell by more than 80% from their 2023 level through the period covered by the IEA's 2025 outlook. The challenge for the battery industry is increasingly about securing reliable, diversified supplies of the right materials as technologies and demand evolve.

name: EPA
title: Budget 2027: Energy and Infrastructure Expenditure - WILLIAM FRY
description:
The Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment (DCEE) has secured €1.28 billion in Budget 2027 to support Ireland’s energy transition, climate action objectives and environmental programmes.
While much attention has focused on affordability measures for households and businesses, Budget 2027 also contains several announcements of particular significance for the energy and infrastructure sector.
While aimed at reducing energy costs and improving energy efficiency, these measures also contribute to the wider decarbonisation of Ireland’s energy system.
Budget 2027 combines continued investment in renewable energy and decarbonisation initiatives with additional resourcing for the regulatory and administrative frameworks that underpin infrastructure development.
For a full briefing of the measures announced across Budget 2027, please see William Fry’s Budget 2027 update here.
text:
The Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment (DCEE) has secured €1.28 billion in Budget 2027 to support Ireland’s energy transition, climate action objectives and environmental programmes.

While much attention has focused on affordability measures for households and businesses, Budget 2027 also contains several announcements of particular significance for the energy and infrastructure sector. The Government repeatedly identifies accelerating infrastructure delivery, streamlining regulatory processes and prioritising critical energy infrastructure as key objectives for 2027, indicating that the focus is increasingly shifting from policy formulation to implementation. Additional investment in renewable energy, district heating, biomethane, regulatory capacity and environmental administration indicates a growing recognition that Ireland’s energy transition will depend not only on policy ambition, but on the State’s ability to facilitate infrastructure development and regulatory decision-making at pace.

Energy Transformation Remains the Central Priority

The most significant allocation in Budget 2027 is the provision of more than €950 million to DCEE’s ‘Energy Transformation’ programme, which intends to support the deployment of renewable energy and the delivery of energy efficiency measures across the built environment. This figure includes a record €655 million in capital funding allocated to SEAI home and community energy upgrade schemes, including enhanced supports for solar PV, battery storage, insulation measures and a new boiler scrappage scheme. While aimed at reducing energy costs and improving energy efficiency, these measures also contribute to the wider decarbonisation of Ireland’s energy system. Further, Budget 2027 seeks to encourage greater participation in microgeneration and rooftop solar by increasing the income tax disregard for households exporting electricity to the grid, from €400 to €600.

Biomethane Continues to Gather Momentum

The most notable sector-specific announcement is the confirmation that a €200 million capital grant scheme for biomethane development will open in the coming days. DCEE’s Budget 2027 press release notes that seven anaerobic digestion plants have recently been completed or are under construction, highlighting the growing role of biomethane in Ireland’s long-term energy infrastructure.

Biomethane has increasingly been identified as a key renewable gas solution in Ireland’s decarbonisation strategy, particularly for sectors where full electrification may not be feasible. As discussed in our previous article, Biomethane Production Facilities in Ireland, the development of a large-scale biomethane industry will require not only financial support but also effective planning, environmental and regulatory frameworks capable of facilitating project delivery. The announcement of a dedicated €200 million capital support scheme therefore represents a significant indication of the Government’s commitment to advancing the sector beyond the policy stage and towards project delivery. This investment is also significant in the context of the proposed Renewable Heat Obligation (RHO). Once introduced, the RHO will require suppliers of fossil fuels used for heating to ensure that a proportion of the energy they supply is from a renewable source. The RHO Bill is now at an advanced stage of priority drafting; however, the European Commission has found the Bill’s proposed multiplier for indigenously produced biomethane to be incompatible with EU law. Further detail is set out in our previous article, Ireland’s Renewable Heat Obligation.

Continued Support for District Heating Infrastructure

District heating systems generate heat at a central source and distribute it as hot water through a network of insulated pipes, providing space heating and hot water to homes and businesses. DCEE confirmed that, in addition to the operational district heating network in Tallaght, Dublin, nine projects have received pre-construction funding through the Climate Action Fund. DCEE also announced that €50 to €100 million has been allocated from the Infrastructure Climate and Nature Fund for future district heating projects, with the district heating capital funding scheme expected to open during the first quarter of 2027.

Although the district heating sector is still nascent, it is expected to play an increasingly important role in Ireland’s energy transition with the repeated allocation of public funding demonstrating an ongoing commitment to establishing a pipeline of viable projects. For developers, investors and local authorities, the continued availability of funding is a promising sign that projects will continue to progress from concept stage towards construction and operation.

Increased Resourcing for Maritime and Environmental Regulation

Beyond direct project funding, Budget 2027 also acknowledges the role of regulatory capacity in delivering major infrastructure projects. The allocation of more than €10 million to the Maritime Area Regulatory Authority (MARA) is intended to support the continued development of Ireland’s maritime planning and consenting framework, including administrative reforms aimed at improving the efficiency of decision-making processes. This is particularly significant for the offshore renewable energy sector, where regulatory certainty and timely consenting remain key considerations for developers and investors.

There are set to be further benefits to the offshore renewable energy sector in the form of continued investment in maritime data and mapping infrastructure. The ‘Budget 2027 Expenditure Report’ confirms ongoing support for the INFOMAR marine mapping programme and associated maritime data collection initiatives, which provide important baseline information for offshore development. These investments contribute to the technical and regulatory foundations required to support the delivery of large-scale offshore renewable energy projects.

Additional funding has been allocated to the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), with the DCEE highlighting ongoing reforms aimed at improving the efficiency and predictability of licensing processes while maintaining environmental standards. Environmental licences and approvals are often critical path items for project delivery, and greater certainty around regulatory timelines can play an important role in project planning, financing and risk allocation.

A Focus on Delivery

Ireland’s ambitious climate and energy objectives are well publicised. To achieve these aims, the State is focusing its efforts on ensuring that the infrastructure required to meet those objectives can be delivered efficiently and at scale. Budget 2027 combines continued investment in renewable energy and decarbonisation initiatives with additional resourcing for the regulatory and administrative frameworks that underpin infrastructure development.

This funding should not be viewed in isolation and is supported by a pipeline of upcoming new legislation. The Government’s Autumn 2026 Legislation Programme includes several bills that will provide the legal framework for these investments. The Heat (Networks and Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill will establish a regulatory model for district heating, the Offshore Transmission Asset Investment Fund Bill will underpin a €2 billion State equity investment in EirGrid to support offshore grid infrastructure, and the Renewable Heat Obligation Bill has been designated for priority publication (see our recent article, Energy Legislation: What’s Moving This Autumn?). Taken together, these measures demonstrate an increasing focus on implementation and project delivery as the next phase of Ireland’s energy transition.

For a full briefing of the measures announced across Budget 2027, please see William Fry’s Budget 2027 update here.

Contributed by Kate Lyttle

text:
Renewable energy developer Zelestra has secured $350 million in green financing for its 203 MW Reclamation Solar project in Gibson County, Indiana.

Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce (CIBC), BBVA, and Societe Generale provided the financing.

The project is backed by a long-term power purchase agreement with Meta and is expected to become operational by the end of 2027. The Reclamation Solar project is under construction on land previously used for coal mining operations in southwestern Indiana. It is expected to support approximately 200 jobs during peak construction.

Sybil Milo Cioffi, Zelestra’s US CFO, said: “Passing $1 billion in U.S. project financing this year is a milestone we are pleased to share with our lenders and our customers. Reclamation is a major project that will deliver many benefits to our customer, and to the wider community. We are pleased that CIBC, BBVA and Societe Generale are backing our ambition. These partnerships enable us to keep building at the pace this market needs.”

With this transaction, Zelestra’s total project financing raised in the U.S. in 2026 has reached $1.14 billion. According to the company, the financing will support the construction of more than 800 MW of new solar capacity across the country.

In August 2026, the company closed $181 million in green project financing for its 136 MW Skull Creek solar project in Anderson County, Texas, which is under construction and is expected to begin commercial operations by the end of 2027.

Zelestra also secured a $600 million green financing credit facility in March with Société Générale and HSBC for the 252 MW Echols Gove project in Lamar County and the 187 MW Cedar Range solar project in Hopkins County in Texas.

Zelestra is expanding its U.S. operations to meet growing demand for renewable energy from hyperscalers and corporate customers. Headquartered in Arlington, Virginia, the company has a development pipeline of approximately 16 GW across major U.S. markets.

text:
The Climate Action Tracker has just published what it views as two extremely disappointing country analyses: the US ("Critically insufficient"), and Canada ("Highly insufficient"), as both governments roll back climate policies.

The Trump Administration continues its unprecedented rollback of climate mitigation measures (see list below). The CAT still rates the US climate agenda under the Trump Administration as "Critically insufficient".

Prime Minister Mark Carney admits that the country will miss its 2030 and 2035 targets under his plan. Canada continues with a "Highly insufficient" overall rating, but the CAT has downgraded its sub-rating for Canada's Policies & action to "Critically insufficient".

"The Trump Administration continues to escalate the most aggressive, comprehensive, and consequential rollback of climate mitigation targets, policies, and funding that the Climate Action Tracker has ever analysed," said CAT US country lead Finn Hossfeld of CAT partner organisation NewClimate Institute.

In neighbouring Canada, the CAT projected that implemented and planned policies two years ago would cut emissions by 30% below 2005 levels by 2030. With many of those policies now removed or weakened, planned policies are now projected to cut emissions by less than half, to 14%.

"What is shocking to us is the true extent to which Prime Minister Carney has rolled back climate policies, largely in favour of the fossil fuel industry," said Bill Hare, CEO of Climate Analytics, a CAT partner.

"This Carney climate carnage, while not quite as bad as Trump's, is rapidly heading in the same direction, despite the country being hit by record wildfires and other devastating climate impacts. Based on this assessment, as it presently stands, if the European Union were to import the Canadian policies it would further undermine the EU‘s own climate action," said Hare.

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government has dismantled or weakened many of the climate policies introduced and implemented by the previous Liberal government. Canada has:

Removed the consumer carbon price

description:
For the South Central Regional Transit District (SCRTD) in southern New Mexico, the answer has been to think beyond the bus.
Our approach combines zero-emission vehicles, renewable energy generation, charging infrastructure, facility modernization and expanding regional transit service into a single strategy.
That creates a direct relationship between the energy SCRTD produces and the transportation service we deliver.
Sunlight collected at a transit facility in southern New Mexico can ultimately help power the vehicles moving passengers throughout the region.
Growth is driving the transformation SCRTD's investments are occurring at the same time that demand for regional transit is increasing substantially.
text:
Public transit agencies across the country are confronting the same fundamental question: How do we transition to cleaner transportation while continuing to provide reliable, affordable service to the communities that depend on us?

For the South Central Regional Transit District (SCRTD) in southern New Mexico, the answer has been to think beyond the bus.

Our approach combines zero-emission vehicles, renewable energy generation, charging infrastructure, facility modernization and expanding regional transit service into a single strategy. At the center of that effort is the SCRTD's Sunland Park Mobility and Energy Hub, a facility that is becoming the foundation for SCRTD's transition toward a cleaner and more resilient regional transportation system.

What makes the project especially significant is where it is happening.

SCRTD is not a major metropolitan transit authority with thousands of employees and a multibillion-dollar capital program. We serve communities throughout southern New Mexico and provide regional connections into El Paso, Texas. Our routes connect rural communities, small cities, employment centers, colleges, medical services, downtown destinations and major transfer points across a large geographic area.

Yet many of the challenges facing our region are the same challenges facing the largest transit systems in the country: rising transportation demand, air quality, energy costs, fleet modernization and the need to build infrastructure capable of supporting the next generation of public transportation.

Building the infrastructure before expanding the fleet

The transition to zero-emission transit involves much more than purchasing an electric bus.

Transit agencies must address charging capacity, electrical infrastructure, utility coordination, maintenance requirements, workforce training, facility design and operational planning. For agencies operating long regional routes, vehicle range and charging strategy become even more important.

SCRTD recognized early that fleet electrification had to be accompanied by a broader energy strategy.

In 2025, the district acquired and opened its new headquarters and operations facility in Sunland Park, N.M. The approximately 7.5-acre property now serves as the operational center for a growing regional transit network and provides SCRTD with something it had never previously possessed: sufficient space to integrate transportation operations with energy infrastructure.

Rather than viewing the project simply as a solar installation, SCRTD views it as transportation infrastructure.

The solar array, energy-storage system and charging equipment are being developed as an integrated system capable of supporting approximately 12 BEBs and electric vehicles while also supplying energy to district facilities.

That creates a direct relationship between the energy SCRTD produces and the transportation service we deliver.

Sunlight collected at a transit facility in southern New Mexico can ultimately help power the vehicles moving passengers throughout the region.

Zero emissions where air quality matters

The environmental benefits are particularly important in the southern portion of SCRTD's service area.

Sunland Park and Santa Teresa, Texas, are located within the greater El Paso metropolitan area, a region facing significant air-quality challenges. Transportation investments that reduce tailpipe emissions therefore have benefits extending beyond the transit agency itself.

Every diesel vehicle that can eventually be replaced by a zero-emission vehicle represents another opportunity to reduce transportation-related emissions in communities where air quality is already a public concern.

SCRTD currently operates BEBs and electric support and passenger vehicles and continues to expand its clean-vehicle fleet.

The district is also pursuing additional battery-electric vehicles for new mobility programs, including complementary ADA paratransit service serving Sunland Park and Santa Teresa.

This is important because zero-emission transportation should not be limited to traditional fixed-route buses.

The same clean-energy strategy can support smaller vehicles providing paratransit, microtransit and community mobility services. For SCRTD, electrification is increasingly becoming a systemwide strategy rather than an isolated fleet demonstration.

Growth is driving the transformation

SCRTD's investments are occurring at the same time that demand for regional transit is increasing substantially.

The district began operating regional transit service in 2016. Since then, ridership has grown dramatically, as SCRTD has expanded its network and strengthened connections between communities in Doña Ana, Sierra and Otero counties in New Mexico and El Paso County in Texas.

For fiscal year 2026, SCRTD is projecting approximately 204,785 passenger trips, representing approximately 24% annual ridership growth.

Over the district's first decade, ridership growth has exceeded 900%.

Those numbers have changed the conversation about public transportation in southern New Mexico.

What began as a relatively small regional transit operation is becoming an increasingly important component of the region's transportation infrastructure.

Our passengers include employees traveling to jobs, students traveling to colleges and universities, seniors reaching medical appointments, residents accessing government and commercial services and passengers connecting to the larger Sun Metro transit network in El Paso.

The district's Yellow, Silver and Purple routes, for example, help connect communities in Sunland Park, Santa Teresa and Anthony with destinations and transit connections in El Paso.

As ridership grows, SCRTD is simultaneously preparing to introduce complementary ADA paratransit and microtransit services and to expand transportation serving one of New Mexico's most important employment centers, the Santa Teresa Industrial Park.

That means our clean-energy investments are not being made for a static transit network. They are being built for a system that is continuing to grow.

A different model for smaller transit agencies

There is a misconception that major transit innovation occurs only in the nation's largest metropolitan areas.

Smaller transit agencies can be exceptional laboratories for innovation because they often have the ability to connect projects that would otherwise be developed independently.

At SCRTD, fleet planning, renewable energy, facility development, passenger service and regional economic development are increasingly part of the same strategy:

The Sunland Park project illustrates that philosophy.

A traditional transit facility stores and maintains buses.

A mobility and energy hub can do much more.

It can produce electricity. It can store energy. It can charge buses and smaller electric vehicles. It can support maintenance and workforce training. It can serve as the operational center for fixed-route transit, paratransit and emerging mobility services.

And it can demonstrate to the community that investments in public transportation can also be investments in infrastructure resilience and cleaner air.

Preparing the workforce

The transition also requires investment in people.

Battery-electric vehicles introduce new technologies for operators, mechanics, supervisors and facility personnel. Charging infrastructure requires employees to understand equipment and operating procedures that were not part of conventional diesel transit operations.

SCRTD has therefore made workforce development an important component of its zero-emission transition.

Drivers and maintenance employees are being trained on BEB systems, and specialized manufacturer training is helping mechanics understand the charging and electrical systems associated with the fleet.

The objective is not simply to acquire new technology. It is to develop the institutional knowledge necessary to operate that technology successfully for decades.

That may ultimately be one of the most important lessons for agencies considering similar projects: the transition to zero emissions is as much an organizational transformation as it is a technological one.

Looking toward the next decade

The Sunland Park Mobility and Energy Hub is only one component of SCRTD's long-term capital program.

The district is also advancing development of a future transit facility on the East Mesa of Las Cruces, N.M., that is planned to accommodate buses, charging infrastructure, light maintenance operations and future service expansion.

Additional buses are being added to the fleet, including vehicles supported through competitive federal transit grants.

Together, these investments are creating a network of facilities and vehicles designed around the transportation needs SCRTD expects to face during its second decade of service.

Our experience in southern New Mexico demonstrates that zero-emission transit does not need to be limited to large urban systems.

Rural and regional transit agencies can participate in the clean-energy transition as well.

But doing so requires looking beyond individual vehicle purchases and asking a larger question: What transportation and energy infrastructure will our communities need 10 or 20 years from now?

For SCRTD, that question has led us from operating buses to building a mobility and energy system.

The solar panels rising above our Sunland Park facility are therefore more than another capital improvement.

They represent where the district is headed next—a regional transit system where mobility, renewable energy, clean air and community connectivity increasingly work together.

description:

text:
Realising the wider benefits

Despite the scale of the REIPPPP pipeline, local manufacturing has struggled to reach sufficient scale and competitiveness. Structural factors – including inconsistent procurement pipelines, global competition, and the timing mismatch between project delivery and industrial investment – have typically limited the growth of domestic supply chains. These are the challenges the SAREM initiative is designed to address.

This experience mirrors debates in the UK’s offshore wind sector, particularly for fixed-bottom wind. The UK has been highly successful in rapidly deploying large-scale offshore wind using global supply chains, achieving world-leading capacity deployment. Yet this speed has often come at the expense of local industrial capability, with supply chains remaining internationally dispersed and domestic manufacturing opportunities not always fully captured.

In the South African context, SAREM makes clear that the energy transition is not only a procurement challenge, but an industrialisation opportunity. The risk is that the jobs, skills, local manufacturing, supplier development and innovation potential of this investment are diluted if delivery becomes a race to import equipment from established global players, including China. The alternative is not protectionism, but a pragmatic view of where South Africa can build competitive capability across renewable energy and battery storage value chains, supported by clear demand signals, skills development, emerging supplier participation and targeted industrial policy. That vision needs to sit at the centre of the transmission and generation build-out, so that the energy transition creates long-term structural benefits for people, businesses and the domestic economy. This is particularly relevant in South Africa given its vast metals and critical minerals deposits – promising an opportunity for the whole country to finally benefit from national resources.

Recent reports of Chinese backing for a potential R2.2 trillion energy expansion programme underline the scale of international interest in South Africa’s transition. If realised, such investment could bring much-needed capital, technology and delivery capacity; but its long-term value will depend on whether it strengthens local manufacturing, skills and supply chains rather than simply accelerating imports. The question, therefore, is not whether South Africa should welcome international partners. It should. The question is how those partnerships are structured so that external capital and technology help build domestic capability over time.

The list of challenges related to this promise and potential, is long. How to expand domestic renewable energy industrial capacity and capability. How to develop a workforce with the skills for each stage of that industrial supply chain and operations. How to develop local strengths in energy innovation and research. And how to make an inclusive shift of South Africa’s electricity supply industry from a centralised, carbon-intensive model to a decentralised, low-carbon structure.

Each of these goals supports the others, requiring an orchestration of effort to unlock the energy transition’s greatest potential.

Renewables, market signalsand employment growth

The orchestration question is not unique to South Africa. Indeed, the parallels between the UK and South Africa continue as both countries enter the next phase of their energy transition investments. In the UK floating offshore wind presents an opportunity to do things differently. The UK is actively exploring how to capture greater industrial value, with projections suggesting floating wind could support up to 97,000 jobs and contribute £47 billion to the economy by 2050 if supported effectively (according to the Floating Offshore Wind Taskforce).

South Africa’s Independent Transmission Programme (ITP) offers a similar moment of opportunity. Designed as a flagship public–private partnership to deliver over 14,000km of new transmission infrastructure, the programme is intended not only to unlock generation capacity but also to drive investment, innovation and industrial development., If a programmatic, strategic approach is taken transmission infrastructure with long-term commitment, standardised components and repeatable delivery methods can be developed, providing a stronger foundation for building local supply.

Critically, the challenge is not unique to South Africa or the UK. Globally, energy transition programmes are grappling with how to balance pace, cost and industrial value. The fundamental constraint is timing. Developers cannot place orders until projects reach financial close, while manufacturers need early visibility of demand to invest in facilities, skills and supply chains. By the time procurement signals are clear, it is often too late to localise production at scale.

The coordination factor

Addressing this requires a new ethos and new models of coordination. In the UK, initiatives such as the Strategic Investment Model (SIM) (an industry-led, collaborative framework initially developed by the Scottish Offshore Wind Energy Council (SOWEC) to coordinate infrastructure and supply chain funding and developed with Arup) have demonstrated how structured collaboration between government, developers and the supply chain can unlock investment confidence and accelerate industrial readiness. By aligning project pipelines with supply chain investment decisions, SIM has helped progress dozens of infrastructure and manufacturing projects representing billions in potential investment.

Applying similar approaches to South Africa’s ITP could enable the programme to fulfil its industrialisation potential. Coordinated planning, clear long-term pipelines, and early engagement with manufacturers will be essential to avoid repeating the challenges seen in generation.

There are encouraging UK precedents for this. In floating offshore wind, the Floating Offshore Wind Manufacturing Investment Scheme (FLOWMIS) has shown how targeted public funding can give ports and manufacturers the confidence to invest ahead of demand. Arup supported the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) as technical advisor, helping to assess which projects could genuinely strengthen the UK’s industrial base.

In Scotland, the Strategic Investment Model developed with SOWEC took this further by creating a shared view of the infrastructure and supply-chain investments needed to support the offshore wind pipeline. That work helped bring forward a portfolio of port, cable and manufacturing opportunities worth several billion pounds, including projects at Kishorn, Hunterston, Nigg and Scapa. The same logic can be seen in earlier manufacturing investments such as Siemens Gamesa’s Hull blade factory, where early confidence in the UK offshore wind market helped anchor a major industrial facility that has since created more than a thousand jobs and continued to expand. The lesson is not that these models can simply be copied, but that clear pipelines, credible coordination and early technical confidence can turn infrastructure ambition into real industrial commitments.

title: Stellantis CEO sees eventual US EV shift, says auto industry becoming more regional
description: PARIS, Oct 13 (Reuters) - The US auto market will eventually embrace electrification despite a slow uptake of electric vehicles so far, Stellantis CEO Antonio Filosa said on Tuesday, predicting
text:
Antonio Filosa, CEO of Stellantis, gestures as he speaks during the Paris Automotive Summit as part of the 2026 Paris Auto Show in Paris, France, October 13, 2026. REUTERS/Benoit Tessier

PARIS, Oct 13 (Reuters) - The US auto market will eventually embrace electrification despite a slow uptake of electric vehicles so far, Stellantis CEO Antonio Filosa said on Tuesday, predicting the shift will happen more slowly than in other regions.

Speaking at an event on the sidelines of the Paris motor show, Filosa said EVs accounted for 7% of US auto sales this year, unchanged from five years ago.

"It has been a bubble driven by regulation. But then, when the administration has decided to deregulate, the consumers have been preferring other powertrains", he said.

For Stellantis, which counts North America among its key markets, interest is growing in the US for range-extender technology in large pickups and SUVs.

It is "not regulation driven, it's customer driven", Filosa said.

Despite the slower pace of adoption, Filosa said he "truly" believed electrification would eventually take hold in the US.

"The level of magnitude and the speed of transition is going to be lower for sure than other regions."

He said Stellantis would be able to draw on lessons learned from Europe's EV rollout as demand develops in North America.

Filosa also said the automotive sector was becoming less global as trade barriers reshape markets.

"The recent trade regimens around the world have triggered the process of regionalisation. So, what was the global industry before, now it's less global and more regional," he said.

As a result, automakers need to focus more closely on local customer preferences and regulations while maintaining global scale, particularly in technology, which is playing an increasingly important role in the industry.

"Techs are important, so it's very important for the companies to adapt to the trend and find a way. Our way is partnerships. So we see so many important partnerships that we can explore," he said.

(Reporting by Giulio Piovaccari and Gilles Guillaume. Editing by Mark Potter)

title: The Senate's Surprisingly Populist Permitting Reform Deal | Washington Monthly
authors: Kainoa Lowman, Richard Kahlenberg, Lief Lin, Ralph Nader, Jonathan Alter, Anne Kim, Daniel A. Hanley, Arnav Rao, Gillen Tener Martin
description:
America needs a massive expansion of its electrical grid—particularly long-distance transmission lines connecting remote clean generation sites to population centers.
They earn more reliable returns on smaller, piecemeal upgrades within their own service areas, while larger transmission projects require costly coordination with neighboring utilities.
Long-distance lines also threaten the profits of utilities that own power plants by exposing them to competition from cheaper electricity elsewhere.
Local transmission projects appeal to utilities partly because many fall outside state or federal regulators’ purview.
Together, these competition and oversight provisions would squeeze utilities towards investing in long-distance transmission.
text:
In September, after months of negotiations and to much fanfare, a bipartisan group of senators introduced a major package of energy reforms. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) has been enthusiastically championed by luminaries of the “Abundance” movement, since parts of the bill would ease regulatory bottlenecks that hinder new energy projects. Economic populists on the left have not embraced the bill in the same way, though they should. BAAJA would take meaningful steps to prevent unpopular corporate interests—namely, utility companies—from hindering the transition to cheaper, cleaner energy sources.

America’s flimsy electrical grid is the top constraint on clean energy expansion. To avoid overwhelming the strained system, developers must complete complex grid-impact assessments for projects they propose. This study process takes three to five years on average and has created a backlog of over 8,000 proposed projects—most of them renewable—waiting to connect to the grid. Even after years of waiting, developers often discover their projects require expensive upgrades to the wider grid, not just a simple connecting line. Faced with exorbitant costs, many abandon their projects altogether.

America needs a massive expansion of its electrical grid—particularly long-distance transmission lines connecting remote clean generation sites to population centers. But utilities are averse to building these kinds of lines. They earn more reliable returns on smaller, piecemeal upgrades within their own service areas, while larger transmission projects require costly coordination with neighboring utilities. Long-distance lines also threaten the profits of utilities that own power plants by exposing them to competition from cheaper electricity elsewhere. Consumers ultimately pay the price through wasteful utility spending on upgrades that do little to strengthen the grid, and high electricity bills that competition would help bring down.

BAAJA would jumpstart the long-distance transmission buildout in a couple of ways. First, the bill makes it easier for private “merchant” transmission developers to build these lines. Today, merchant projects are rare because developers struggle to secure private financing and obtain regulatory approval from multiple jurisdictions that interstate lines cross, often amid local opposition. To ease the financing challenge, the bill allows merchant developers to recover the costs of new lines from ratepayers who stand to benefit—effectively allowing developers to usurp local utilities and do their job for them. As for permitting, the bill empowers the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to approve high-priority interstate transmission lines if states and municipalities don’t do so within a year.

Allowing merchant developers into the market could also spur utilities to build long-distance lines themselves. Today, utilities prefer investing in smaller projects, but “if a big new interregional line comes in and it relieves a ton of congestion and adds a bunch of reliability, the smaller projects they wanted to do are no longer justified” in the eyes of regulators, Aidan Mackenzie, an infrastructure analyst at the Institute for Progress, says. Better for utilities to cooperate on long-distance lines than have developers beat them to it. The bill further facilitates cooperation by mandating new long-distance planning processes based on nationally standardized models.

Another provision discourages utilities from pursuing wasteful local projects in the first place. Local transmission projects appeal to utilities partly because many fall outside state or federal regulators’ purview. BAAJA allows FERC, at a state’s request, to review such projects and penalize utilities for imprudent investments.

Together, these competition and oversight provisions would squeeze utilities towards investing in long-distance transmission. “Essentially, the bill would make it harder for utilities to act on their incentives,” Mackenzie said, adding that it would represent “a pretty big expansion of what federal power over utilities has been.”

To be sure, BAAJA is not a panacea for America’s inadequate grid. As Grayson Flood of Groundwork Collaborative notes, much would depend on how FERC implements and enforces key provisions, and the bill does not deliver the centralized transmission planning and financing authority Flood and other progressives have called for. Still, it is a big step forward—“necessary, but insufficient,” he told me. Preliminary modeling suggests it could shave billions from Americans’ electricity bills and promote renewable power.

But that depends on whether BAAJA’s transmission provisions survive the utility lobby. Some have argued that the very introduction of these reforms reflects a decline in the industry’s political power amidst public outrage over skyrocketing utility bills. But David Pomerantz, Executive Director of the Energy and Policy Institute, told me it would be unwise to write off a well-resourced adversary that has defeated numerous congressional and regulatory efforts to make it easier to build transmission lines in the past. “Electric utility companies will do anything they can to undermine the elements of the BAAJA that seek to encourage regional transmission planning and development that they find threatening to their monopolies,” Pomerantz said.

text:
Africa holds billions of barrels of oil, trillions of cubic metres of gas and produces most of the world’s cobalt and manganese for electric car batteries.

This week, energy ministers, investors and oil executives are meeting in Cape Town for African Energy Week, which runs until October 16. The conference focuses on investment in oil and gas, energy finance and ending energy poverty.

In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera maps where Africa’s oil, gas and critical minerals are found, how its electricity is generated and who still goes without it.

How much oil does Africa have?

Africa holds about 125 billion barrels of proven crude oil reserves, representing 7.2 percent of the global total. Proven reserves are oil that has been discovered and can be extracted commercially with existing technology, but is still in the ground.

Libya and Nigeria account for nearly 70 percent of Africa’s reserves, with 48.4 billion and 36.9 billion barrels, respectively. Algeria ranks third, with 12.2 billion barrels. Angola follows with 7.78 billion barrels, while South Sudan and Egypt hold 3.75 billion and 3.3 billion barrels, respectively.

Nigeria was Africa’s largest oil producer in 2024, accounting for about 23 percent of the continent’s output. Algeria and Angola followed with about 17 percent each, and together the three produced 56 percent of Africa’s oil. The top five producers accounted for more than 80 percent. Africa as a whole produced 7.6 percent of the world’s crude oil, roughly in line with its share of global reserves.

Libya, which holds Africa’s largest proven reserves, ranked only fourth in production. Italy’s Eni, France’s TotalEnergies and Spain’s Repsol are among the foreign companies operating in the country, where political disputes and blockades have repeatedly disrupted output.

Where are Africa’s natural gas reserves?

Africa held almost 18 trillion cubic metres of proven natural gas reserves at the end of 2023.

Nigeria and Algeria hold about 58 percent of the total, followed by Mozambique with 2.84 trillion cubic metres, Egypt with 2.21 trillion and Libya with 1.51 trillion.

Algeria and Nigeria are also among Africa’s leading gas exporters, while much of Mozambique’s reserves, discovered offshore in the 2010s, remain largely undeveloped.

Where do the critical minerals come from?

The African continent supplies a large share of the minerals used in electric vehicles, batteries and renewable energy technologies.

In 2025, African countries accounted for 71.2 percent of global cobalt production and 72.4 percent of manganese production.

Cobalt is used in rechargeable batteries. Manganese is mainly used to strengthen steel, but it is also used in some electric vehicle batteries and in batteries that store renewable energy.

The Democratic Republic of the Congo produces nearly 70 percent of the world’s cobalt. Some of it is dug by hand by artisanal miners, and Amnesty International has documented dangerous and often deadly conditions in some of the country’s mines.

South Africa produces nearly 38 percent of global manganese, followed by Gabon with nearly 25 percent. Together with Ghana, the three countries account for 72.4 percent of global production.

Zimbabwe, Africa’s largest lithium producer, accounted for 9.6 percent of global production in 2025. Lithium is used in rechargeable batteries that power electric vehicles and store electricity from solar and wind.

Madagascar, Mozambique and Tanzania produced a combined 222,000 tonnes of natural graphite in 2025, or 11.9 percent of the global total. Graphite is used in the anodes of most lithium-ion batteries, the negative electrodes that store and release energy, as well as in steel manufacturing, lubricants and pencils.

How many African countries produce electricity from renewables?

Renewable energy accounted for all electricity generated in Ethiopia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2024. Uganda, Namibia and Eswatini each generated more than 96 percent from renewables, mostly hydropower.

At the other end, renewables made up less than 5 percent in Algeria, Libya, Niger and Tunisia, which rely mainly on gas or oil.

Ethiopia’s electricity comes mostly from hydropower, led by the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Blue Nile, Africa’s largest hydroelectric project. The dam began generating power in 2022 and was officially inaugurated in September 2025.

Where do people have access to electricity?

In 2024, six African countries reported universal electricity access: Algeria, Egypt, Mauritius, Morocco, Seychelles and Tunisia. Together, they are home to about 215 million people, or roughly 14 percent of Africa’s population.

Elsewhere, access varies widely. In South Sudan, only 5.4 percent of people had electricity. The figure was 15.6 percent in Malawi and 22.5 percent in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, even though the DRC generates all its power from renewables.

Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country, had an access rate of 62.5 percent, leaving roughly 85 million people without electricity, the largest number of any country in the world.

In rural areas, where access is far lower than in cities, many families still rely on kerosene lamps, candles or torches to light their homes after dark.

text:
The Trump Administration is restricting access to a federal rural energy program for farmers in another move against renewable energy. But the major change to the Department of Agriculture’s Rural Energy for America Program (REAP) that eliminates upfront funding would make energy efficiency projects and cheaper energy for farmers inaccessible to many of them, analysts say.

The USDA’s new rules, unveiled at the end of September and effective October 16, aim to eliminate taxpayer funding for “unreliable energy sources”, protect farmland from oversized solar arrays, and reduce imported components from adversaries.

“For too long many applicants have prioritized unreliable energy sources and have not fully delivered on their stated goals, as of today that ends,” Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins said.

Apart from cutting red tape, the changes to the REAP protect “productive American farmland from oversized solar developments and ensuring taxpayer-supported energy investments don’t put components from foreign adversaries on American farms,” said Under Secretary for Rural Development, Glen Smith. Related: Black Sea Oil Shipping Insurance Costs Surge to $2.5 Million

“REAP should work for rural America, not foreign supply chains or projects that take good farmland out of production.”

The changes include Secretary Rollins’ direction “to disincentivize solar photovoltaic and wind energy systems on cropland.”

More importantly, projects must be fully built, operational, and should be able to demonstrate the project’s actual documented output, energy savings, costs, and system performance before applying for funding.

Under the previous rules of the program launched in the 2000s, funding could cover up to 50% of the costs of the energy project, and farmers were able to apply for it before construction began.

REAP invested almost $4.8 billion in projects across the country between 2012 and 2025, making it the agency’s second-largest business program, according to USDA-Rural Development.

Since the program was created, over two-thirds of REAP’s grants have gone to districts currently represented by Republicans. The districts receiving the highest total funding are largely clustered in the Midwest, where the majority of projects are also located, the Brookings Institution said in a report last year.

This year, there has been no funding from REAP because USDA halted applications pending the rule review.

The new rule – requiring operational projects with proven energy savings before application – would put energy-saving projects of any kind out of reach for many farmers, according to analysts.

The new rule would also be another hit to farmers who want to cut on utility bills and energy costs, according to the National Sustainable Agriculture Coalition (NSAC). America’s farmers have been reeling from record-high diesel prices and from the Trump Administration’s trade policies.

“For a lot of farmers, that just simply won’t be possible, especially with these times already being so financially uncertain,” Richa Patel, policy specialist at NSAC, told Reuters.

Environmental organizations and farmers’ unions took the U.S. Administration to court over the new rule that significantly restricted access to funding for energy projects.

The Environmental Law & Policy Center (ELPC) and Earthjustice have filed a lawsuit against the USDA challenging USDA’s efforts to write solar energy out of the Renewable Energy for America Program (REAP).

Importantly, the Iowa Farmers Union and other farmers have joined the lawsuit, which argues that “More farmers and rural small businesses who would like to access the benefits of solar energy systems, but who cannot afford the upfront costs of installation without the support of a REAP grant or loan guarantee are also harmed by the policy.”

“As finances get tighter and margins thinner, we cannot pull the rug out from the people who grow our food,” said Alex Beld, Communications Director at RENEW Wisconsin, which is also part of the group of plaintiffs.

“REAP is supposed to help farmers keep their energy costs low. Instead, the USDA has blocked solar, an incredibly affordable source of energy, and made the change retroactive—leaving farmers with bills they were told the government would cover.”

The PJM Interconnection has accepted the first projects under its Expedited Interconnection Track (EIT), including 2.1 GW of power generation and storage capacity developed by Engie North America and LS Power across the PJM market in the United States (PJM Interconnection press release, 08/10/2026).
The selected projects are among the first to benefit from PJM's accelerated interconnection process designed to bring new generation online more rapidly.
The approved portfolio includes 1.7 GW of storage capacity proposed by Engie (two standalone storage projects of 860 MW in Crawford, Pennsylvania, and 800 MW in Morrow, Ohio) and a 455 MW gas-fired power project in Adams, Pennsylvania, proposed by Hunterstown Generation, a subsidiary of LS Power.
The projects were selected because they can be connected to the grid with limited network upgrades and are expected to help address forecast capacity shortages within the PJM region.
The EIT programme was introduced by PJM to accelerate the interconnection of projects capable of reaching commercial operation within a shorter timeframe than projects progressing through the standard queue process.
