text:
Qcells, one of the most prolific solar manufacturers operating in the U.S., is staking a claim on the next generation of solar power.

Laboratory scientists have established that solar panels convert sunlight to electricity with much higher efficiency if traditional silicon cells are paired with layers of perovskites, a type of crystal that can be synthesized with a wide range of ingredients. These constructions have set stunning efficiency records in the lab, but break down far too quickly out in the real world.

A number of startups — including Tandem PV, Oxford PV, and Caelux — have been trying to solve this problem and commercialize these so-called tandem perovskite panels. But none of them are mass producing and selling tandem panels with a commercial warranty akin to conventional solar.

Qcells aims to be among the first to make that leap. Qcells is testing full-size tandem panels in the field and plans to open a gigawatt-scale factory to produce them in 2029, Global Chief Technology Officer Danielle Merfeld told Canary Media.

That means competition is heating up in the race to build large-scale perovskite solar factories, even as the contenders still must prove that their tandem products survive long enough to be commercially viable.

Chinese company GCL said it opened a 1-GW factory last year in Kunshan, near Shanghai; that said, factory developers in China can avail themselves of many types of direct public support that aren’t available to companies in other countries, making it hard to extrapolate lessons about perovskites’ commercial readiness. In the U.S., Tandem PV is targeting 2028 for building a gigawatt-scale factory, CEO Scott Wharton told Canary Media. ​“I think we’ve seen enough on the product side. It’s more you’ve got to raise money,” he said.

Qcells, originally a German firm that was acquired by South Korea’s Hanwha in 2012, has been developing tandem cells since 2016. It opened a pilot R&D line to make tandem prototypes in Germany in 2022, then, in 2024, launched a 40-megawatt pilot line in South Korea that produces full-size tandem panels. That sizing is notable in itself, as the competing perovskite startups are still transitioning from smaller test cells to bigger systems.

Current high-performance solar panels convert the sunlight with around 24% efficiency. That number has been inching higher as manufacturers hone their craft, Merfeld said: Over the last decade, the rate has improved by half a percentage point each year.

Qcells set a tandem efficiency record in 2024, when an independent body confirmed a rate of 28.6% for a standard-size silicon cell layered with perovskites. That’s like gaining eight years of incremental progress, instantly. Conventional panels will have narrowed the gap a bit by 2029, but Merfeld expects another cycle of process improvements once tandem hits mass production.

Should Qcells or any competitors succeed in bringing perovskites to market, that could profoundly accelerate the adoption of solar power, which has already become the top new power source getting built in the U.S. and around the world.

Tandem panels produce more energy in the same size package as conventional panels. That means installers could turn rooftops or fields into more productive clean power plants in the same footprint. Or they could generate the same amount of electricity in a smaller space, with compounded savings on all the non-panel costs, like wiring, auxiliary equipment, land, and labor.

Leapfrogging clean energy hardware is painstaking work fraught with setbacks — just ask anyone hoping to bring solid-state batteries to market, or actually install a small modular nuclear reactor. Silicon Valley has invested billions of dollars in the belief that nimble, venture-backed startups are best suited to invent these new climate solutions, rather than the ossified incumbent energy companies. Qcells proposes a different theory of the case.

“We’re not a startup, unlike a lot of the Western tandem developers,” Merfeld said. ​“We don’t need to raise money. We don’t need to excite investors, except for our own internal owners. We’re only working on commercial scale.”

In other words, setting new records with tiny sample cells might make sense if the goal is to generate headlines and stimulate venture capitalists, but that is a separate pursuit from honing a product for mass manufacturing.

Qcells has spent years studying the ​“killer issues” that degrade silicon cells over time, such as light, heat, and dampness. ​“We have the right muscles to solve those problems,” Merfeld said.

To that end, in July Qcells announced its tandem panel passed testing against the solar panel quality standards set by UL and the International Electrotechnical Commission. The panels had to withstand a barrage of highly calibrated physical stresses and still produce power reliably. Since no tandem panel has actually operated for 20-plus years, these third-party accelerated degradation tests offer a necessary proof point for the banks that will ultimately need to finance installations of the technology.

There’s more to do to keep building that confidence. Qcells declined to share the ingredients it chose for its perovskites, or to share degradation data from early field testing. But Merfeld said the company installed tandem panels at its own test sites over the last year, and is also getting them to potential customers so they can see for themselves how they work. Waiting until 2029 to launch the gigascale factory allows time to convince large buyers of solar panels that they should make the jump to perovskites.

The location of that proposed factory has not been decided yet (though a company presentation in Seoul last week seemed to indicate that Jincheon, South Korea, was the pick). Qcells designed its new, vertically integrated solar factory in Cartersville, Georgia, to easily upgrade to tandem fabrication when the time comes, Merfeld noted.

But Merfeld argued that supportive industrial policy will be a determining factor in where the tandem factory goes. Qcells has previously advocated for domestic manufacturing incentives and trade protections against cheap imports from China-linked firms, to bolster U.S. solar manufacturing as a strategic industry. The company suffered from the absence of such policies in Germany, which let that country’s ​“Solar Valley” get wiped out by competition from state-backed Chinese manufacturers in the early 2010s. (Qcells survived that episode because Hanwha bought it out of bankruptcy for nearly $45 million.)

“We learn by doing,” Merfeld said. ​“If you support the innovation here, you build that cycle that you need to build more and learn more.”

title: 6 leaders on what must happen to solve the new energy equation | World Economic Forum
description:
The convergence of energy infrastructure, digital technologies, advanced manufacturing, storage, mobility and clean fuels can help strengthen energy systems and industrial competitiveness.
Zhang Chao, Co-President, Mingyang Smart Energy “ Energy issues are no longer limited to security, affordability and sustainability.
As energy systems become more complex, the focus must shift beyond expanding generation capacity to building resilient, flexible and integrated power systems that can reliably deliver affordable, clean energy at scale.
” To solve the new energy equation, we must address a critical timeline mismatch: energy infrastructure and grids take five to 10 years to build, while digital and industrial demand can scale in mere months.
” One of the defining challenges of our time is building sustainable energy systems to power a growing, increasingly electrified world.
text:
Energy is increasingly central to economic competitiveness, amid rising demand from artificial intelligence, data centres, electrification and manufacturing.

Energy security is becoming broader and more complex, making innovation and cooperation more critical.

Six co-chairs of the Forum's recent Energy Forum 2026 provide perspectives here on the practical action needed to ensure reliable, sustainable energy while strengthening economic resilience.

The WEF's Energy Forum 2026 in September brought together 150 leaders from businesses, governments, academia and civil society to explore one defining question: how can energy systems meet rapidly growing demand, while also strengthening security, affordability, sustainability and competitiveness in a fast-changing global context?

Four themes stood out from the discussions:

Energy is becoming even more central to economic resilience and competitiveness. Electrification, artificial intelligence, data centres, industrial policy and new manufacturing models are increasing demand for reliable and affordable power.

Energy security is becoming more complex. It now extends beyond fuel supplies to include grids, critical infrastructure, technologies, materials and industrial systems.

Innovation is creating new opportunities for investment and growth. The convergence of energy infrastructure, digital technologies, advanced manufacturing, storage, mobility and clean fuels can help strengthen energy systems and industrial competitiveness.

International cooperation is adapting, not disappearing. Cooperation is becoming more focused on practical areas of shared interest. At the same time, geopolitical uncertainty is pushing governments and businesses to diversify supply chains, strengthen resilience and develop greater strategic independence.

These themes point to a broader conclusion: the next phase of the energy transition will depend on coordinating infrastructure, markets, policy and industrial capacity to build resilient, flexible and integrated energy systems.

In the reflections that follow, the Energy Forum's six co-chairs share their perspectives on the barriers leaders should not underestimate, and the practical action needed to accelerate the transition to more secure, competitive, resilient and sustainable energy systems.

Zhang Chao, Co-President, Mingyang Smart Energy

“

Energy issues are no longer limited to security, affordability and sustainability. Competitiveness has become an equally critical priority.

”

Energy issues are no longer limited to security, affordability and sustainability. Competitiveness has become an equally critical priority. These four objectives are deeply interconnected, and energy has become critical economic infrastructure underpinning industrial competitiveness, technological leadership and long-term growth.

As energy systems become more complex, the focus must shift beyond expanding generation capacity to building resilient, flexible and integrated power systems that can reliably deliver affordable, clean energy at scale. This requires investment in grids, storage, digital technologies and the capabilities that connect them.

In an increasingly complex geopolitical and economic environment, no country or company can achieve this transformation alone. By building trusted partnerships that combine complementary strengths, and judging technologies by the value they deliver rather than their origin, we can accelerate innovation, strengthen resilience and build a more competitive, secure and sustainable energy future.

Gyanesh Chaudhary, Chairman and Managing Director, Vikram Solar

“

Energy sovereignty is now economic sovereignty.

”

The greatest risk leaders underestimate is delivery, on two fronts. More than 2,500 gigawatts of projects remain stuck in grid-connection queues worldwide, with capital and clean electricity delayed by transformer, permitting and infrastructure bottlenecks.

At the same time, manufacturing has expanded in response to short-term demand signals rather than long-term supply-chain visibility, resulting in overcapacity in some regions and shortages in other fast-growing markets.

The countries expected to drive around 80% of future electricity demand growth also face financing costs two to three times higher than those of advanced economies. Energy sovereignty is now economic sovereignty. Countries that can build cells, modules and batteries will increasingly shape the terms of their own transitions.

Governments and businesses should work together to procure firm, dispatchable renewable power under stable and predictable policy frameworks. Government creates the long-term certainty that enables investment, while industry delivers globally competitive technology, manufacturing capacity and innovation.

Cheap solar got us here; delivery takes us the rest of the way.

Faheem Haider, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer, Mari Energies

“

The opportunity is to move beyond a technology-by-technology approach towards integrated system planning.

”

One barrier leaders may still be underestimating is system readiness. The energy transition is often discussed in terms of how quickly we can add new production, power generation and clean technologies. Yet the real constraint may be whether the wider system can absorb and manage that growth.

This is particularly important for growing economies such as Pakistan. If investment in oil and gas production or power generation moves ahead of transmission and distribution, storage, demand growth, technical skills, regulatory capacity or policy support, we risk creating stranded or underutilized assets while consumers continue to face unreliable and expensive energy.

The transition becomes more costly without necessarily becoming more sustainable.

The opportunity is to move beyond a technology-by-technology approach towards integrated system planning. Governments and businesses should identify policy gaps and infrastructure bottlenecks while developing a jointly prioritized and bankable project pipeline.

Aligning production, generation, grids, demand and financing from the outset will reduce execution risk, improve affordability and enable capital to deliver greater impact.

Georgios Stassis, Chief Executive Officer, PPC

“

Governments and businesses must collaborate to enable investment ahead of demand.

”

To solve the new energy equation, we must address a critical timeline mismatch: energy infrastructure and grids take five to 10 years to build, while digital and industrial demand can scale in mere months.

The most significant barrier is the lack of predictable regulatory frameworks to support anticipatory grid investments. Renewables are being built rapidly but regulatory models often force utilities to remain reactive, requiring them to build networks only after demand has been established.

Governments and businesses must collaborate to enable investment ahead of demand.

Until these regulatory updates materialize, PPC is addressing grid bottlenecks through ecosystem co-location. Our flagship project at Agios Dimitrios in Western Macedonia, Greece, is repurposing former lignite lands into an energy-self-sufficient digital hub through co-located solar, energy storage and flexible generation.

Platforms such as WEF can help bridge this gap by convening policymakers and industry leaders around a common objective: giving utilities the confidence and regulatory certainty to build tomorrow’s grid today while keeping electricity affordable for consumers.

Sama Bilbao y León, Director General, World Nuclear Association

“

For too long, energy decisions have been optimized around individual objectives without sufficient regard for the wider system.

”

One of the defining challenges of our time is building sustainable energy systems to power a growing, increasingly electrified world.

My main takeaway is that we continue to underestimate a fundamental reality: energy is not simply a sector of the economy; it is the engine of the economy. It underpins industrial competitiveness, economic growth, technological leadership, national security and quality of life.

For too long, energy decisions have been optimized around individual objectives without sufficient regard for the wider system. The Energy Forum was structured around four imperatives: security, affordability, sustainability and economic growth. The challenge is not to choose between them but to build systems that can deliver all four simultaneously.

That requires governments and industry to align infrastructure, permitting, financing, workforce development and industrial strategy with future energy demand.

Long-term policy certainty and stable market signals are not simply energy priorities; they are economic priorities. When energy is treated as a strategic enabler of prosperity, investment follows, innovation accelerates and growth becomes possible at scale.

Varun Sivaram, Founder and Chief Executive Officer, Emerald AI

“

From India to Europe, countries pursuing AI face the same challenge: connecting the infrastructure of future economic growth while keeping electricity affordable and reliable.

”

AI’s future depends on a very physical constraint: getting connected to power.

At the Energy Forum 2026, we launched the AI Energy Management Alliance to help address that challenge, bringing together companies across the AI and energy ecosystems to make AI data centres better citizens of electricity grids and local communities.

Data centres are projected to consume only around 3% of global electricity in 2030. Yet AI deserves a prominent place on the energy agenda because of its speed, scale and economic significance.

Electricity consumption at AI-focused data centres surged 50% in 2025; their concentrated power requirements can overwhelm local infrastructure and countries increasingly view AI infrastructure as foundational to economic growth, competitiveness and sovereignty.

However, we can make these facilities more flexible. By coordinating computing workloads, batteries and other resources, data centres can reduce electricity demand when grids are under stress. As NVIDIA explains, this can free capacity for faster connections, avoid costly infrastructure built for rare demand peaks and support reliable electricity for surrounding communities.

At the Energy Forum, we discussed a grand bargain in which governments and regulators offer AI data centres that are good grid citizens faster and larger power connections. Although the Alliance begins with an American focus, the opportunity is global.

text:
Pasay City – First Gen Corporation subsidiary Bac-Man Geothermal, Inc. (BGI), the owner and operator of the 197.27-megawatt (MW) Bac-Man geothermal power plant in Bicol, received a special recognition on Oct. 7, 2026, during the 2026 Asean Energy Awards in Pasay City.

BGI earned the National Strategic Excellence Award under the Asean Renewable Energy category from the Asean Centre for Energy (ACE), a Jakarta-based intergovernmental organisation which sponsors the Asean Energy Award, Southeast Asia’s highest recognition, to promote private sector participation in the development of the region’s energy sector.

A part of the First Gen Renewables portfolio, Bac-Man was recognised for its operational excellence and compliance—highlighted by its National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) Blackstart Service Accreditation and a win at the Department of Energy’s 2025 Sustainable Energy Awards for On-Grid Renewable Energy Projects.

Bac-Man’s geothermal steamfield, which sits on Manito, Albay and Bacon, Sorsogon, has been supplying steam to the Bac-Man Geothermal Power Plant since 1993.

Before First Gen acquired it in 2010, the facility was not producing any electricity as it suffered extensive damage from a previous typhoon.. Post-acquisition, it underwent extensive rehabilitation and modernisation, and within two years, the facility was restored to its full capacity.

In 2020, the plant faced another challenge when Super Typhoon Rolly, recognised as the world’s most powerful cyclone in that year, left a trail of devastation across the country. Already grappling with the impact of the pandemic, Bicol further endured the loss of lives and the destruction from the super typhoon.

During this challenging time, Bac-Man (BGI) extended its services to the public beyond its contracted obligations by providing power to the Bicol grid, making them the lone power provider. Its ‘islanding operations’ have helped Bicolanos recover from the aftermath of the super typhoon and the pandemic.

In 2025, the facility avoided emissions of close to a million tons of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e) or exactly 955,757.77 tCO₂e, by maintaining 100-percent renewable energy use in its operations and keeping zero discharge through complete geothermal fluid reinjection. The avoided emission was equivalent to keeping more than 200,000 gasoline-powered cars off the road for a year.

Bac-Man was also recognised for putting heavy priority on local economic participation, with over 90 per cent of its 2025 procurement spend sourced from local contractors and vendors.

The Asean RE Project Awards is one of the categories under the Asean Energy Award, and the National Strategic Excellence award acknowledges renewable energy projects that hold strong national relevance, demonstrating contributions to the acceleration of RE growth at the national level.

name: Congress
title: Can Congress Hand EPA the Power to Pick Winners? - New Civil Liberties Alliance
description:
Mark Chenoweth: Welcome to Unwritten Law with Mark Chenoweth and John Vecchione.
This is the RMS of Georgia doing business as Choice Refrigerants v. EPA case.
Because the point of Congress – Mark Chenoweth: Justice Cavanaugh would.
Zhonette Brown: Congress didn’t do that here, yeah.
Zhonette Brown: Congress literally said nothing here.
text:
Mark Chenoweth: Welcome to Unwritten Law with Mark Chenoweth and John Vecchione. We are joined today by NCLA General Counsel, Zhonette Brown. Zhonette, welcome back to Unwritten Law.

Zhonette Brown: Thank you. Good to be here.

Mark Chenoweth: And Zhonette is here because she has just filed a petition for writ of certiorari with the US Supreme Court, in a case you have been since day one, Zhonette. This is the RMS of Georgia doing business as Choice Refrigerants v. EPA case. Can you just briefly remind folks who might have heard us on the podcast talking about this case before, what the underlying issue is. And then we’ll just ahead to what the issues are – what the main issue is that we’re taking up with the Supreme Court.

Zhonette Brown: Sure. The wheels of justice move slow. So, going back, RMS does business as Choice Refrigerants of Georgia. They are a small company based in Alpharetta, Georgia. They developed patents for certain refrigerants that came after other products had been phased out by the EPA.

Mark Chenoweth: Right. As part of the Clean Air Act in the early 90s, right?

Zhonette Brown: Correct. And so, they invested, became an entrepreneur. They did all of the things that you’re supposed to do in the land of opportunity. And then, in 2020, Congress came around and said, “Actually, there’s too many of those products, as well. We’re going to create a Cap and Trade regime. We’re going to cut your market – the market – by 85%. EPA, you figure out how that gets allocated.”

Mark Chenoweth: But this wasn’t a complete phase out. This was a phase down. Unlike, what happened with the prior generation of –

Zhonette Brown: That’s correct. So, under this vision, under the statute, the market continues indefinitely. By 2036 it gets phased down 85%, but there’ll still be millions of what are now called allowances. Which are what allows people to participate in the market.

Mark Chenoweth: So, no one is going to be happy when the government comes in and says, “Hey. You’re going to have to do a lot less of what you were doing before.” But my sense is that the EPA made this even worse. Or, I guess you could say Congress made this even worse because it left so much up to the EPA here. Tell me about – what does the AIM Act do and what doesn’t it do?

Zhonette Brown: Sure. Well, the AIM Act identifies a certain group of refrigerants that says, these refrigerants have to be reduced over time in phases. So, down 10 percent in the first phase, down 40 percent in the next phase, etc. But Congress didn’t tell EPA how that should be done. And the effect of that was that the EPA had the ability to decide, “Do you Choice, lose your rights? Or does Dupont? Or Honeywell? Or a foreign company? Or does someone else lose their rights, and why?”

So, Congress didn’t make up the reasoning as to why anyone’s market share would be reduced. They left it to EPA to do. And in this particular case, EPA did it worse than usual.

Mark Chenoweth: Leaving EPA to their own decide is never a good idea, John?

John Vecchione: No. Well, any of the administrators, when you don’t tell them what to do or why to do it, certainly, they’re going to make up their own – their own system. Which is not going to be the way Congress would do it. Which is usually split the baby, and they didn’t split the baby here. Certain people got hurt a lot worse.

Zhonette Brown: Yeah, our client got their ox gored. And the point of Congress not telling why, that’s another interesting part about this statute is, not only did Congress not tell EPA why to take anyone’s given market share. Congress didn’t say in the statute why it was requiring a phase down of this market. So, EPA being EPA said, “Oh, well clearly it’s for environmental reasons.” But there’s nothing like that in the statute. And in fact, since the 90s Congress hadn’t passed that kind of an environmental statute.

John Vecchione: So, originally, as I recall, and correct me if I’m wrong. The refrigerants had to be eliminated because they’re making a hole in the ozone. Right? And now we don’t have a hole in the ozone.

Zhonette Brown: Way back in the 1990s, it was a different product. It was not –

Mark Chenoweth: Right.

Zhonette Brown: – the refrigerants of day. Way back in the 90s those types of refrigerants and products created a hole in the ozone.

Mark Chenoweth: And when they made that law, Congress actually said, “We’re doing this because there’s a hole in the ozone.”

Zhonette Brown: And in that law, Congress actually said, “When we phase this out in these steps, those phases apply to the people who are making the product beforehand.” They didn’t allow new market entrants, and they specified that this was a direct, proportional phase out.

John Vecchione: I recall that.

Mark Chenoweth: So, how’s this one different?

Zhonette Brown: This one is different, because again, Congress just said, “EPA, you establish a cap and trade regime and do so within – it was roughly 180 days.” And EPA, in the rule making, recognized that they had all sorts of discretion on how to allocate the market. Recognized in its view that it wasn’t limited to how it had been done before. And so –

Mark Chenoweth: Sort of rubbing its hands together.

Zhonette Brown: Exactly. And on top of its list, social and environmental justice. So, EPA sliced off part of the market of people who had invested in it, had patents like our client, and just gave them away to new market entrants who may have been disadvantaged. And then EPA moved in the direction of favoring administrative ease, i.e., if you had been a good boy, filed paperwork with the EPA; you got rights. Even if those rights didn’t necessarily belong to you.

Mark Chenoweth: And none of this was in what Congress wrote?

Zhonette Brown: None of it.

John Vecchione: And none of that also effects the environment. For instance, it isn’t like they did any studies and said, “Well, this refrigerant is causing more damage than that refrigerant. So, we have to – we’ll allow this one that’s a little less damaging to last a little longer.” Nothing like that. No scientific expertise was applied.

Zhonette Brown: That’s correct. That’s the whole point of the allowances in the AIM Act, is that they are fungible and tradable between products. And so, the more damaging a product is the more allowances it requires, etc. So, none of that is part of what figured into EPA’s calculation.

Mark Chenoweth: So, we might not like this, but under current law Congress is allowed to delegate some of its legislative power to an agency if it gives enough instruction to the agency. So, what’s wrong with what the AIM Act did here?

Zhonette Brown: Well –

Mark Chenoweth: What was missing?

Zhonette Brown: I don’t know if I would 100% agree with the way you’ve raised it. Because the point of Congress –

Mark Chenoweth: Justice Cavanaugh would.

Zhonette Brown: Well, the point of Congress having to give direction, is that that direction, those standards, those rules that Congress has to give to an agency – that is what is supposed to make it so the agency is implementing or executing on the law, rather than making the law.

Mark Chenoweth: Right. So, just to give everybody a little bit of lawyer speak here, under current doctrine the Congress has to specify an intelligible principle in the law that the agency can then use in order to implement it. And we’re saying – part of what we’re saying in this surrepetition is, Congress didn’t do that.

Zhonette Brown: Congress didn’t do that here, yeah. And the point of the intelligible principle is, like I said, it’s supposed to separate legislative power from executive power. If Congress gave enough rules, gave an intelligible principle, then what EPA is doing in theory is executing the law instead of making it up.

Mark Chenoweth: The other thing that’s interesting to me about this case, and it’s different, John, from a lot of the other cases we’ve seen, is a lot of times there’s an argument over, “Well, did they say enough? Was there enough here?” Congress literally said nothing here about 98% of the allowances.

Zhonette Brown: Congress literally said nothing here. And there’s a number of other reasons why this is a great vehicle to take up what’s called the Nondelegation Doctrine. There’s no – we do not argue, and I don’t think it would qualify as a major question in doctrine case, where Congress can say, or the court can say, “Did Congress actually delegate that power?” There’s no question Congress delegated power. And there’s no question of, “Did they give enough of a principle that it’s an intelligible principle?” There’s none of that here.

And this isn’t a case, for example, that I think Justice Thomas, under his dissent in the tariffs case would say involves privileges, rather than rights. We’re stalking specifically about reliance interest. The ability to do the business that you have invested in, your patented products, etc. So, this is a pure legislative power case.

Mark Chenoweth: Right. So, you have Congress might have the power to take these rights away. I don’t think we’re challenging here, at least, the ability for Congress to reduce the size of the market.

Zhonette Brown: Right.

Mark Chenoweth: But we’re saying, “Congress, you have to decide who is going to have to give up market share. You can’t just tell EPA to do it and not give them any direction or instruction.”

Zhonette Brown: Right. And the point of that, obviously, is accountability. If Congress are going to make decisions that are going to cost people their business, Congress has to make that decision itself, rather than let EPA make the decision. Congress can’t just say, “You know, we have too many of any given product cars on the road. EPA go figure out who doesn’t get to drive their car anymore.” It’s the rights impacting decision that has to be made by Congress.

John Vecchione: And what did the court below say, what court was it, and what did we say in the Supreme Court?

Zhonette Brown: Sure. So, the court below, because it’s a case that incorporated parts of the Clean Air Act – not the relevant parts, but the procedural parts, it had to be in front of the DC circuit. So, the DC circuit is the original court that heard our petition. And they denied our petition. They found the statute was sufficiently intelligible. But not the statute and what’s written in the statute. Instead, what the DC circuit found was that Congress obviously intended to incorporate part of the Clean Air Act.

Mark Chenoweth: Clearly.

Zhonette Brown: Clearly. Although it didn’t mention it by name anywhere – mentioned other parts of the Clean Air Act.

Mark Chenoweth: Well, that sounds very helpful. The DC circuit’s trying to supply the intelligible principle that Congress didn’t supply. What’s wrong with that?

Zhonette Brown: That’s a whole different constitutional problem. So, that is the judiciary, instead of Congress now supplying intelligible principle. So, instead of an Article II branch supplying the Article I power; now you have the Article III branch. Which is even less accountable, theoretically, supplying the intelligible principle. So, you cannot fix a constitutional wrong with another constitutional wrong.

John Vecchione: It’s like –

Mark Chenoweth: I think I said in the surrepetition, two constitutional wrongs don’t make a right.

John Vecchione: It’s as if they took the rational basis test and said, “We’re going to make a rational basis test for the intelligible principle. And if we can think of an intelligible principle then they win.” That’s what it strikes me as.

Zhonette Brown: Right. Well, that’s a version of today’s constitutional avoidance, which is another problem here. But yeah, the worst part – even worse than what the DC circuit did – is it said, “Okay. We’re going to incorporate what we call the market share version of what existed under the Clean Air Act.” And so, what EPA did is fine. But EPA didn’t do a market share version. EPA took away part of the market to give it to new market entrants. That’s by definition not market share. And then EPA figured out the rest of it by doing, again, who filed paperwork with them. Which is in no way, shape, or form what any business person would consider being part of the market.

Mark Chenoweth: So, the question presented in this case is whether Congress violated the vesting clause of Article I, by giving it executive agency, unbounded discretion to choose which private parties are entitled to participate in this multi-billion dollar market. So, the vesting clause of Article I, for folks who maybe aren’t steeped in the Nondelegation Doctrine. What’s the connection between those two things?

Zhonette Brown: Well, the vesting clause basically says all legislative power that is granted in the constitution shall be vested in the Congress of the United States. And so, it takes legislative power to make these impact in rules. The Nondelegation Doctrine is a question. It questions whether it’s the test for deciding whether Congress has inappropriately given away its legislative power. And under the Nondelegation Doctrine, as you mentioned before, so long as Congress – now, so long as Congress gives intelligible principle, the courts have found that there is no violation of the constitution.

Mark Chenoweth: Sorry, I lost my train of thought. I don’t know if you want to –

Male Speaker: I’ll cut this up.

Mark Chenoweth: Yeah, mark that. Did you have something else?

John Vecchione: I can. So, what are they asking the court to do, though, with this intelligible principle? We don’t come out – what I’m saying is, we don’t come out of the box and say, “Oh, get a new test.”

Zhonette Brown: We don’t. We basically say, “This should be the metric by which it’s determined whether or the intelligible principle actually does its job. Because if this statute which gives no guidance, if it provides – if it passes the intelligible principle test, then the intelligible principle test is dead. But we don’t argue for a new test at the outset.”

John Vecchione: And so, a lot of our listeners know this case. So, is this better or worse that Gundy?

Zhonette Brown: This case is a better case. It’s a way better case –

John Vecchione: Why?

Zhonette Brown: – than Gundy. Because –

Mark Chenoweth: Because it doesn’t involve sexual predators, John.

John Vecchione: I mean, not just for the elite old folk.

Mark Chenoweth: Oh, okay.

Zhonette Brown: Well, what’s an issue in this case as I said is pure legislative power, number one. So, there is no overlap of executive, legislative, judicial power in the criminal area like you had both in Mistretta and in Gundy and –

John Vecchione: Right.

Zhonette Brown: – some of the titling, the drug cases as well.

John Vecchione: Right.

Zhonette Brown: So, that’s one reason. The other reason is in Gundy, the court, in a different context had already filled in what the statute meant in terms of saying, “Under the Gundy event, that sexual predators or people who are subject to the law had to register as soon as possible.” Right? And so, there’s nothing, there’s no pre-existing interpretation here. There’s no long standing history. This is all fresh.

Mark Chenoweth: Yeah. I think the quote in the brief is that if the abject lack of direction in the [inaudible] [00:14:51] doesn’t violate the test, it’s hard to see what could. And so, to me that’s what makes this such a great vehicle. Because if – I mean, it’s been what, 90 years since the Supreme Court has set aside the statute under the Nondelegation Doctrine? But this seems like a pretty good candidate. This seems like a law that, if they’re ever going to do it, this would be an easy one for them to do.

Zhonette Brown: Yeah. If you look back again, at the tariffs case, at the FCC vs. Consumer Research case, so many of the cases – Gundy, Mistretta – so many of the cases over the last few decades that the Supreme Court has taken up do involve some sort of arguably overlapping power. Whether it’s foreign affairs, whether it’s crime, whether it’s managing federal assets, federal land; that sort of thing. Whether it’s privileges instead of rights, the way that Thomas was talking about in the tariffs case. This case doesn’t have any of those complications.

John Vecchione: And what is the remedy we’re looking for? The whole statute being struck down, or what happens?

Zhonette Brown: No. Because there’s a lot more to the AIM Act that we haven’t talked about. So, there’s just the narrow cap and trade part that would be struck down. There are other elements to the statute that allow EPA to ratchet down certain market sectors in a different way. So, there’s a lot that would survive. It’s just a little bit that would really be struck.

Mark Chenoweth: So, you’re asking the court to reinvigorate the intelligible principle test or the Nondelegation Doctrine, or?

Zhonette Brown: They either need to articulate the intelligible principle test in a way that shows how this statute fails to meet it, or they need to come up with a new test.

Mark Chenoweth: One of the things the surrepetition talks about is a judicially administrable test. So, I think one of the problems that particularly lower courts have had with these nondelegation cases is, they don’t know how they’re supposed to decide how much is too much, or how much isn’t enough, or what have you. Well, the problem is that really should be on Congress to establish what it’s doing in a way that the judge can look at what Congress did and say, “Oh, okay. There are enough – there’s enough guidance in this statute, there’s enough guardrails that have been given to the agency that we can judge as judges, whether or not the agency is following the will of Congress or not.”

When those aren’t there at all there’s no way for the judge to tell. And so, what they ought to do is say, “Look. That statute doesn’t meet the standard of giving enough.” They haven’t been willing to do that. But at least here where there’s, like we say, literally nothing. It ought to be relatively easy for them to say, “Well, whatever else might pass muster under our somewhat toothless existing test, this doesn’t pass.”

Zhonette Brown: Right. That’s exactly right. And it is high time; it’s been 91 years. And if you go back to the old cases they did say there had to be a judicially administrable standard. That means as a judge you have to be able to look at what the agency did, compare it to the statute that was written, and say either, I can tell that the agency followed the will of Congress in the letter of the statute, or they didn’t. But this, “I can’t tell.” Which has led to deference and a lot of it – a lot of other problems. That’s then not a judicially administrable standard that Congress has given. And therefore, it would fail.

Mark Chenoweth: Absolutely. So, as I said you’ve been on this case from the beginning. But we’ve added some help here at the Supreme Court stage, a couple of lawyers from Clement & Murphy, namely Clement and Murphy. And so, Erin Murphy is the counsel record on this case. Former Solicitor General Paul Clement has been helping out. But also, Erin Hawley has been helping out. How has that process gone? Do you want to say anything about the work that those folks have been doing on the surrepetition?

Zhonette Brown: All of them are experienced Supreme Court litigators. All of them have clerked in front of the Supreme Court. Paul Clement obviously was the former Solicitor General of the United States. But they all contributed to forming these arguments, the way to present them to the Supreme Court. And Erin Hawley was actually involved a little bit earlier in trying to get the DC circuit en banc to reconsider what the panel had done. But just helping to frame the case in a way that the Supreme Court will understand that this is the perfect vehicle for them to take up.

John Vecchione: Murphy, the day we’re taping, she just argued today, as a matter of fact. I was just listening.

Mark Chenoweth: Oh, okay. I didn’t know that. Well, so, we worked in parallel with Paul Clement to dispose of the Chevron deference doctrine, John. And so, one of the things I said in our press release is that it’s exciting to work even more directly with Erin and Paul to give the Nondelegation Doctrine its day of reckoning. So –

John Vecchione: Yes.

Mark Chenoweth: – it would be fun to see not just the Chevron doctrine go down in relentless, but to see the Nondelegation Doctrine either go down or –

John Vecchione: Revivified, I think is what Alito told Neal Katyal. “You don’t want to be the guy who revivifies the –“ I remember. I think that’s what it was.

Mark Chenoweth: Yeah. So, the thing to me, Zhonette, that was exciting because this isn’t the first time I’ve asked Paul or Erin if they might want to help us out on a case. And they’re often busy. They don’t have – but they took a real interest in this case. They said, “You know what? I know we’ve said no a bunch, but yeah, we’ll help you on this one. Because they’re real believers in the case that you have here. They think this is a cert-worthy issue.”

Zhonette Brown: This is a very unique statute. It’s a very pristine set of circumstances that serves it up on a silver platter to the Supreme Court. If you’re ever going to do your job in this area of separation of powers, now is the time to do it.

Mark Chenoweth: Yeah. So, I have an unfair question for you. The court just looked at nondelegation last term, right, in the Consumer’s Research v. FCC case. Does that make you concerned the they’re not going to be willing to do it again so soon, or does that make you think, “Look. They’re obviously in a mood to consider or think about these things. So, maybe they’ll take on our case.”

Zhonette Brown: Well, I think at least some of the justices were not happy with the way that the court, in that case, again, filled in frankly, the intelligible principle. Because the interpretation the majority gave the Communications Act in FCC was inconsistent with all the interpretations that had been given by courts below. The court put boundaries and strictures on the FCC that nobody else thought existed. There’s also though some language. There’s multiple pieces actually of language in the opinions and the dissents that I think give hope that the Supreme Court would take this.

The Supreme Court indicated that context matters, right? The discussion was, are we delegating the power to design a tax stamp, or are we delegating the power to reorder the entire national economy? Well, one of the other examples that Justice Gorsuch gave was controlling and market and industry. Right? And so, this gives the Supreme Court the opportunity that it should take, and it frankly owes to the lower court to take. To sort out how that scale works. What happens here when we’re talking about a multi-billion dollar industry with a product that’s in almost everybody’s home and vehicle? But it’s still not a major Questions Doctrine case.

Mark Chenoweth: Yeah. John, what is your prediction here? Do you think this is the kind of case that’s likely to get the court’s attention?

John Vecchione: I will say this: the problem with nondelegation is that it is hit or miss. There seems to be appetite. But is there appetite by four? Is the question I have. And I think there has to be after Gundy, right? There were four –

Mark Chenoweth: Well, they keep saying that there’s five-ish votes, maybe six.

John Vecchione: Yeah. So, therefore, I say yes. I think it’s a good vehicle. We’ll see what they do. It’ll be interesting to see if it’s relisted one time.

Mark Chenoweth: Let me ask you this.

John Vecchione: Not seven times, not eight times; one time.

Mark Chenoweth: Yeah. Let me ask you this: so, the head of the EPA, I’m blanking on his name, the former –

Zhonette Brown: Lee Zeldin.

Mark Chenoweth: Lee Zeldin. Thank you. He’s likely to agree with us on what needs to happen to the nondelegation issue –

Zhonette Brown: Well, if you –

Mark Chenoweth: Why is the EPA going to fight us on this? They should just role over.

John Vecchione: For the same reason that Gene Scalia liked the Chevron deference. That he wrote about why he liked it. Well, Lee Zeldin’s the head of the EPA. By saying his title you said his interest and then you said why.

Mark Chenoweth: They like it when Congress just hands over lots of things for them to do.

John Vecchione: Exactly. “I have more power, not less power. Oh, I guess I’ll keep quiet for now.” And I will say this: more seriously, but only a little more seriously. They have a duty to protect the statute and their regulations. And that’s their duty and that’s their client. So, that’s – that’s the non-cynical reason.

Mark Chenoweth: Yeah. That’s what Solicitor General Sauer would say, or Sarah Harris would say, as to why they have to defend this –

John Vecchione: Correct.

Mark Chenoweth: – this statute So, what happens now, Zhonette?

Zhonette Brown: Now we wait. We wait to see if the Supreme Court is going to grant cert or not. The EPA and a couple of trade associations who are in the case have 30 days to file some briefs. We have 30 days from when the case is docketed for some – hopefully for some amici to come in and support our argument, that the Supreme Court should take this case. And then after that passes –

Mark Chenoweth: If you’re listening, potential amici.

Zhonette Brown: Please join us.

Mark Chenoweth: There’s still time. By the time you’re hearing this, there’s at least three weeks to get your act together and file an amicus brief and be in the case that’s going to rewrite the Nondelegation Doctrines.

Zhonette Brown: There you go.

Mark Chenoweth: Yeah. Well, I think this is an exciting case. Maybe one final word about our client, and Ken Ponder, and Choice Refrigerants. And there’s a wonderful video that our Erin Reese has put together that features you that folks can go watch and learn more about this case.

Zhonette Brown: Yeah. You can really see when you watch that video how Ken Ponder built this business from ground up. Literally starting by cleaning refrigerants out of air conditioners and refrigerators in dumps.

Mark Chenoweth: Yeah.

Zhonette Brown: And building this –

Mark Chenoweth: At the garbage dump that people just left there.

Zhonette Brown: Right. .

Mark Chenoweth: Yeah.

Zhonette Brown: Because those products couldn’t be vented to the air. So, then he is a guy who just comes up with solutions for his customers all the time. And that’s how he came up with these patented products. You had to get rid of certain types of refrigerants, R21, etc.. He had to come up with a new product that would work there in those systems without completely redesigning the system and redoing everything about the way the product worked. And he found those kinds of solutions. Like I said, he’s exactly what you envision when you think of small business entrepreneur. Part of what he said is because he’s small, he can move quicker than big corporations and get things done.

Mark Chenoweth: Yeah.

Zhonette Brown: And he did.

Mark Chenoweth: We used to call that Yankee ingenuity. I don’t know if they like that term down in Georgia, John.

Zhonette Brown: Yeah. I’m going with no.

Mark Chenoweth: But I wish you well, Zhonette. I think this is a fantastic case, I think a fantastic client, a great issue. Thrilled that we have the Clement & Murphy folks on board helping along with Erin Hawley. And I’m optimistic that we’re going to get four votes for cert here. We’ll see what the – see what the government’s brief says. We’ll see what the amici say and so forth. But we will certainly keep folks apprised of what’s happening. So, thank you for joining us on Unwritten Law.

title: Democratic Party Rep. Lee Un-ju Condemns Chinese EV Subsidies as Treasonous
description:
The lawmaker emphasized that “without technological sovereignty, jobs disappear” and stressed the need to shift industrial policies to protect domestic production bases.
The U.S. imposes high tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, while the European Union (EU) has levied tariffs of up to 45.3% on Chinese electric vehicles and is pushing to restrict hybrid vehicle imports.
In contrast, South Korea applies a basic 8% tariff on Chinese vehicles and continues to provide purchase subsidies for Chinese-made electric vehicles.
New registrations of Chinese electric vehicles in the first half of 2026 reached 69,513 units, a 178.7% increase from the same period last year.
She introduced a bill to amend the Special Taxation Restriction Act, applying tax credits to electric vehicles produced and sold domestically or exported.
text:
“Supporting Chinese electric vehicles with the blood tax paid by our citizens must stop immediately.”

Democratic Party of Korea lawmaker Lee Un-ju (3rd term, Yongin, Gyeonggi Province) criticized the government’s policy of providing purchase subsidies for Chinese-made electric vehicles during a recent interview with the Chosun Ilbo. The lawmaker emphasized that “without technological sovereignty, jobs disappear” and stressed the need to shift industrial policies to protect domestic production bases. During last month’s National Assembly questioning of the government, she also denounced subsidizing overseas-produced electric vehicles with taxpayer money as “an act of betrayal in this era,” warning that it threatens the domestic manufacturing ecosystem and technological sovereignty.

Lee’s warnings come amid growing concerns that Chinese automakers could intensify low-price offensives in the South Korean market to bypass trade barriers in the U.S. and Europe. The U.S. imposes high tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, while the European Union (EU) has levied tariffs of up to 45.3% on Chinese electric vehicles and is pushing to restrict hybrid vehicle imports. In contrast, South Korea applies a basic 8% tariff on Chinese vehicles and continues to provide purchase subsidies for Chinese-made electric vehicles.

◇U.S. and Europe Lock Out Chinese Cars… Korea Faces Accelerating Market Erosion

The EU is advancing a plan to limit annual imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles to 350,000 units over the next four years, increasing the quota by 6% annually starting from the second year. The EU expects significant import suppression effects, as Chinese hybrid vehicle imports this year are projected to reach up to 800,000 units. The Chinese Ministry of Commerce argues that the quota would still allow for increased exports compared to last year’s 302,000 units.

South Korea’s automotive industry fears a “balloon effect,” where Chinese vehicles, facing narrowed sales channels in the U.S. and Europe, flood the Korean market. According to the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers, domestic sales in China fell 21.8% year-on-year in January–August 2026, while exports surged 66.7% to 7.153 million units. Chinese automaker BYD recently launched a four-wheel-drive version of its plug-in hybrid SUV, the Sealion 6 DM-i, in South Korea for 41.9 million Korean won—approximately 30 million Korean won cheaper than its European pricing.

Chinese vehicles’ share of South Korea’s electric vehicle market has rapidly expanded. According to the Korea Automobile & Mobility Association, Chinese-made electric vehicles accounted for 4.7% of new registrations in 2022 but rose to 35.0% in the first half of 2026. New registrations of Chinese electric vehicles in the first half of 2026 reached 69,513 units, a 178.7% increase from the same period last year. Domestic production accounted for only 57.5% of the market. The “Chinese” category includes not only Chinese brands but also foreign brands like Tesla produced in Chinese factories.

Lee stated, “Electric vehicles are a core strategic industry connected to batteries, semiconductors, software, robots, and physical AI. Protecting domestic electric vehicle production is about safeguarding the ecosystem of future high-tech manufacturing and jobs.”

◇“Tax Credits for Production Instead of Purchase Subsidies… Korea Needs Its Own IRA”

Lee’s proposed solution is to shift the focus of electric vehicle support policies from purchases to production. She introduced a bill to amend the Special Taxation Restriction Act, applying tax credits to electric vehicles produced and sold domestically or exported. The bill includes a preferential coefficient of up to 1.5 times for vehicles produced outside the capital region—a so-called “Korean version of the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA).”

Lee argued, “While purchase subsidies have contributed to expanding eco-friendly vehicle adoption, the policy should now shift to benefit companies that maintain domestic production and employment.” During a National Assembly Finance and Economy Planning Committee meeting last month, she criticized the government’s exclusion of electric vehicles from its domestic production tax credit proposal, stating, “The industry urgently needs incentives to continue and expand domestic production.”

She also raised data security concerns linked to the spread of Chinese electric vehicles. “Autonomous and connected vehicles collect not only vehicle data but also detailed road networks, infrastructure, and the movement patterns of drivers and pedestrians,” Lee said. “The government must verify at the national level whether data from overseas-manufactured vehicles is transmitted abroad or subject to remote control.” She argued that South Korea should treat information sovereignty as an economic security issue, similar to the U.S., which is tightening regulations on connected and autonomous vehicle systems linked to China and Russia.

◇“Nations That Make Electric Vehicles Will Make Robots”

Lee emphasizes electric vehicle production as the foundation for future AI industries. “Nations that make electric vehicles will make robots,” she said. “Batteries, motors, sensors, semiconductors, and software in electric vehicles connect to autonomous vehicles, humanoid robots, and physical AI.”

While acknowledging that South Korea may struggle to catch up with the U.S. and China in AI models and software, Lee highlighted the country’s hardware strengths in semiconductors, automobiles, batteries, and precision manufacturing, which present opportunities in physical AI. She explained that in an era where factories, robots, and vehicles operate autonomously through AI, existing manufacturing technologies and production experience will be critical assets.

Urgent action is needed to prevent the hollowing out of domestic manufacturing. Data Lee disclosed during a parliamentary audit revealed that 1,090 companies in 35 national industrial complexes across the country closed or suspended operations last year, a 48.9% increase from the previous year. Localization rates for drone core components remain low: 25.6% for motors, 36.8% for batteries, and 37.5% for flight controllers.

“How can we protect technological sovereignty in advanced industries if our manufacturing capabilities disappear?” Lee asked. “It’s contradictory to abandon today’s manufacturing base and expect to build tomorrow’s robot and drone industries.” She stressed that even if automakers expand overseas production, “mother factories” (core technology and process development sites) and key suppliers must remain in South Korea.

◇“Alliances Are No Longer Free… U.S. Investments Must Deliver Tangible Benefits”

In her recent book “The Free Order Has Ended,” Lee analyzes shifts in the free trade system and U.S.-China technological rivalry, outlining South Korea’s economic security strategy. The book’s core argument is that semiconductors, AI, energy, supply chains, and the U.S.-South Korea alliance are not isolated issues but part of a single structure determining national production capacity and bargaining power.

“Free trade is over,” Lee said. “Now, even alliances require contributions. For resource-poor South Korea with a small domestic market to negotiate equally with major powers, it must secure technologies that cannot be easily replaced.”

She emphasized prioritizing tangible benefits over investment scale in U.S.-South Korea economic cooperation. Citing U.S. liquefied natural gas (LNG) projects in Alaska and nuclear power investments, Lee said, “The question isn’t whether to invest because the U.S. asks, but what strategic benefits South Korea gains.” She stressed securing long-term contracts, refining and processing capabilities, and outcomes linked to domestic production and employment for critical minerals like rare earths and tungsten.

Lee also proposed cultivating “energy physical AI”—efficiently combining nuclear power, renewable energy, and energy storage systems (ESS)—as a key national strategic industry in the AI era.

◇“U.S.-China Rivalry Is an Opportunity… Don’t Miss the Next 5–10 Years”

Lee views the U.S.-China rivalry as both a crisis and an opportunity for South Korea. As the U.S. excludes China from advanced technology supply chains, South Korea’s semiconductor, battery, shipbuilding, and nuclear power industries could play new roles.

“Significant opportunities are emerging in supply chains that exclude China,” she said. “This situation may last 5–10 years, but we don’t know how long. We must secure markets and invest in core technologies during this time.”

The book proposes a national strategy of becoming a “connected nation,” linking South Korea’s technology with Middle Eastern and Singaporean capital, Indonesian raw materials, and ASEAN markets to expand its economic territory. “Other countries have what we lack,” Lee said. “Connecting with nations that need our technology allows us to transcend the limitations of our land and domestic market.”

Lee defines the current era as South Korea’s third industrial transformation, following Park Chung-hee’s heavy chemical industrialization and Kim Dae-jung’s IT industry development. This transformation centers on AI.

“It’s not just about the president, bureaucrats, or companies like Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix performing well,” she said. “Politicians must stop focusing solely on political debates like prosecutorial reform and explain to the public why the global order is changing and what South Korea will live on in the future.”

“South Korea lacks resources but possesses technologies, manufacturing capabilities, and skilled workforce the world needs,” Lee concluded. “By securing technological sovereignty and connecting with other nations’ capital, resources, and markets, we can open a new path to growth.”

title: Power requires hardware, Houston can build it
description:
Recent work by the Houston Energy Transition Initiative has examined the supply- and demand-side solutions needed to support that growth.
But that buildout creates another economic-development opportunity: manufacturing more of the equipment required to make it happen.
Demand for U.S. power equipment is growing.
Houston is already building the hardware The greater Houston region is already part of this supply chain.
Houston is already preparing to power the next wave of industrial growth.
text:
Houston’s rising electricity demand is creating an opportunity that extends beyond adding power generation: manufacturing more of the equipment needed to support that growth. Recent work by the Houston Energy Transition Initiative has examined the supply- and demand-side solutions needed to support that growth.

But that buildout creates another economic-development opportunity: manufacturing more of the equipment required to make it happen.

Every megawatt added to the system requires physical infrastructure. Transformers move electricity between voltage levels. Switchgear controls and protects electrical systems. Turbines, drives, power electronics, substations and control systems help generate, move and manage power.

Demand for U.S. power equipment is growing. The U.S. Department of Energy has identified limited domestic production capacity, extended procurement timelines and dependence on foreign supply chains as constraints for critical grid equipment. Demand for distribution transformers has increased 41% since 2019, according to Wood Mackenzie, while lead times for some large transformers now extend to three to four years.

Houston is already building the hardware

The greater Houston region is already part of this supply chain. Houston-based Powell Industries manufactures medium-voltage switchgear and other electrical systems for industrial and infrastructure markets, and Aksa Power Generation USA manufactures standby and mobile generator systems at its Conroe facility.

In September 2026, TMEIC Corporation Americas expanded its regional manufacturing footprint with a new Waller County facility for uninterruptible power supplies and medium-voltage drives.

Also in 2026, GEIS Electrical Protection selected Houston for a new manufacturing and service hub for medium- and low-voltage switchgear. The company cited Houston’s position at the center of North American energy and industrial markets, along with its “skilled workforce and strong logistics connectivity.”

The site-selection question goes beyond the site

For a power-equipment manufacturer, proximity to demand matters. So does access to the companies that design, specify, finance, install and operate that equipment.

Manufacturers can operate alongside engineering firms, EPC contractors, fabricators, utilities, skilled trades, industrial customers and logistics providers accustomed to complex energy projects.

RELATED: Build Here, Scale From Here: Why Greater Houston Works for Energy Manufacturing

For companies evaluating where to establish or expand U.S. production, that means they do not have to build an entire operating ecosystem around the factory from scratch.

Houston is already preparing to power the next wave of industrial growth. The next opportunity is to manufacture more of what powers it.

text:
The Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA) is providing up to $31.1 million to establish solar robotics manufacturing facilities in Melbourne and Brisbane, supporting faster, safer and more efficient construction of large-scale solar farms across Australia.

Funded under Round 2 of ARENA’s Solar Sunshot Program, the projects will manufacture two complementary technologies in Australia; robots that install solar panels and autonomous systems that drive foundation piles.

The new facilities in Victoria and Queensland will help improve productivity, reduce construction costs and ease workforce constraints as large-scale solar deployment grows, supporting Australia’s goal of ultra low-cost solar.

ARENA CEO Darren Miller said these projects will advance the development of technologies previously demonstrated in Australian conditions into locally manufactured products that can be deployed at scale.

“Installing foundations and placing panels are two of the most labour-intensive parts of solar farm construction. It’s hard work in the hot sun,” Mr Miller said.

“Australia needs to install large volumes of solar quickly and cost-effectively. Local manufacturing and automation can improve the way solar farms are built by reducing construction costs and making installation faster, safer and more efficient; an important part of ARENA’s ultra low-cost solar vision.

“Manufacturing these technologies in Australia will help to strengthen local supply chains, develop specialist skills and give solar projects better access to advanced construction equipment when and where it is needed.”

ARENA is providing up to $17.8 million to Luminous Robotics to establish a Melbourne manufacturing facility for its autonomous solar panel installation robots, called LUMIs. The facility is expected to support the manufacture and deployment of around 100 LUMI robots by 2029, helping automate solar panel installation on large-scale solar farms.

Luminous Robotics came through ARENA’s 2024 Solar Challenge, an initiative designed to supercharge innovation and crowdsource ideas from across the world on how to reduce the cost of large-scale solar.

ARENA supported demonstrations of LUMI robots at solar farms in Victoria and New South Wales, where the technology was tested under Australian construction and environmental conditions. The new funding will enable moving the technology from field demonstration to industrial-scale manufacturing in Australia.

“We’ve proven LUMI on real solar farms in Australia, in the heat and dust, doing some of the hardest work on site. With ARENA’s support, the next step is to turn that into scale,” Tenzin Crouch, General Manager, Luminous Robotics Australia said.

“Building a production line in Melbourne, delivering our first hundred robots, and then growing from there. If Australia is going to build renewable energy at the scale and speed we need, robotics will have an important role to play and we are building it.”

Built Robotics Australia will receive up to $13.3 million to establish a Brisbane manufacturing hub and operations centre for autonomous piling systems used in utility-scale solar construction. The facility will manufacture and deploy 12 robotic piling systems, helping automate one of the most labour-intensive stages of solar farm construction.

The project builds on previous ARENA-supported deployments of Built Robotics’ autonomous piling technology in Australia, establishing domestic capability to manufacture, integrate and test piling systems for solar projects.

“Australia has shown the world that construction robotics and physical AI work in the field. Now we’re going to build that technology here,” Paul Kelly, Vice President of Business Development, Built Robotics, said.

“Our Brisbane hub will make Queensland a home for autonomous solar construction, creating skilled local jobs and a supply chain that serves projects in Australia, building on nearly a decade of work we’ve done here.”

Together, the projects will build Australian manufacturing capability at two critical stages of solar farm construction. By moving proven robotics into larger-scale production and deployment, they can help create a domestic equipment supply chain for Australia’s growing large-scale solar industry.

About Solar Sunshot

The Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA) is delivering the $850 million Solar Sunshot Program to support innovation in Australia’s solar PV manufacturing industry. Solar Sunshot was announced by the Australian Government in March 2024 and aims to uncover and support innovation to drive scale and diversity in a critical industry.

Australia benefits from strong renewable energy potential, high-quality, abundant raw materials and a long track record of excellence in research and development. Solar Sunshot aims to harness these advantages so that Australia can strengthen and diversify its supply chains and create economic opportunities.

name: Detroit Environment
title: Voices: Strength in numbers. Tribal Nations are building energy sovereignty together.
authors: Daniel Wiggins Jr, Hadassah GreenSky, Gleb Tsipursky, Charles Griffith
description:
Collective action is the idea behind the Midwest Tribal Energy Resources Association (MTERA).
In this environment, Tribal Nations face complex technical, regulatory, and financial decisions; not just to keep up, but to grow and secure their own energy sovereignty.
“Energy sovereignty is no longer a theoretical concern for rural Tribal Nations like Bay Mills.
That is why MTERA is launching Tribal Energy Voices, a dedicated space for Tribal Nations to tell their own energy stories in their own words.
You could even share your story of how energy has impacted your life through our Tribal Energy Voices initiative.
text:
Tribal Nations have long understood that a community’s strength is not measured by what one member can do alone, but by what the whole is willing to build together. That principle now connects Tribal energy projects across Michigan and the Midwest.

Collective action is the idea behind the Midwest Tribal Energy Resources Association (MTERA). Founded in 2014 by a small group of Tribes facing similar challenges, today MTERA brings together 33 Tribes across Michigan, Minnesota, and Wisconsin. We are a group of Tribes helping Tribes build the capacity to plan, finance, and operate energy projects on their own terms.

What’s possible together is real. In 2024, we aligned more than $62 million in federal funding to bring residential solar to Tribal Nations across EPA Region 5, with a plan in place to reach every reservation. In August 2025, the Solar for All program was terminated, cutting more than $500 million earmarked for Tribal clean energy nationwide.

While this termination decision is still being challenged in federal court, this was not the first reversal Indigenous peoples have absorbed in this country. What happened next is the part worth paying attention to. Rather than seeing the loss of funding as a failure, our Member Tribes used it as a catalyst to deepen collaboration, strengthen resolve, and innovate new paths forward together.

Energy work is unfolding faster than ever. Utilities are building new infrastructure, data centers are driving record-high electricity demand, and the grid is transforming in ways not seen for generations. In this environment, Tribal Nations face complex technical, regulatory, and financial decisions; not just to keep up, but to grow and secure their own energy sovereignty.

“Energy sovereignty means every Tribal Nation has the right to determine its own energy future based on its priorities, values, and the needs of its community,” said Bill Bernier, Environmental Services Director for the Inter-Tribal Council of Michigan. “Working together doesn’t diminish that sovereignty. It strengthens our collective ability to exercise it.”

For some Tribes, those decisions are urgent. “Energy sovereignty is no longer a theoretical concern for rural Tribal Nations like Bay Mills. It’s a daily reality,” said Whitney B. Gravelle, President of the Bay Mills Indian Community. “Stronger storms, high winds, ice events, and flooding are causing more frequent and longer outages that put our most vulnerable citizens at risk.

“The ongoing risks posed by the Line 5 dual pipelines make it clear that we cannot depend on aging external systems that threaten our homelands. Building our own energy systems, like our solar farm, allows us to create power that is stable, local, and designed for the conditions we actually live in.”

A few Tribes have been doing this work for decades. Others are just beginning. No single blueprint exists, and there shouldn’t be. What we share is the goal: that every Tribal Nation has the knowledge, capacity, and resources to decide its own energy future.

Long before anyone called this energy policy, our Nations moved knowledge the way we always have: through story. Stories carried instruction, warning, wisdom, and memory.

They still do. That is why MTERA is launching Tribal Energy Voices, a dedicated space for Tribal Nations to tell their own energy stories in their own words. Not case studies written about us, but firsthand accounts of what we tried, what failed, what held, and who stood beside us when it did.

Those stories deserve an audience beyond our own communities, and I believe every single one of us, including newsrooms, has a part to play in carrying them forward, because the decisions Tribal Nations are making about energy are shaping policy at the state, regional, and federal level.

Which brings me to what I would ask of you.

If you are non-Native, and you have never set foot on a reservation, and you are not certain which Tribal Nations reside in your state or what sovereignty actually means, that is not something to be embarrassed about.

The problem was never not knowing. The problem is allowing unfamiliarity to become a barrier to connection and understanding. Not knowing is natural; choosing not to learn or engage is how perspective and progress are lost.

Start somewhere. Learn whose ancestral homelands you reside on. Michigan is home to 12 federally recognized Tribal Nations, each with its own government, history, and cultural traditions.

Each is making its own decisions right now. When your utility, your employer, or your municipality holds a proceeding on energy, ask whether Tribal Nations were invited, and ask early enough that the answer can still change. And when you find a Tribal Nation already doing what your community is still debating, ask how it was done.

If you are Native and wondering where this work begins in your tribal community, it begins with a conversation. Reach out to your Tribal Council, ask how your community is approaching energy.

You can even reach out to us. We’d be happy to share how we created a coalition of Tribal Energy Leaders and partners working together to empower Tribes to manage their energy resources.

You could even share your story of how energy has impacted your life through our Tribal Energy Voices initiative.

The future of Tribal energy will not be built by one project or one funding cycle. We will build it through relationships that hold when funding does not. That is the power of collective action, and it is how we will keep building for our future generations.

Planet Detroit’s Voices column includes opinion pieces from our community of partners and readers. These pieces express the voices of the authors and not necessarily those of the publication.

text:
Italian long-duration energy storage (LDES) company Energy Dome has opened a manufacturing plant in Piacenza, Italy, as it expands production of its CO2 Battery technology for international projects.

The facility will manufacture key components, including the large domes used in the company’s carbon dioxide-based energy storage systems.

Energy Dome said it has shipped the first dome manufactured entirely in-house to India for the 20 MW/160 MWh Kudgi project with state-owned power company NTPC. Production is underway for the 20 MW/200 MWh Columbia Energy Storage Project in Wisconsin, United States, with Alliant Energy. The next component is destined for a 23 MW/200 MWh project in Rhode, Ireland.

The company invested approximately €2 million ($2.2 million) in the Piacenza site over the past year to upgrade the building, acquire machinery and improve electrical and network infrastructure. It plans to increase total investment to approximately €6.5 million over the next two years, with the goal of tripling production capacity and expanding the local workforce from 30 employees to between 80 and 90 by 2028.

Energy Dome said its technology relies on European manufacturing supply chains, including steel and turbomachinery, rather than supply chains located outside Europe.

The company reports a presence across four continents, with more than 2 GWh of projects operational or under contract, more than 3 GWh of authorized projects and a development pipeline exceeding 30 GWh. Its customers and partners include Google, Engie, Alliant Energy, NTPC, SEC and SRP.

Energy Dome also cited Italy’s National Integrated Energy and Climate Plan, grid operator Terna’s stated need for 50 GWh of storage by 2030 and the new MACSE storage procurement mechanism as factors supporting demand for energy storage.
