title: State EV Incentive Programs Beyond NEVI: Grants, Tax Credits & Rebates
description:
This article maps the major categories of state EV incentives, explains how they interact with federal programs, and gives you a practical checklist for pursuing funding in your state.
The Federal Baseline: IRC §30C and Bonus Depreciation Before diving into state programs, understand the federal tax tools that underpin most state incentive designs.
Disadvantaged community set-asides: Many state programs reserve a portion of funding for sites in low-income or environmental justice communities.
State Tax Credits State tax credits reduce your state income tax liability dollar-for-dollar.
How State Programs Interact with NEVI NEVI carries an 80% federal cost share, meaning the site host or state must provide at least 20% of project costs.
text:
Why State EV Incentives Matter for Fuel Retailers

The federal National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (NEVI) Formula Program allocated $5,000,000,000 over FY2022–2026 to build out EV charging along designated Alternative Fuel Corridors — but NEVI is not the only game in town, and it is not available to every site. State plan approvals were suspended on February 6, 2025, and while interim final guidance issued August 11, 2025 restarted the process, individual state pipeline status varies. Operators should confirm their state's current plan status with their state DOT before counting on NEVI dollars.

Fortunately, dozens of states have built their own parallel incentive stacks — grants, tax credits, rebates, and low-interest loan programs — that fuel retailers can pursue independently of NEVI or layer on top of it. Understanding these programs is increasingly important as you evaluate whether adding EV charging infrastructure makes financial sense for your site. (For a detailed look at how to model the numbers, see our guide on EV charger ROI: how to build the model for your site.)

This article maps the major categories of state EV incentives, explains how they interact with federal programs, and gives you a practical checklist for pursuing funding in your state.

The Federal Baseline: IRC §30C and Bonus Depreciation

Before diving into state programs, understand the federal tax tools that underpin most state incentive designs.

Alternative Fuel Vehicle Refueling Property Credit (IRC §30C)

The federal Section 30C credit applies to qualified alternative fuel vehicle refueling property — including EV charging equipment — placed in service at a business location. Important deadline: Under P.L. 119-21 (the One Big Beautiful Bill), property placed in service after June 30, 2026 is not eligible for the IRC §30C credit. If you are planning a charger installation, the placed-in-service date relative to this cutoff is critical. Consult your tax advisor immediately if your project timeline extends into the second half of 2026 or beyond.

Bonus Depreciation

For qualified property acquired after January 19, 2025, the bonus depreciation rate is 100% (permanent) under P.L. 119-21 (as of July 4, 2025, IRS guidance). This means the full cost of eligible EV charging equipment can be deducted in the year it is placed in service, dramatically improving first-year cash flow on capital investments.

Section 179 Expensing

For tax years beginning in 2026, the Section 179 expensing limit is $2,560,000, with a phase-out threshold of $4,090,000 (Rev. Proc. 2025-32). Most single-site fuel retailers will fall well below the phase-out, making Section 179 a straightforward tool for expensing charger hardware and installation costs.

State incentive programs are typically designed to complement — not duplicate — these federal tools. Many states explicitly require applicants to disclose federal credits received and reduce the state award accordingly, so accurate tax planning is essential before you apply.

Categories of State EV Incentive Programs

1. State Capital Grants

Capital grants are direct awards that do not need to be repaid. They are the most valuable form of incentive but also the most competitive. State energy offices, departments of transportation, and public utility commissions administer the majority of these programs.

Common grant structures for fuel retailers include:

Site-host grants: Awards to the property owner or operator for hardware purchase and installation. Eligibility often requires the site to be open to the public and to meet minimum uptime standards similar to NEVI's requirement of greater than 97% average annual uptime per charging port (23 CFR 680.116).

Make-ready grants: Cover the electrical infrastructure — trenching, conduit, panel upgrades, transformer upgrades — rather than the charger hardware itself. These are particularly valuable because make-ready costs often exceed hardware costs at legacy fuel retail sites.

Disadvantaged community set-asides: Many state programs reserve a portion of funding for sites in low-income or environmental justice communities. If your station is in a qualifying census tract, you may face less competition for a larger share of available funds.

States with historically active grant programs include California (through the California Energy Commission and CARB), New York (through NYSERDA), Colorado (through CDOT and CDLE), and Washington. Program availability, funding levels, and application windows change frequently — always verify directly with the administering agency.

2. State Tax Credits

State tax credits reduce your state income tax liability dollar-for-dollar. They are less immediately valuable than grants (you must have tax liability to use them) but are often available on a rolling basis rather than through competitive application windows.

Several states have modeled their EV infrastructure credits directly on the federal IRC §30C structure, which means the June 30, 2026 federal termination date may or may not affect state credit eligibility — state conformity to the federal code varies. Check whether your state has a "rolling conformity" or "static conformity" date with the Internal Revenue Code.

3. Utility Rebate Programs

Electric utilities — investor-owned, municipal, and cooperative — are often the fastest and most accessible source of EV charging incentives for fuel retailers. Utility programs are funded through rate cases approved by state public utility commissions and do not depend on legislative appropriations cycles.

Common utility rebate structures include:

Hardware rebates: A fixed dollar amount per DC fast charger port or per kilowatt of installed capacity.

Make-ready rebates: Utility pays for or reimburses the cost of upgrading service to the meter. Some utilities own the make-ready infrastructure outright and provide it at no cost to the site host.

Demand charge mitigation: EV fast chargers create large, brief demand spikes that can dramatically increase your monthly demand charge. Some utilities offer special EV rates, demand charge caps, or battery storage incentives to offset this. This is often more financially significant than the hardware rebate itself.

Time-of-use (TOU) rate incentives: Preferential rates for charging that occurs during off-peak hours, which can improve the economics of overnight fleet charging at your site.

To find utility programs in your area, the U.S. Department of Energy's Alternative Fuels Station Locator and incentive database at afdc.energy.gov maintains a searchable database of utility and state programs updated regularly.

4. State Revolving Loan and Low-Interest Financing Programs

Not all state support comes as grants or credits. Several states offer low-interest loans through green banks, state infrastructure banks, or energy revolving loan funds. These programs are particularly useful for operators who need to bridge the gap between grant awards and project completion, or who want to finance make-ready costs that grants do not fully cover.

How State Programs Interact with NEVI

NEVI carries an 80% federal cost share, meaning the site host or state must provide at least 20% of project costs. State grants and utility rebates can be used to satisfy all or part of that 20% non-federal match — but only if the total federal share (NEVI plus any other federal-aid highway funds) does not exceed 80%. State-only funds and private funds face no such restriction.

This stacking structure means a well-positioned fuel retailer could theoretically cover a substantial portion of total project cost through a combination of NEVI (80% federal share), a state make-ready grant, a utility hardware rebate, the federal IRC §30C credit (if placed in service by June 30, 2026), and 100% bonus depreciation on the remaining basis. The complexity of stacking these programs makes early engagement with a tax advisor and your state energy office essential.

For a broader look at how EV charger revenue and costs interact over time, see our analysis of EV charger revenue projections: will charging pay for itself?

Pricing and Metering Compliance: A Prerequisite for Incentive Eligibility

Most state grant and rebate programs require that funded chargers comply with applicable weights and measures laws. This is not a minor administrative detail — it affects how you price and meter charging sessions.

Under NIST Handbook 130 (section 2.33) and NIST Handbook 44 (section 3.40, effective January 1, 2023), electricity sold as a vehicle fuel must be sold by the kilowatt-hour (kWh). An EVSE may not sell electricity as vehicle fuel by units of time. Time-based charges are lawful only as separately disclosed occupancy or overstay fees. Many state incentive programs now explicitly require kWh-based pricing as a condition of award — and some states have enacted their own weights and measures statutes reinforcing this requirement.

NEVI-funded chargers carry additional technical requirements: OCPP 2.0.1 network protocol (23 CFR 680.108), at least four DC fast charging ports each capable of simultaneously delivering at least 150 kW of continuous power with at least one permanently attached CCS Type 1 connector per port, and a contactless payment method accepting major debit and credit cards (23 CFR 680.106). State programs that are designed to complement NEVI often adopt these same technical standards as eligibility criteria even when NEVI funds are not involved.

State-by-State Research: What to Look For

Because state programs change frequently and vary enormously in structure, the most reliable approach is to research your specific state directly. Here is a framework for that research:

Key Questions to Ask Each Administering Agency

Is the program currently accepting applications, or is it between funding rounds?

Is there a minimum or maximum project size?

Are fuel retail sites (as opposed to fleet depots or parking garages) explicitly eligible?

Does the program require the site to be publicly accessible 24/7?

What uptime and reporting requirements apply post-installation?

Does the program require kWh-based metering and pricing?

How does the program treat federal credits and other incentives received for the same project (offset, stacking, or disclosure only)?

What documentation is required at application and at project closeout?

Where to Search

AFDC Incentives & Laws database: afdc.energy.gov — searchable by state, fuel type, and incentive type

State energy office websites: Most states publish their EV infrastructure programs through the energy office or department of environmental quality

State public utility commission dockets: Utility make-ready and rebate programs are approved through rate cases; commission websites publish approved tariffs

State DOT: For programs tied to transportation funding or Alternative Fuel Corridor designations

Common Pitfalls and Compliance Risks

Missing the IRC §30C Deadline

The June 30, 2026 termination date for the federal Section 30C credit is the single most time-sensitive compliance issue for any fuel retailer currently planning an EV charger installation. "Placed in service" means the equipment is installed, operational, and available for use — not ordered, not permitted, not under construction. Supply chain delays and utility interconnection timelines routinely push projects past their anticipated completion dates. Build significant schedule contingency into any project targeting this credit.

Failing to Disclose Stacked Incentives

Most state grant agreements require disclosure of all other incentives received for the same project. Failure to disclose can result in grant clawback, disqualification from future programs, and in some cases referral for fraud investigation. Maintain a complete incentive log for every project.

Uptime and Reporting Obligations

Grant agreements typically impose multi-year post-installation obligations: minimum uptime requirements, data reporting to the state agency, and sometimes public data sharing through the AFDC or a state portal. Failure to meet these obligations can trigger repayment provisions. Factor ongoing compliance costs into your project economics.

Equipment Eligibility Restrictions

Some state programs restrict eligible equipment to products on an approved list, require specific network protocols, or mandate domestic content. Verify equipment eligibility before purchasing hardware. For a detailed look at charger hardware options and specifications, see our EV charger cost for gas stations: a pricing guide.

Action Items: Pursuing State EV Incentives

Immediate (Next 30 Days)

Search the AFDC database at afdc.energy.gov for all active incentive programs in your state

Contact your electric utility's key accounts or commercial team to ask about EV make-ready and rebate programs

Consult your tax advisor about the IRC §30C June 30, 2026 placed-in-service deadline and whether a project can realistically meet it

Confirm your state's NEVI plan status with your state DOT before assuming NEVI funds are accessible

Short-Term (60–90 Days)

Request pre-application meetings with your state energy office and any relevant utility program administrators

Obtain a preliminary electrical service assessment from your utility to understand make-ready scope and cost

Identify whether your site is in a qualifying disadvantaged community census tract (check EPA's EJScreen tool at epa.gov)

Begin assembling required documentation: site control evidence, electrical single-line diagram, business entity documents, prior-year tax returns

Before Submitting Any Application

Confirm that all incentives you plan to stack are disclosed in each application

Verify that your planned equipment meets the program's technical specifications (OCPP version, connector type, kWh metering, uptime capability)

Review the grant agreement's post-installation obligations and confirm you can meet them operationally

Have legal counsel review the grant agreement before signing — clawback provisions and reporting obligations can be significant

text:
Swedish autonomous technology company Einride has deployed autonomous electric trucks without a driver’s seat for real freight transport in the United States. It is applying autonomous driving technology to routine logistics work beyond test runs, accelerating the commercialisation of unmanned freight transport.

CleanTechnica recently reported that Einride is operating 2 Level 4 (L4) autonomous electric trucks in Marysville, Ohio. The vehicles transport freight daily, shuttling between warehouses operated by logistics company EASE Logistics.

The vehicles are designed with no driver’s seat. They drive themselves without a driver on designated sections, while an external remote operator monitors operations and can intervene when needed.

The route includes not only internal roads at logistics facilities but also nearby public roads. The two companies began actual transport in September and are collecting data such as mileage, freight volume and vehicle operating time. Based on the data, they plan to expand the number of vehicles and operating routes.

The project is part of the Truck Automation Corridor initiative being 추진 by the U.S. states of Ohio and Indiana. The project, which began in 2021, has received a total of $8.8 million (about 11.8 billion won) and aims to verify the safety and efficiency of autonomous driving technology on major freight routes.

A key segment is the 166-mile (about 267 km) stretch of Interstate 70 linking Columbus, Ohio, and Indianapolis, Indiana. However, Einride’s vehicles are operating on a limited section in Marysville, not the full length of the highway.

In March, carrier Nussbaum Transportation deployed 3 trucks equipped with automation technology to the related project.

Work is also under way to build charging infrastructure for electric freight vehicles. Tesla and U.S. truck stop operator Pilot are expanding a Megacharger charging network for the Semi electric truck.

With autonomous driving demonstrations and expansion of charging facilities for large electric trucks proceeding in parallel, attention is also focusing on the shift to electrification and automation in the U.S. freight transport industry.

title: The Return of the Brazilian Far Right Is a Climate Catastrophe - Amazon Watch
description:
His victory will be a catastrophe for many reasons, but there’s one looming disaster that will extend far beyond Brazil’s borders: The fate of the Amazon rainforest, the world’s largest, hangs in the balance.
The Amazon rainforest is our planet’s biggest carbon sink.
In recent years, climate scientists point out that some 17 percent of the Amazon has already been burned or otherwise destroyed.
Under the elder Bolsonaro, rainforest destruction had accelerated dramatically, as the fazendeiros, or large-scale ranchers, had demanded.
Defending the Amazon rainforest is a dangerous business, and the killing didn’t stop with Chico Mendes.
text:
On October 25, Brazilians will vote in the second round of their presidential elections. The matter might not be all that suspenseful. The far right-wing candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, is widely favored to defeat the incumbent, President Lula da Silva, especially after Bolsonaro’s unexpectedly strong showing in the first round, which found both him and the members of his far-right movement broadly in the ascendance. His victory will be a catastrophe for many reasons, but there’s one looming disaster that will extend far beyond Brazil’s borders: The fate of the Amazon rainforest, the world’s largest, hangs in the balance. Its stepped-up destruction will likely dramatically accelerate global warming.

What’s more, Donald Trump has personal ties to one of the Brazilian oligarchs who is most directly responsible for the ongoing destruction of the Amazon, and Trump actually hosted him in the White House on August 20.

And yet the mainstream U.S. media is ignoring the rising danger to the Amazon. Ominously, climate scientists have warned that increased destruction will push the vast rainforest toward a “tipping point,” after which recovery will be difficult, if not impossible.

Here, briefly, is the science behind the warnings. The Amazon rainforest is our planet’s biggest carbon sink. Its 2.3 million square miles of thick vegetation pull dangerous carbon dioxide from the global atmosphere, and safely store it in the forest’s thick vegetation. Burn the forest, and carbon dioxide, the worst of the greenhouse gases, remains in the atmosphere, damaging the climate everywhere on the planet.

In recent years, climate scientists point out that some 17 percent of the Amazon has already been burned or otherwise destroyed. Estimates are that 20 to 25 percent would be the tipping point, after which the end result will be treeless savannah and scrubland. Naturally, these predictions are not facts, but as Thomas Lovejoy, the great American scientist and environmentalist who devoted his life to the Amazon, used to say, “Multiply the risk of a catastrophe by its disastrous consequences, and you will see that inaction is impossible.”

Once you witness the aftermath of the rainforest destruction, you will never forget it. Take, for instance, the construction of BR-317, the two-lane highway that runs southwest from the city of Rio Branco in Brazil’s western state of Acre to the Bolivian border. Once, triple-canopy forest reached right to the highway’s edge on both sides. Now, green pasture stretches into the far distance, with occasional dead tree trunks and blackened stumps a reminder of what happened. Once, you would have struggled to peer more than 50 feet into the forest. Now, you can see for miles.

These days, huge herds of dewlapped, humped, white Brahma cattle roam across the huge fazendas, or ranches. Patches of sickly orange-brown soil are the giveaway; the topsoil is actually shallow and not fertile. In the rainforest, falling vegetation from the thick forest cover is regularly recycled into new forest growth. Destroy the original dense tree cover, and the rainforest dies.

Of course, along highway BR-317, the rainforest’s rich and interdependent insect, bird, and animal life has also retreated into the far horizons. From time to time, you might see a couple of parrots; they sometimes fly in matrimonial pairs. On a rare occasion, you might catch sight of a dazzlingly blue morpho butterfly dancing along the highway. But the life form you are most likely to notice is gray-headed vultures.

Xapuri, a small town along the highway, was once the home to Chico Mendes, the legendary environmentalist and rubber-tapper leader who was murdered back in 1988. The local ranchers who later burned the forest killed him first, to get him out of the way. Several books have been written about his life; he is also the subject of an excellent feature film.

Destroying the trees to create pasture for beef cattle is one of the main reasons the rainforest is dying, and powerful cattle ranchers are one of the major supporters of the far right in Brazil. Flávio Bolsonaro, the current candidate, is a stand-in for his father, Jair, who was president from 2018 to 2022 (and is presently in prison for plotting to overthrow the incumbent president, Lula da Silva, who defeated him in the 2022 election). Under the elder Bolsonaro, rainforest destruction had accelerated dramatically, as the fazendeiros, or large-scale ranchers, had demanded. After Lula won, the burning dropped 34 percent in his first six months in office.

Another contributor to rainforest destruction is JBS, the gigantic global foods company that originally started in Brazil but which has now expanded, including into the United States. JBS is the world’s largest meat-processing company. Environmentalists and others have credibly accused it of exporting meat from Brazilian pastures that replaced stretches of burned-out rainforest. JBS denies the allegations, but Senator Ron Wyden held a series of hearings from 2021 to 2023, and he concluded that JBS “was turning a blind eye as parts of its supply chain burn down the Amazon, push the world toward climate catastrophe, and undercut American ranchers who play by the rules on international trade.” Human Rights Watch also reported in 2025 that JBS “may have exported beef … sourced from illegal ranches.”

It was one of the principal owners of JBS, Joesley Batista, who met Donald Trump face to face in the White House on August 20. Batista apparently successfully lobbied Trump to lower U.S. tariffs on imported Brazilian beef, in an effort to reduce consumer prices in the United States. But you can bet that Trump never raised the fate of the Amazon – nor will he, if Flávio Bolsonaro wins on October 25.

Defending the Amazon rainforest is a dangerous business, and the killing didn’t stop with Chico Mendes. A 2022 report by Global Witness found that more than 1,700 environmental activists had been murdered in the previous decade across the global south. Brazil was in first place, with 342 killings. Indigenous people are among the victims. A remarkable 2022 film, The Territory, actually documented one such murder.

Cattle ranches are not the only threat to the Amazon. High global gold prices have stimulated feverish efforts to invade the forest, as Amazon Watch, the influential U.S.-based environmentalist organization, warned last May. Large mining corporations, and the individual artisanal miners called garimpeiros, are both to blame. Amazon Watch indicted “a predatory logic that turns rivers into sludge, strengthens illegal networks, and deepens violence.”

There is unfortunately yet another threat. Rising global demand for soybeans is also triggering rainforest destruction.

Under President Lula, a Brazilian government agency called IBAMA fought hard to protect the forest. IBAMA agents are authorized to carry weapons, and they do often get into gunfights with forest destroyers. If Flávio Bolsonaro wins, he and his allies in the Brazilian Congress, which will be dominated by the far right, will surely neuter the agency. What’s more, for now the Brazilian Constitution bans industrial mining in Indigenous territories. But the fear is that the incoming far-right majority will change the law.

Amazon Watch’s program director is Christian Poirier. His organization, like the others in the global environmental movement, regards the news from Brazil as a true climate emergency: “The Trump administration is openly sympathetic to the Bolsonaros, and has been working to subvert and interfere in Brazil’s election. We need to vote in a Democratic Congress in November, and then push it to put the brakes on Trump’s pro-Bolsonaro, anti-rainforest moves.”

Andrew Miller is Amazon Watch’s advocacy director, in Washington, D.C. He recognizes that certain progressive members of Congress, like Representatives Delia Ramirez and Mark Pocan, are already taking a direct interest in the Brazil environmental crisis. But he warns that Congress is also afflicted by what is called “climate hushing.”

“It’s crazy,” he says. “Studies show a measurable decline in the number of press releases and public statements about the environment coming out of Congress. The number of congressional interventions on the climate is decreasing – at a time when the actual global crisis is greater than ever, and growing.”

text:
KENITRA, Morocco (MNTV) — Morocco is preparing to advance its electric vehicle battery manufacturing industry as Gotion Power Morocco plans to begin commissioning production equipment at its Kenitra gigafactory during the week of October 20.

Moroccan subsidiary of China’s Gotion High-Tech announced the timetable for starting up equipment at the industrial facility, which is intended to produce lithium iron phosphate battery cells.

The project’s first phase represents an investment of approximately 13 billion Moroccan dirhams, equivalent to about $1.3 billion, and targets an initial annual capacity of 20 gigawatt-hours.

Located in Kenitra’s Atlantic Free Zone, the facility is designed to serve the automotive and energy storage industries.

Its potential markets include Morocco, other African countries, Europe, the Middle East and the United States.

Construction began in September 2025, with the company’s buildings and infrastructure completed over approximately 13 months.

The project required large-scale shipments of production equipment from China, supported by Moroccan port and customs authorities.

Gotion Power Morocco president Khalid Qalam described the equipment startup as an initial step toward developing a wider battery manufacturing ecosystem in the country.

The company has recruited more than 400 Moroccan employees, including engineers, technicians and production workers. Many received training at Gotion facilities in China before joining the Kenitra project.

The company expects the gigafactory to create more than 2,300 direct jobs when fully developed. Its longer-term plans include expanding production capacity and manufacturing battery materials for electric vehicles and energy storage systems.

The project also forms part of a broader partnership involving Gotion and Volkswagen’s battery subsidiary, PowerCo. The companies announced a separate Moroccan joint venture in September to produce lithium iron phosphate cathode materials.

That venture is expected to involve an investment of approximately €480 million, or about $547 million, with planned annual production capacity of 100,000 metric tons.

The developments strengthen Morocco’s ambitions to attract advanced manufacturing investment and establish a larger role in international electric vehicle supply chains.

text:

The Detroit, Michigan-based automotive manufacturer said battery-electric vehicles, plug-in hybrid electric vehicles and extended-range electric vehicles accounted for over 60% of vehicles sold, amounting to "the highest NEV penetration rate ever recorded for the third quarter."

"We are strengthening a competitive and sustainable business in China, guided by our commitment to meeting the evolving needs of Chinese customers," said John Roth, GM senior vice president and president of GM China and Asia.

title: Volkswagen, Audi, and Porsche All Lost US Sales in Q3 2026 - autoevolution
description:

Jetta sales rose 24.9 percent to 14,092 units, while the Taos crossover held flat at 9,780 deliveries.
Said gains weren't enough to cover falling Q6 e-tron deliveries, and it's really bad.
Of course, e-tron GT sales fell as well.
Of the 16,026 vehicles Porsche dealers moved in the US in Q3 2026, the Cayenne was the biggest winner, contributing 5,837 sales compared to 5,519 for the Macan.
text:
The Volkswagen Group's core brands in the United States market had a rough third quarter. For starters, Volkswagen sold 11,481 fewer ID.4 electric crossovers than a year earlier. Its collapse helps explain why the internal combustion Tiguan and Jetta could not prevent an overall decline, while Audi and Porsche faced their own problems with electric vehicles and product transitions.

Altogether, these brands reported 133,956 deliveries in the third quarter of 2026 stateside. Compared to 152,866 in the third quarter of 2025, that's down 12.4 percent. Volkswagen's total fell 10.9 percent to 78,179 units, Audi deliveries contracted 15 percent to 39,751 vehicles, and Porsche dropped 12.9 percent to 16,026 deliveries in the United States of America.

As noted earlier, the gas-powered Tiguan and Jetta provided some relief for the corest of Volkswagen Group brands. Tiguan sales improved 27.4 percent to 28,091 units, making it the best-selling Volkswagen of the quarter. Jetta sales rose 24.9 percent to 14,092 units, while the Taos crossover held flat at 9,780 deliveries. Those increases lifted passenger car sales 16.6 percent.

The SUV line had it worse, for combined sales of the Atlas and ID. models fell sharply enough to drag total sport utility vehicle volume down 16.2 percent. Atlas fell 19.5 percent, Atlas Cross Sport slipped 9.5 percent, and the ID.4 recorded a pitiful 989 deliveries compared to an even worse 432 for the ID. Buzz family hauler.

There is, however, some context at play here. Federal tax credits are no longer a thing, and the ID.4 is no longer available to configure stateside. Production came to a screeching halt earlier this year, freeing valuable Chattanooga plant output for the redesigned Atlas and Atlas Cross Sport. The existing ID.4 inventory could last into 2027.

There is a planned future version of the ID.4 for North America, and that vehicle is called the ID. Tiguan. With a bit of luck, the newcomer should hit dealer lots in the latter half of 2027 as a 2028 model. Audi's story is a bit more complicated, with the premium-oriented automaker from Ingolstadt delivering 39,751 vehicles in the past quarter.

Several recently introduced models gained ground, of which the A5 stands out for improving 53 percent. A6 volume rose 36 percent, Q3 sales 24 percent, and the Q5 improved by 17 percent. While it may be pricier, the Q7 advanced 42 percent to 6,071 units. The aging Q8, meanwhile, more than doubled sales to 4,095 units.

Said gains weren't enough to cover falling Q6 e-tron deliveries, and it's really bad. The Premium Platform Electric-based model nosedived from 10,059 units to 619 last quarter, whereas the Q4 e-tron dropped from 2,956 to 8 examples of the breed. The A6 Sportback e-tron, which uses similar underpinnings to the Q6 e-tron, also slid a lot. Of course, e-tron GT sales fell as well.

Porsche's decline is noteworthy as well, a decline attributed by the Zuffenhausen-based marque to the lower volume of 718 sales. Both gas-powered models are on their way out for good to make room for the 718 Electric line, and yes, Porsche is not bringing the gas-powered 718 back. Instead, the full-electric version will have to suffice from 2027 forward.

Of the 16,026 vehicles Porsche dealers moved in the US in Q3 2026, the Cayenne was the biggest winner, contributing 5,837 sales compared to 5,519 for the Macan. The internal combustion 718, by comparison, sold 8 units. The Taycan, which is clearly showing its age, didn't fare well. Instead of 1,553 deliveries in Q3 2025, it fell to 537 this past quarter.

MARYSVILLE, Ohio (WKRC) - Autonomous electric freight transports have begun operating in the State of Ohio.

Autonomous electric trucks without cabs are now moving freight each day between EASE Logistics facilities in Marysville, according to WSYX.

Einride AB and EASE Logistics announced Tuesday that two SAE Level 4 trucks have begun operating on scheduled routes across company property and nearby public roads.

The vehicles move freight between EASE facilities without anyone inside. Remote operators monitor each truck from another location and can intervene if necessary.

The deployment is part of the Ohio-Indiana Truck Automation Corridor Project, a collaboration involving the Ohio Department of Transportation, DriveOhio and the Indiana Department of Transportation.

Einride Chief Technology Officer Henrik Green said the Marysville operations show its autonomous system can operate with remote supervision in real-world conditions.

“This deployment reflects the maturity of our purpose-built autonomous stack, combining driverless operation with remote oversight to run safely in real-world operations,” Green told WSYX. “Daily operations in Marysville give us the proof points we need to keep expanding autonomous freight across the corridor and beyond.”

Launched in 2021, the $8.8 million project aims to support automated freight along key Ohio and Indiana routes. Its goals include improving safety, cutting fuel use and emissions, increasing efficiency and helping fleets gain experience with automation.

EASE Logistics President and CEO Peter Coratola Jr. said the company’s third autonomous trucking deployment with DriveOhio builds on its efforts to use innovation in freight transportation.

“This deployment builds on that commitment while helping advance the adoption of autonomous freight across the transportation industry,” Coratola told WSYX.

text:
This article is Part 2 of a series that examines the policy prescriptions coming from the left-wing group Carolina Forward. With North Carolina at a crossroads, it’s a good time to evaluate the sort of policies advanced by those that desire to move our state in a more “progressive” direction.

You can read the complete introduction in Part 1 here.

This article focuses on Carolina Forward’s recommendations for North Carolina regarding transportation, housing, and population shifts.

Transportation

Carolina Forward’s report rightly acknowledges that North Carolina’s days as the “good roads state” are in the past. Heavy traffic congestion on crowded urban highways combined with rural roads overdue for maintenance are problems in need of attention. These factors combine to be costly for drivers: costly in time while sitting in traffic and costly in car maintenance and repairs due to driving on undermaintained roads.

North Carolina is unique in that the state maintains the majority of roads throughout the state, with no county-owned roads at all.

The report further notes that the primary funding mechanism for North Carolina’s roads — the gas tax — may be becoming outdated owing to the increase in highly fuel efficient cars and electric vehicles. The less gas drivers require, the less revenue raised for North Carolina’s roads and highways.

On these points, the Locke Foundation can find broad agreement. Differences begin to emerge, however, in the Carolina Forward report’s disappointment in the lack of light rail and commuter rail. Light rail in particular is one of the least efficient means of transporting people that exists in modern society.

For example, we can look at construction costs of a recently completed stretch of four-lane highway in Craven County, which averaged out to about $32 million per mile. Compare that with a recent addition to Charlotte’s light rail “Silver Line,” with capital costs of $3.3 billion for 10 miles, averaging $330 million per mile, more than 10 times as expensive as the four-lane highway. In other words, these figures suggestion that, for about the same amount of money as one 10-mile stretch of light rail, transportation planners could build 100 miles of four-lane highways.

Also, four-lane highways can move a lot more people than light rail. Years ago, it was estimated that a proposed light rail in Durham County would average 622 passengers per hour (actual light rail ridership often falls short of estimates, however). By comparison, highways can accommodate 2,200 cars per lane per hour, meaning a four-lane highway could accommodate 8,800 cars per hour. Even assuming one passenger per car, it means highways can move 14 times more commuters per hour than light rail even under optimistic estimates.

In short, light rail is more than 10 times more expensive per mile than a four-lane highway and could move a mere fraction (1/14 at best) of the amount of people. Which option do you think would best mitigate congestion? For some reason, the Carolina Forward report insists on diverting billions of dollars more to light rail at the expense of building more roads and highways.

The policy recommendations the Carolina Forward report puts forth in response to North Carolina’s growing transportation needs are at best a mixed bag.

“Boost Funding and Embrace New Revenue”

Here the report recommends phasing in a vehicle-miles-traveled fee on drivers for better capturing revenue from road use by electric vehicles and highly fuel-efficient cars. This is something the Locke Foundation has also suggested. The report’s recommendation, however, also includes a policy of steady, automatic gas-tax increases to ensure steadily increasing revenue. This would, of course, be a regressive tax — something progressives claim to oppose — and make commuting and travel less affordable for working-class North Carolinians. Instead of reflexively searching for ways to increase taxes, policymakers should task the North Carolina Department of Transportation with finding methods to spend our tax dollars more carefully, targeting the highest-priority projects.

“Accelerate Highway Maintenance and Expansion”

This recommendation includes suggestions that are largely unobjectionable, such as prioritizing needed maintenance and projects in high-growth areas to relieve bottlenecks.

“Invest in Transit and Mobility Alternatives”

Here the report recommends prioritizing local transit projects like light rail. The gross inefficiency of such projects is addressed above, but suffice it to say these projects get little bang for the buck and take resources from much more beneficial priorities such as road maintenance and real congestion relief. For rural areas, the report recommends more state grants (i.e., taxpayer funds) for local, low-impact initiatives like dial-a-ride programs or public/private ride-share partnerships to serve low-density areas. This recommendation would require still more taxpayer funds, diverting them from higher-impact projects.

“Encourage Smart Growth and Multi-Modal Transportation”

This is especially where the Carolina Forward report’s inner central planner reveals itself. Here the report calls on government to “encourage” and “incentivize” certain choices — no doubt through strict regulations and taxpayer handouts — to shape what communities look like. Recommendations include government regulations ordering housing to be built near transit stops and directives to build more bike lanes and greenways, though those receive virtually no traffic but pull scarce resources away from more productive uses.

Outside of agreement on a vehicle mileage tax as a more sustainable means of revenue, the contrast with Locke is clear: Carolina Forward advocates for more centralized planning of communities and taxpayer funding of nice-sounding but wildly inefficient projects. Locke’s policy recommendations include more usage of market-based user fees and directing taxpayer funds to the most productive and efficient means of moving people.

Housing

The Carolina Forward report correctly identifies one of North Carolina’s most pressing economic problems: We do not have enough housing. The report estimates that the state faces a shortfall of 764,000 homes through 2029 and that more than one million North Carolinians are already spending more than 30 percent of their income on housing. Median home prices have also risen 58 percent since 2017, but incomes have grown by 38 percent. These are real problems, and North Carolina needs significantly more housing to be built to keep up with population and job growth.

Where Carolina Forward goes wrong is in how it proposes to address that shortage. What North Carolina needs is policymakers to focus on removing the regulatory barriers that make housing artificially scarce and to allow builders to respond to consumer needs. Instead, the Carolina Forward report calls for expanding housing supply through zoning reform, government spending on infrastructure, and government incentives for mixed-income development.

“Dramatically Increase Housing Supply”

The Carolina Forward report calls for expanding housing supply through zoning reform, infrastructure investment, and incentives for mixed-income development.

“Invest in Affordable and Workforce Housing”

This is where Carolina Forward’s supply-side diagnosis gives way to a much larger role for government subsidies. The report calls for state funding and incentives to promote mixed-income development and expand housing opportunities in communities struggling with affordability. (Once again, it is important to note that by “invest,” the report means spending taxpayer dollars, while the report neglects to acknowledge the tax increases that will be necessary to finance these “investments.”)

Apart from growing governmental intervention, spending more money on subsidized housing does not necessarily mean getting more housing overall. Research on the federal Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) illustrates why. A 2010 study in the Journal of Public Economics by Michael D. Eriksen and Stuart S. Rosenthal found that LIHTC construction substantially crowded out new, unsubsidized rental construction in the same markets. Its most robust estimates suggested that nearly every subsidized unit was offset by a reduction in newly built unsubsidized rental units, although the authors cautioned that the range of estimates allows for less dramatic effects.

The study showed that subsidies can end up changing who pays for housing rather than substantially increasing how much housing exists. In a state facing a shortage of hundreds of thousands of homes, that distinction matters.

Housing vouchers present a similar unintentional tradeoff. A 2015 study by Eriksen and Amanda Ross in the American Economic Journal: Economic Policy found that expanding vouchers did not raise rents across the entire rental market, but they did increase rents for units near the voucher program’s maximum allowable rent in cities where housing supply was relatively difficult to expand. In other words, when there aren’t enough homes available, giving households more purchasing power can bid up the limited housing that already exists.

North Carolina should therefore prioritize policies that make it possible for builders to provide more housing in the first place. New market-rate construction adds to the housing stock and gives people more housing options, while removing zoning, permitting, and other regulatory barriers allows private investment to respond to demand without requiring taxpayers to subsidize each additional unit.

“Keep Housing Markets Local and Empower Renters”

The report also calls for limiting the role of large institutional investors in the single-family housing market and expanding protections for renters. The concern about institutional ownership is now being addressed at the federal level. The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, enacted in July 2026, includes provisions restricting large institutional investors from acquiring additional single-family homes. HUD has already begun implementing those requirements in federal housing transactions.

That makes additional state restrictions on institutional investors less compelling, especially given the shortage of supply. Restricting who can purchase existing housing does not create new housing. Policymakers should concentrate on policies that allow more homes to be built, giving renters and would-be homeowners more choices and reducing the leverage that comes from a persistently undersupplied market.

The Carolina Forward report is on firmer ground in recognizing that renters can face significant barriers in tight housing markets. But policymakers should be cautious about responding with additional mandates on landlords without addressing the supply constraints that give those landlords greater market power in the first place. North Carolina policymakers can do more for renters by making it easier to build apartments, townhomes, duplexes, and other forms of rental housing. A larger supply of homes gives renters more options and forces landlords to compete for tenants rather than relying on regulation to hold down costs.

“Revitalize Housing in Rural and Declining Areas”

As the Carolina Forward report points out, housing challenges are not limited to fast-growing metropolitan areas. Some rural communities face aging housing stock, vacant properties, and limited new construction. Improving housing quality and making better use of existing properties can be worthwhile goals, but the solution should not be to make state government the primary financier of housing.

Rural housing markets face different constraints from metropolitan markets, which is precisely why policymakers should be cautious about relying on broad, government-directed housing programs. Research examining rural and suburban development separately found that infrastructure constraints play a much larger role in suburban development, while rural residential development is more likely to rely on private wells and septic systems. The same study found that zoning restrictions on maximum residential density reduced the likelihood of higher-density rural development.

Rather than assuming that rural communities need another state-funded housing program, policymakers should give property owners and entrepreneurs more flexibility to respond to local conditions. Reusing vacant buildings, allowing a wider range of housing types, reducing unnecessary lot-size and density restrictions, and streamlining permitting can make smaller-scale development more feasible without requiring the state to decide which projects or communities deserve taxpayer support. The goal should be to remove barriers where they are actually constraining development while allowing communities to respond to their own housing needs.

The Carolina Forward report correctly notes that infrastructure and housing are connected. New housing cannot be built where roads, water, sewer, and other infrastructure cannot accommodate additional development. But infrastructure policy should support housing growth rather than become another vehicle for government-directed development. The goal should be to alleviate infrastructural problems affecting housing construction, not to use public spending to subsidize particular developments or locations.

Population Shifts

North Carolina is one of the most rapidly growing states in the nation, but that growth isn’t spread out evenly. Urban and suburban centers are seeing significant population growth, while many rural areas are losing residents.

The fast growth of urban areas puts additional demands on local infrastructure and services like roads, schools, and sewage, according to the report, while dwindling or stagnant populations in rural areas face pressure to sustain such amenities with a shrinking tax base.

Despite the contrast in demographic trends, however, the recommendations of the Carolina Forward report remain consistent: centralized direction from the political class as the answer to almost every challenge. Specifically, the report states that “[c]lear-eyed planning is needed to manage booming growth in some regions while revitalizing others.” There’s little to no room for consideration of removing government barriers to make it easier for local communities to determine for themselves — through the actions of individual residents, entrepreneurs, and consumers — the best path forward.

This reflexive call for more centralized control becomes readily evident upon examination of the report’s recommendations:

“Promote Balanced Regional Development”

The report encourages a greater use of government “economic incentives” for rural areas to aid their economic development. Such programs, however, involve taking taxpayer dollars and handing them to politically selected businesses. Governments have a very poor track record with these programs, and more importantly, the process of government bureaucrats picking winners and losers in the economy is patently unfair.

“Strengthen Regional Planning”

Here the report urges more involvement by “metropolitan planning organizations” and “regional councils of government” to coordinate a “statewide framework for regional planning.” This is supposedly to ensure that infrastructure decisions “align with where people are settling.” At best, this recommendation would merely further the kind of infrastructure planning that already exists. At worst, it represents a consolidation of more planning power into centralized planning bureaus to override local actors.

“Enhance Rural Quality of Life”

This recommendation calls for greater government spending by rural communities on amenities that may attract more people to live in rural areas. The report encourages spending on such items as broadband internet, health care facilities, and recreation. While they may sound beneficial, many of them already are, or should be, provided by entrepreneurs operating in a free enterprise environment. Taxpayers shouldn’t be forced to pay for them. Moreover, the report conveniently leaves out any admission that such “investments” raise the burden on taxpayers, leaving them with less money to pay for the amenities and recreation of their own choosing.

“Plan for Aging and Migration Patterns”

Here the report comes closer to hitting the mark. While recognizing the dwindling population in rural areas, it recommends “rightsizing” infrastructure, such as consolidating schools and health care services. These choices should be fairly obvious.

Other helpful recommendations the report offers is “streamlining” processes like professional licensing and also expanding housing supply (which, as discussed above, the report deals with in a separate section). With respect to professional licensing, one way to aid workers is to have state licensing boards recognize licenses from other states, which would make it much easier and quicker for transplants to begin working in North Carolina. Eliminating Certificate of Need laws and expanding nursing scope of practice would also go a long way toward relieving health care shortages in rural areas, but those needed reforms go unmentioned in the Carolina Forward report.

Next in this series is Part 3, which examines the Carolina Forward report’s recommendations for public education and health care.

text:
Roberto Baldwin

With the EU digital battery passport going into effect on February 18, 2027, and the rise in used EVs entering the market, the need to determine the health of electric vehicle batteries after they've been in use for a few years is growing.

To meet the challenge of investigating what lies in used batteries, Qnovo has developed a yet-to-be-named pilot application to determine the health of these packs.

The system is part of Qnovo's Battery Genome, an extensive database of OEM-partner (like Hyundai) batteries. Regardless of type or manufacturer, the database has detailed information about batteries currently powering vehicles across the planet. The system tracks battery behavior, degradation, the mechanisms that cause degradation, and performance. The system also tracks charge and discharge cycles in real-world conditions. The pilot application takes the genome to the next level and leverages that deep knowledge based on the individual data coming from a vehicle.

"Battery passports are a welcome step towards transparency, but without a better understanding of the battery, it opens OEMs to liability," said Nadim Maluf, CEO of Qnovo, in a press release. "Since the Battery Genome runs in the vehicle where the rich data lives, we know with added certainty what the battery is doing and what it is not doing. That gives the OEM more insight over what is out in the field and more confidence in every assessment."

According to Qnovo, in the vehicles with its Battery Genome system deployed, the system has a full electrochemical record. That includes changing behavior, operating history, environmental exposure, and variations at the cell level. The new pilot software identifies signifiers of accelerated aging and any defects that may have happened over the life of the pack. That information produces a view of the battery's health and even includes the residual value of the pack as a data point.

Because the Battery Genome stack is already deployed to partner OEM vehicles, the information is already accessible by Qnovo and the OEMs. The application just takes that information and determines the potential for problems and the battery's current issues.

Qnovo told SAE Media that the application and Battery Genome are "built on OEM-grade vehicle data, meaning high-quality data provided by the vehicle manufacturer for each vehicle, rather than the aftermarket data available through an OBD. Working from OEM data lets the application deliver deeper and more reliable battery intelligence, tailored to each vehicle platform and the real-world conditions it operates in."

While the health of a battery is important to OEMs, regulators, and potential buyers, insurance companies are also interested in this data to help determine the value of a vehicle. Typically, more than half the cost of a new vehicle s the battery pack. That data point doesn't disappear as the vehicle ages. A vehicle with a severely degraded battery pack is worth far less than one that's only lost a few percentage points of pack capacity.

Qnovo's Battery Genome is powered by over 2,000,000 km (1,243,000 miles) of road data and over 200 million deployed vehicles. According to Qnovo, the real-time insights provided by its software is 98.7% accurate in detecting potential safety issues.

text:
We know that people work at the White House: Presidents and press secretaries, c…

NBA Courtside: LeBron James says you can’t count out OKC on making a championshi…



President Donald Trump eliminated the once-popular $7,500 tax credit for electric vehicle buyers in the United States over a year ago, and signs now point to some clear winners and losers of that decision.

That tax credit, which was first adopted during former President George W. Bush's administration in 2008 to help spur EV adoption, was eliminated on Sept. 30, 2025, by a law passed by Republicans in Congress and signed immediately by Trump.

EV sales have plummeted since then, although a spike in gas prices this year has led to a bit of a renaissance for plug-in models in 2026. The elimination of the EV tax credits has had impacts on other parts of the industry too: Carmakers canceled production on several low-selling electric models that they could no longer market with the big discount, and they have also revived some popular gas-guzzlers.

Additionally, as consumers sought fuel efficient models in the wake of average gas prices rising above $4 per gallon, hybrid vehicles saw a big uptick in interest as carmakers who were moving away from EVs pitched those to gas price-conscious consumers.

Carmakers have sold over 12 million new cars so far in 2026, similar to their pace in the first nine months of 2025, according to Cox Automotive. Only about 6% of those new car sales this year have been electric cars, which was down from nearly 10% last year, although used EV sales are up in recent months, according to the group.

With that in mind, the USA TODAY Cars team compiled a list of the top winners and losers of Trump's decision to cut EV tax credits.

Winners include Tesla, foreign automakers

1. Tesla

First half of 2026 EV sales: 242,100

Best-selling EV model this year: Tesla Model Y

Why they're a winner: Tesla had a 10-year headstart as the main U.S. electric car maker, with its shoppers having access to federal tax credits since the discount was first created under former President George W. Bush's administration. Even now, with company CEO Elon Musk taking political positions that riled some of Tesla's supporters, Tesla sells over 50% of the EVs that are on U.S. roads today. But as more of their competitors are coming online with new electric models, the $7,500 discount is gone.

2. Toyota

First half of 2026 EV sales: 21,855

Best-selling EV model this year: Toyota bZ

Why they're a winner: Toyota faced criticism from environmental groups for their decision to keep relying on hybrids instead of full electric vehicles, even when the federal government was pumping out EV tax credits under former Presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden. The end result is the company had a lineup full of hybrids ready to go this year as car shoppers pivoted to those cars as gas prices spiked due to the Iran war. Toyota also successfully pushed back on an effort under the Biden administration to give extra EV tax credits to Detroit carmakers, and the company has announced three new electric models.

3. Hyundai

First half of 2026 EV sales: 26,936

Best-selling EV model this year: Hyundai Ioniq 5

Why they're a winner: Like Toyota, Hyundai also had several hybrids in their lineup that were able to market to fuel-efficiency hungry car shoppers who didn't want to go fully electric. Hyundai also has several fully electric models that they have marketed to people who are open to plug-in models, so they have multiple options in both categories.

4. Kia

First half of 2026 EV sales: 12,627

Best-selling EV model this year: Kia EV9

Why they're a winner: Like its South Korean-sibling brand, Kia also has several hybrids in their lineup that were already on the market. Also, like Hyundai, Kia has several fully electric models that they have marketed to people who are open to plug-in models even without the federal discount.

Losers, including Detroit automakers, Volkswagen

1. General Motors

First half of 2026 EV sales: 56,679

Best-selling EV model this year: Chevrolet Equinox EV

Why they're a loser: GM touts that it is the nation's second-largest EV seller, behind only Tesla. The company's CEO, Mary Barra, said during a recent appearance on Fortune's "Titans" podcast that her company is still committed to a future of developing mostly electric vehicles, although that appears now to be much further off than most of the industry's initial projections were.

"I don't think it's shifted our mission," Barra said in an interview. "We still think EVs are the endgame." GM's EV sales in the first half of 2026 were solid compared to competitors. But, unlike Tesla, which built their dominant EV presence with help from the federal tax credit, GM now faces a future where car shoppers aren't going to be incentivized by the federal government to buy EVs for the foreseeable future. GM sold more than 78,000 EVs in the first half of 2025, when tax credits were still available. But this year with no tax credits, their EV sales fell below 57,000.

2. Ford

First half of 2026 EV sales: 16,606

Best-selling EV model this year: Ford Mustang Mach-E

Why they're a loser:  Ford CEO Jim Farley said in a July 2026 interview with USA TODAY that his company's new $30,000 Fathom electric pickup truck would be its most important car of the future. But the Dearborn automaker also announced plans this year to transition its F-150 Lightning pickup, which was once seen as game changing EV, from a fully electric car to a type of hybrid car known as an Extended Range Electric Vehicle (EREV). So the company now enters the next phase of the EV transition without an electric version of its signature pickup.

3. Volkswagen

First half of 2026 EV sales: 3,768

Best-selling EV model this year: Volkswagen ID.4

Why they're a loser: After years of heavily investing in electric cars, in part because of a decade-old settlement with the federal government over diesel emission cheating, Volkswagen announced earlier this year that was ending production of its U.S.-built ID.4 electric crossover, which was its most popular domestic EV and the only VW model that saw an increase in U.S. sales in 2025. The company has said it plans to introduce a successor electric vehicle for the United States and it introduced a ID.3 Neo that it said it would begin selling this year in "Germany and many European markets." But as more shoppers are considering EV amid rising gas prices, Volkswagen's only domestic electric car now is the ID. Buzz minivan. Even hybrid versions of its most popular SUVs are years away.

Engineers, OEMs, regulatory experts, and first responders each see a different piece of the thermal runaway problem, and this panel puts those perspectives on one stage.”

— John Redman, COO of Americase International

WAXAHACHIE, CO, UNITED STATES, October 12, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- As lithium battery energy density climbs and deployment scales across electric vehicles, stationary storage and industrial applications, meeting a safety standard does not guarantee that a thermal runaway event stays contained. Americase International will address that challenge in a panel at The Battery Show North America on October 14 in Detroit.

The session, “Engineering Containment for the Next Generation of Batteries: Mitigating Thermal Runaway in Transport and Storage,” takes place Wednesday, October 14, at Huntington Place during the show’s October 12–15 run. Americase International Chief Operating Officer John Redman will moderate, joined by Chief Revenue Officer Chris Egloff and Ryan Paquet, president of HazMat Safety Consulting, an Americase International company, along with experts from General Motors, Power-Metric and Energy Security Agency.

The panel will explore what “safe and compliant” actually requires today and how those expectations continue to change as the industry scales.

According to the U.S. Department of Energy, the volumetric energy density of lithium-ion battery packs rose more than eightfold between 2008 and 2020, from 55 to 450 watt-hours per liter. Total capacity is also growing: in 2025, the average battery in a U.S. battery electric car held about 90 kilowatt-hours of energy, according to the International Energy Agency. Researchers report a persistent trade-off between energy density and safety in lithium-ion batteries.

“Compliant is not necessarily contained,” said John Redman, COO of Americase International. “Containment has to keep pace with the chemistry. Engineers, OEMs, regulatory experts, and first responders each see a different piece of the thermal runaway problem, and this panel puts those perspectives on one stage.”

The 45-minute session, part of the show’s Battery Chemistry, Materials & Cell Innovation track and Battery Safety theme, will cover thermal runaway behavior across chemistries and formats, the materials science behind effective transport and storage design, how containment engineering, regulatory compliance and emergency response intersect, and where containment standards and best practices are headed next.

Americase International will also showcase its battery transport and storage solutions at Booth 3508 throughout the four-day event, October 12–15.

Moderator and Panelists

- John Redman (Moderator), COO, Americase International — Redman oversees operations across Americase International's containment, testing, and regulatory compliance businesses, including HazMat Safety Consulting, Americase, and Fulcrum Testing.

- Chris Egloff, Chief Revenue Officer, Americase International — Egloff works with OEMs, logistics providers, and battery manufacturers to address real world battery transport and storage challenges. Egloff is a co-author of Mastering Lithium-Ion Battery Safety.

- Michael Colaianne, Senior Manager of Dangerous Goods Transportation, General Motors — Colaianne leads General Motors' global dangerous goods transportation compliance program across manufacturing and pre-production sites. He is a Certified Dangerous Goods Professional (CDGP) through the Institute of Hazardous Materials Management (IHMM) and a subject-matter expert in multimodal lithium battery transportation.

- Ryan Paquet, President, HazMat Safety Consulting, an Americase International company — A former PHMSA official with more than 20 years of experience in hazardous materials transportation safety, Paquet is also co-author of Mastering Lithium-Ion Battery Safety.

- Jun Shin, Executive Partner, Power-Metric — Shin focuses on the materials science and engineering side of battery safety and performance.

- Dalan Zartman, CEO, Energy Security Agency — Zartman brings hands-on expertise in emergency response, risk mitigation and incident command for battery-related hazards.

text:
KKR is expanding its investment in U.S. solar power through a third transaction with TotalEnergies, adding to a series of renewable energy deals involving European utilities as the Trump administration rolls back federal support for U.S. wind and solar development.

KKR and TotalEnergies inked an agreement to add three utility-scale solar projects in Texas and Ohio to their 50-50 U.S. joint venture, bringing its portfolio to 2.1 gigawatts (GW) from 1.4 GW. The 700-megawatt (MW) addition carries an enterprise value of $1.2 billion. The projects are expected to begin commercial operations by the first quarter of 2027.

TotalEnergies will retain responsibility for operating the assets, whose electricity production has either been contracted to third parties or will be marketed by the French energy company. The transaction is expected to close before year-end, subject to customary conditions.

The expansion follows the model established when the North American partnership was established in September 2025. At that time, TotalEnergies agreed to sell a 50% stake in six utility-scale solar projects and 41 distributed generation assets to insurance vehicles and accounts managed by KKR.

That portfolio, consisting primarily of U.S. assets, was valued at $1.25 billion, with TotalEnergies expecting to receive $950 million at closing through the stake sale and a bank refinancing.

The arrangement allows TotalEnergies to retain an ownership interest and operating control while bringing in institutional capital to fund its renewable energy business. For KKR, it provides exposure to electricity generation assets with contracted revenue or power marketed by TotalEnergies.

“We have long been investors in renewables through our infrastructure platform, having committed more than $23 billion to date in energy transition investments,” Cecilio Velasco, managing director at KKR, said when the partnership was first announced in 2025.

KKR and TotalEnergies extended that relationship to Europe in August 2026, agreeing to a transaction involving a 1.2 GW portfolio of onshore wind and solar projects in Germany, Spain, France and Poland. An insurance account managed by KKR agreed to acquire a 50% stake in the portfolio, which carries an enterprise value of €1.8 billion and is expected to close this year.

As with the U.S. arrangements, TotalEnergies will retain half the equity and continue operating the assets.

U.S. renewables investment amid policy changes

The agreements come during a period of policy changes affecting renewable energy development in the U.S., where the second Trump administration has moved to withdraw federal support for projects and restrict access to tax incentives.

On his first day back in office in January 2025, President Donald Trump signed the Unleashing American Energy executive order, directing federal agencies to pause disbursements under the Inflation Reduction Act and Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act while reviewing programs for consistency with administration policy. Offshore wind development subsequently faced project suspensions and legal challenges.

The administration followed with legislation and executive action in July 2025 curtailing clean electricity production and investment tax credits for wind and solar projects. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act established an accelerated termination schedule for those credits, while a subsequent executive order directed the Treasury Department to enforce the changes and implement restrictions involving foreign entities.

Under the legislation, wind and solar facilities that begin construction after July 4, 2026, generally lose eligibility for the credits if they enter service after Dec. 31, 2027. The administration also tightened the rules governing when construction is considered to have begun.

Several foreign-backed renewable energy manufacturing projects were paused or reconsidered following the policy changes. These included solar manufacturing plans involving Singapore-based Bila Solar in Indiana, Canada-based Heliene in Minnesota and Norway’s NorSun in Oklahoma.

The three solar projects in the KKR-TotalEnergies transaction are scheduled to enter commercial operation before the end of 2027. The companies did not disclose their construction-start dates or eligibility for federal tax credits.

Despite — or because of — the changing policy environment, KKR has been eager to add U.S. renewable energy assets to its portfolio. In June, the firm struck a deal for the U.S. and Canadian operations of EDF power solutions from France’s state-owned EDF Group. The transaction values the equity interest at approximately $4.2 billion, with potential additional payments of up to $390 million.

Under the agreement, KKR will purchase EDF’s North American renewable energy operations, including its project development, construction, operations, maintenance and asset management businesses. The platform owns and operates solar, wind and battery storage assets serving utilities, corporations and institutional investors.

The firm also boosted the capital available for infrastructure investments with the August close of KKR Global Infrastructure Investors V at $19.2 billion, exceeding the $17 billion raised for its predecessor in 2022.

The fund targets core-plus infrastructure investments in North America and Western Europe. As of June 30, KKR reports $119 billion in infrastructure equity assets.

text:
Gevo Inc. on Oct. 1 announced sales of substantially all of the Section 45Z tax credits generated by its ethanol and renewable natural gas (RNG) facilities in 2026, totaling $70 million worth of credits. Gevo has received over $30 million in cash from these credit sales through Sept. 30 and expects the remaining cash to be received over the next six months. The credits were generated through the production and sale of low-carbon transportation fuels and were sold by Gevo pursuant to the credit’s transferability provisions.

On Sept. 30, Gevo sold $50 million worth of credits to a non-financial, publicly traded company. Gevo previously sold $20 million worth of credits to Quill Financial, Inc., the parent company of Quill Bank, a Utah-based community bank providing commercial, agricultural, mortgage and consumer banking services.

"We have successfully sold our expected 2026 45Z tax credit position while broadening participation beyond financial institutions to also include strategic corporate buyers,” said Gevo Chief Executive Officer Paul Bloom. “By efficiently monetizing the value generated through our low-carbon fuel operations, we are increasing cash on the balance sheet, enhancing financial flexibility and creating additional value for shareholders.”

Gevo expects to produce an additional $7 to $10 million worth of Section 45Z tax credits in 2027 due to the anticipated completion of debottlenecking activities at Gevo North Dakota that is expected to increase production capacity and associated carbon capture by 10-15%. The debottlenecking remains on track to be completed by the end of 2026.
